children.title: Generic Convex Program Forms
children.top_down_role: Equivalent high-level containers for finite-dimensional convex optimization models.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Optimization Problem and Inclusion of Linear Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional inequality-form convex programs; this formulation does not address equality constraints or extended-valued functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The problem \(\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} f_0(x)\) subject to \(f_i(x)\le b_i\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), is called a convex optimization problem when each \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), \(i=0,\ldots,m\), is convex, i.e., for every \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\alpha,\beta\ge 0\) with \(\alpha+\beta=1\), \[f_i(\alpha x+\beta y)\le \alpha f_i(x)+\beta f_i(y).\] Every linear function satisfies this relation with equality; consequently, every linear program is a convex optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality-form optimization problem is convex when its objective and all its constraint functions satisfy the convexity inequality for every convex combination of two points. Linear functions satisfy that relation with equality, so every linear program belongs to the class of convex optimization problems.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\forall i\in\{0,\ldots,m\},\ f_i\text{ is convex}\right]\Longrightarrow \text{the stated problem is a convex optimization problem},\qquad \mathrm{LP}\subseteq\{\text{convex optimization problems}\}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity of a generic problem expressed through its objective and nonnegative infeasibility measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A generic problem \(\mathcal P\), equipped with an infeasibility measure satisfying \(X(p)=\{x:\operatorname{Infeas}_{\mathcal P}(p,x)=0\}\), is convex if, for every \(p\in\mathcal P\), both \(p_0:\mathbb R^{n(p)}\to\mathbb R\) and \(x\mapsto\operatorname{Infeas}_{\mathcal P}(p,x)\) are convex. Because the infeasibility measure is nonnegative, \(X(p)=\{x:\operatorname{Infeas}_{\mathcal P}(p,x)\le0\}\), which is convex. Convex inequality programs with \(\operatorname{Infeas}(p,x)=\max\{0,p_1(x),\ldots,p_{m(p)}(x)\}\) satisfy this definition when the objective and constraints are real-valued convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generic problem is convex when every instance has a convex objective and convex nonnegative infeasibility function that vanishes exactly on its feasible set. The feasible set is consequently convex. Convex inequality programs with maximum constraint violation as their infeasibility measure satisfy the definition.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{Infeas}_{\mathcal P}(p,\cdot)\text{ is convex and nonnegative on }\mathbb R^{n(p)}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X(p)=\{x\in\mathbb R^{n(p)}:\operatorname{Infeas}_{\mathcal P}(p,x)\le0\}\text{ is convex for every }p\in\mathcal P

children.title: Functional-Constraint Form
children.top_down_role: Programs organized by convex inequality families and affine equality families.

knowledge_statements.title: Functional-Constraint Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite convex inequalities with affine equalities in a real finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_m:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex functions, let \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^p\) be linear, and let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^p\). The functional-constraint form is
\[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\bigl\{f_0(x): f_i(x)\le 0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ Ax=b\bigr\}.\]
Its feasible set is \(\{x\in\bigcap_{i=0}^m\operatorname{dom}f_i:f_i(x)\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ Ax=b\}\), which is convex. The value is \(+\infty\) when this set is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex program minimizes a convex objective subject to finitely many convex inequalities and affine equalities; their common feasible set is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:f_i(x)\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ Ax=b\}\) is convex on the common effective domain.

notation.meaning: effective domain where the extended-real function is finite

source_refs.locator: 2.2.3 Convex Sets p. 101

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.3 Convex Sets p. 101

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonaffine Equalities Need Not Define Convex Feasible Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp reason that equalities in the generic functional convex form are required to be affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(h(x)=x^2-1\) is convex on \(\mathbb R\), but
\[\{x:h(x)=0\}=\{-1,1\}\]
is not convex. Thus a generic equality involving a nonlinear convex function cannot replace \(Ax=b\) while preserving convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonlinear convex equality can have a nonconvex zero set, so generic equalities must remain affine unless additional structure is established.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonaffine Equalities Need Not Define Convex Feasible Sets

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent single-inequality form for a finite family of scalar convex constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), define \(g(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)\). Then
\[f_i(x)\le0\ \text{for every }i\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad g(x)\le0.\]
If every \(f_i\) is convex, then \(g\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finitely many scalar convex inequalities can be combined exactly into one inequality using their pointwise maximum.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is convex for the convexity conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap_i\{x:f_i(x)\le0\}=\{x:\max_i f_i(x)\le0\}\).

notation.meaning: pointwise maximum of the constraint functions

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation of Finite Scalar Inequalities

children.title: Set-Constrained Form
children.top_down_role: Programs organized by an objective over an explicit convex feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Set-Constrained Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex optimization expressed using one explicit feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex on \(C\). The set-constrained convex program is
\[\inf_{x\in C} f(x).\]
A point \(x^\star\in C\) is optimal exactly when \(f(x^\star)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in C\). Allowing \(C=\varnothing\) under the extended-real convention assigns optimal value \(+\infty\) and yields no minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The set-constrained form minimizes a convex function over an explicitly specified convex set, with optimality defined by comparison against every feasible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\) is a convex optimization problem in set-constrained form.

notation.meaning: an optimal feasible point, when one exists

source_refs.locator: 1.5 Affine Sets and Convex Sets p. 3

source_witnesses.locator: 1.5 Affine Sets and Convex Sets p. 3

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed generic existence theorem; its canonical home is general convex existence theory rather than this representation leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and closed, and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and lower semicontinuous. If some nonempty sublevel set \(\{x\in C:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is compact, then \(\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\) is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact nonempty sublevel set ensures attainment for a proper lower-semicontinuous objective, but this is generic existence theory rather than a defining property of set-constrained representation.
assumptions_latex: Some nonempty sublevel set is compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Attainment in Set-Constrained Form

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the primal optimal value for a continuous convex objective on a bounded closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_1\) be a bounded closed convex set in a finite-dimensional real vector space \(E_1\), and let \(f:Q_1\to\mathbb R\) be continuous and convex, not necessarily differentiable. Define the primal optimal value by \[ f^*=\min_{x\in Q_1}f(x). \]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal set-constrained convex problem minimizes a continuous, possibly nondifferentiable convex function over a bounded closed convex set; its optimal value is denoted by f star.
assumptions_latex: Q_1\subset E_1\text{ is bounded, closed, and convex}
f:Q_1\to\mathbb R\text{ is continuous and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^*:=\min_{x\in Q_1}f(x).

children.title: Domain-Constraint Encoding Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Programs whose domains and set constraints are encoded within convex functions.

children.title: Extended-Value Objective Encoding
children.top_down_role: Objective-domain encoding through extended-valued convex functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Value Objective Encoding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absorption of an explicit convex domain into an extended-real objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex. Define the extended-value function \(\widetilde f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) by
\[\widetilde f(x)=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}\]
Then \(\widetilde f\) is convex, and \(\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\widetilde f(x)\). The two problems have exactly the same minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assigning infinite objective value outside a convex domain converts an explicitly constrained convex problem into an equivalent unconstrained extended-value problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\widetilde f(x)\) and the infimal values agree.

notation.meaning: extension of the objective by positive infinity outside its domain

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Effective Domain and Properness of the Positive-Infinity Extension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effective-domain information retained by extending a restricted objective to the ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\widetilde f\) be the positive-infinity extension of \(f:C\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). Then
\[\operatorname{dom}\widetilde f=\{x\in C:f(x)<+\infty\}.\]
Consequently, \(\widetilde f\) is proper if and only if \(f\) is finite at some point of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive-infinity extension retains exactly the finite-valued part of the restricted domain and is proper exactly when that part is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}\widetilde f=\{x\in C:f(x)<+\infty\}\), and \(\widetilde f\) is proper if and only if this set is nonempty.

notation.meaning: effective domain of the extended objective

knowledge_statements.title: Effective Domain and Properness of the Positive-Infinity Extension

children.title: Indicator-Function Constraint Encoding
children.top_down_role: Set-constraint encoding through convex indicator functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Indicator-Function Constraint Encoding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encoding membership in a convex set by an extended-real indicator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), define its convex-analysis indicator by
\[\delta_C(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}\]
For every extended-real function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\),
\[\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\bigl(f(x)+\delta_C(x)\bigr).\]
The minimizer sets also agree. Moreover, \(\delta_C\) is convex if and only if \(C\) is convex, including the empty-set convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-membership constraint is encoded by adding an indicator that is zero on the set and positive infinity outside it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}(f+\delta_C)(x)\).

notation.meaning: extended-real indicator of the set C

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Properness and Closedness of a Set Indicator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic analytic properties of the indicator used for hard-constraint encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), the indicator \(\delta_C\) is proper if and only if \(C\ne\varnothing\). It is lower semicontinuous, equivalently closed as an extended-real function, if and only if \(C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set indicator is proper exactly for a nonempty set and closed exactly for a closed set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_C\text{ is proper}\iff C\ne\varnothing\), and \(\delta_C\text{ is lower semicontinuous}\iff C\text{ is closed}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Properness and Closedness of a Set Indicator

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Aggregation of Finitely Many Indicator Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of finitely many hard membership constraints to one indicator component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For sets \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb R^n\),
\[\sum_{i=1}^m\delta_{C_i}(x)=\delta_{\cap_{i=1}^m C_i}(x)\quad\text{for every }x.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite sum of set indicators is the indicator of the intersection.
assumptions_latex: The family of sets is finite.
Each indicator takes the values \(0\) and \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_i\delta_{C_i}=\delta_{\cap_iC_i}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation of Finitely Many Indicator Constraints

children.title: Domain–Constraint Encoding Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between explicit domains, set constraints, and function-based encodings.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain–Constraint Encoding Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact equivalence between an explicit domain, positive-infinity extension, and indicator-function encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), and define \(\widetilde f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) by \[\widetilde f(x)=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}\] If \(\bar f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) agrees with \(f\) on \(C\), then \(\widetilde f=\bar f+\delta_C\) pointwise. Consequently, \[\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\widetilde f(x)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\bigl(\bar f(x)+\delta_C(x)\bigr),\] and the three formulations have the same minimizers and the same finite-valued points in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit restriction to a set, extension by positive infinity outside that set, and addition of its indicator give the same objective values on the domain, infimal value, and minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde f=\bar f+\delta_C\), and the explicit-domain and extended-value formulations have equal infimal values and identical argmin sets.

notation.meaning: positive-infinity extension of f outside C
any extended-real function on the ambient space agreeing with f on C

children.title: Composite-Separable Form Family
children.top_down_role: Programs exposing affine compositions, component sums, or separable blocks.

children.title: Affine Composite Convex Forms
children.top_down_role: Convex functions composed with affine mappings.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Composite Convex Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex outer functions composed with affine maps and combined additively.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(h_j:\mathbb{R}^{p_j}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex for \(j=1,\ldots,r\). For linear maps \(A_j:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^{p_j}\) and vectors \(b_j\in\mathbb{R}^{p_j}\), an affine composite convex form is
\[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left(g(x)+\sum_{j=1}^r h_j(A_jx+b_j)\right).\]
The displayed objective is convex on \(\operatorname{dom}g\cap\bigcap_{j=1}^r A_j^{-1}(\operatorname{dom}h_j-b_j)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex outer functions composed with affine maps remain convex, so their sum with another convex term defines a convex program.
assumptions_latex: Each \(A_j\) is linear and each \(b_j\) has compatible dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\mapsto g(x)+\sum_{j=1}^r h_j(A_jx+b_j)\) is convex.

notation.meaning: affine argument supplied to the j-th outer function

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint-domain condition distinguishing a proper affine-composite objective from an identically infinite model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g,h_1,\ldots,h_r\) be proper convex functions and define \(\Psi(x)=g(x)+\sum_{j=1}^r h_j(A_jx+b_j)\). Then \(\Psi\) is proper if and only if
\[\operatorname{dom}g\cap\bigcap_{j=1}^r\{x:A_jx+b_j\in\operatorname{dom}h_j\}\neq\varnothing.\]
If this intersection is empty, \(\Psi\equiv+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine-composite sum is a proper objective exactly when its component domains have a common compatible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Psi\text{ is proper}\iff\operatorname{dom}\Psi\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: effective domain of the affine-composite objective

knowledge_statements.title: Properness of the Affine-Composite Objective

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed general convex-calculus theorem rather than a defining representation fact for this terminal form leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\Psi(x)=g(x)+\sum_{j=1}^r h_j(A_jx+b_j)\). Under a common relative-interior domain qualification, \(\partial\Psi(x)=\partial g(x)+\sum_jA_j^*\partial h_j(A_jx+b_j)\), yielding a zero-subgradient optimality condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A qualified affine chain and sum rule gives an adjoint-pulled subdifferential formula.
assumptions_latex: The component functions are proper convex
A common relative-interior domain qualification holds
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial\Psi(x)=\partial g(x)+\sum_jA_j^*\partial h_j(A_jx+b_j)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Composite Subdifferential and Optimality Rule

children.title: Component-Sum Convex Forms
children.top_down_role: Objectives or constraints assembled from multiple convex components.

knowledge_statements.title: Component-Sum Convex Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite additive decomposition of a convex objective into component functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and suppose their domains have a common point. The component-sum form is
\[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} F(x),\qquad F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x).\]
The function \(F\) is convex with \(\operatorname{dom}F=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}f_i\). Constraints may be included as indicator components without changing this form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A component-sum program minimizes a finite sum of convex functions sharing the same decision variable; indicators may represent constraints among the components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\) is convex and \(\operatorname{dom}F=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}f_i\).

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epigraph Splitting of a Component Sum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lifted epigraph form for a finite shared-variable component sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\),
\[\inf_x\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x)=\inf_{x,t_1,\ldots,t_m}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m t_i:(x,t_i)\in\operatorname{epi}f_i\ \text{for all }i\right\}.\]
If the lifted problem has an optimizer, its \(x\)-component minimizes the component sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite component sum can be represented by one epigraph variable per component and a linear aggregate objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_x\sum_i f_i(x)=\inf\{\sum_i t_i:(x,t_i)\in\operatorname{epi}f_i\ \forall i\}\).

notation.meaning: upper bound on the i-th component value

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Splitting of a Component Sum

children.title: Block-Separable Convex Forms
children.top_down_role: Program structures partitioned across variable or constraint blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Separable Convex Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive convex objectives whose components depend on disjoint variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X_i\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces and let \(f_i:X_i\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). With \(X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_m\) and \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\), the block-separable form is
\[\inf_{x\in X}\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i).\]
Its objective is convex on \(X\), and in the absence of coupling constraints its infimal value equals \(\sum_{i=1}^m\inf_{x_i\in X_i}f_i(x_i)\), under the usual extended-real convention excluding undefined sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block-separable program sums convex terms depending on disjoint variable blocks; without coupling, the blocks can be minimized independently.
assumptions_latex: Each \(X_i\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
Each \(f_i:X_i\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is convex and never equals \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in X}\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i)=\sum_{i=1}^m\inf_{x_i\in X_i}f_i(x_i)\) when the right side is well-defined.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Nonsmooth Models of the Objective Function p. 225

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Product Structure of the Minimizer Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment structure for an uncoupled block-separable objective with finite attained block minima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i)\). If every \(f_i:X_i\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper and attains a finite minimum, then
\[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\prod_iX_i}F(x)=\prod_{i=1}^m\operatorname*{argmin}_{x_i\in X_i}f_i(x_i).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every block has a finite attained minimum, the global minimizers are exactly the Cartesian products of block minimizers.
assumptions_latex: Each \(X_i\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
Each \(f_i\) is proper and attains a finite minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}F=\prod_i\operatorname*{argmin}f_i\).
knowledge_statements.title: Product Structure of the Minimizer Set

children.title: Coupling Across Separable Blocks
children.top_down_role: Residual interactions that connect otherwise separable program components.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Single Affine Equation Can Destroy Blockwise Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal counterexample to independent minimization under cross-block coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[\min_{x_1,x_2\in\mathbb R}(x_1-1)^2+(x_2-1)^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_1+x_2=0.\]
The uncoupled block objectives are uniquely minimized at \(1\), but \((1,1)\) is infeasible, and the coupled problem has the unique minimizer \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One shared affine equation can make independently optimal block choices infeasible and change the optimizer in every block.
knowledge_statements.title: A Single Affine Equation Can Destroy Blockwise Optimality
Coupling Across Separable Blocks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-separable objectives combined with shared affine or conic constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f_i:X_i\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex, let \(A_i:X_i\to Y\) be linear, and let \(b\in Y\). A linearly coupled block-separable program has the form
\[\inf_{x_i\in X_i}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i):\sum_{i=1}^m A_ix_i=b\right\}.\]
The feasible set and objective remain convex, but feasibility no longer factors into independent conditions on individual blocks. More generally, replacing equality by membership of \(b-\sum_iA_ix_i\) in a convex cone preserves convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shared affine or conic constraints couple otherwise separable blocks, preserving convexity while preventing independent blockwise feasibility and minimization.
assumptions_latex: Each \(A_i\) is linear, with a common codomain \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupled feasible set is convex, although it generally is not a Cartesian product of blockwise feasible sets.

notation.meaning: linear contribution of block i to the coupling constraint

children.title: Generalized-Inequality Form
children.top_down_role: Programs whose constraint order is induced by a convex cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cone Orders Need Pointedness for Antisymmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-theoretic boundary distinct from convexity of generalized-inequality feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Y\) be a real vector space and \(K\subseteq Y\) a convex cone. The relation \(u\preceq_Kv\iff v-u\in K\) is reflexive and transitive, and it is antisymmetric if and only if
\[K\cap(-K)=\{0\}.\]
A nonpointed cone therefore induces a preorder rather than a partial order, although it can still define convex generalized inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone-induced comparison is a partial order exactly when the cone is pointed; otherwise it is only a preorder.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\preceq_K\text{ is antisymmetric}\iff K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Cone Orders Need Pointedness for Antisymmetry

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Componentwise Inequalities as an Orthant Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar specialization of generalized inequalities under the nonnegative-orthant order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=(f_1,\ldots,f_m):D\to\mathbb R^m\) and \(K=\mathbb R_+^m\). With \(u\preceq_Kv\) defined by \(v-u\in K\),
\[F(x)\preceq_K0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f_i(x)\le0\ \text{for every }i.\]
Moreover, \(F\) is \(K\)-convex if and only if every component \(f_i\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonnegative-orthant order makes one generalized inequality exactly equivalent to finitely many scalar convex inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)\preceq_{\mathbb R_+^m}0\iff f_i(x)\le0\ \forall i\), and orthant-convexity is componentwise convexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Inequalities as an Orthant Inequality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar characterization of a generalized convex inequality in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Y\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let \(K\subseteq Y\) be a closed convex cone, and let \(F:D\to Y\) on a convex set \(D\). Then \(F\) is \(K\)-convex,
\[F(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\preceq_K\theta F(x)+(1-\theta)F(y),\]
if and only if \(x\mapsto\langle z,F(x)\rangle\) is convex for every \(z\in K^*=\{z:\langle z,k\rangle\geq0\ \forall k\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex ordering cone in finite dimensions, cone convexity is equivalent to convexity of every scalarization by a dual-cone vector.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space
\(K\subseteq Y\) is a closed convex cone
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is }K\text{-convex}\iff\langle z,F(\cdot)\rangle\text{ is convex for every }z\in K^*\).
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Cone Scalarization of Cone Convexity
Generalized-Inequality Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex constraints ordered by a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq Y\) be a convex cone and define \(u\preceq_K v\) by \(v-u\in K\). Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex, let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex, and let \(F:D\to Y\) be \(K\)-convex, meaning
\[F(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\preceq_K\theta F(x)+(1-\theta)F(y)\]
for \(x,y\in D\) and \(0\le\theta\le1\). Then
\[\inf_{x\in D}\{f(x):F(x)\preceq_K0\}\]
is a convex program because its feasible set is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized convex inequality orders vector-valued constraint values by a convex cone; cone-convexity of the constraint map makes the feasible set convex.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is convex, \(f\) is convex, and \(F\) is \(K\)-convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in D:F(x)\preceq_K0\}\) is convex.

notation.meaning: cone order defined by v minus u belonging to K

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cone-Ordered Convex Mappings and Convex Generalized-Inequality Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines vector-valued convexity relative to a cone order and the resulting convexity classification for a cone-constrained problem with a convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq Y\) be a closed convex cone and define \(a\succeq_Q b\) by \(a-b\in Q\). A mapping \(G:\mathbb R^n\to Y\) is convex with respect to \(Q\) if, for every \(x_1,x_2\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), \[tG(x_1)+(1-t)G(x_2)\succeq_Q G(tx_1+(1-t)x_2).\] For a convex domain \(C\), the problem \(\min_{x\in C}f(x)\) subject to \(G(x)\in K\) is convex when \(f\) is convex and \(G\) is convex with respect to \(Q=-K\). Every affine mapping is convex with respect to every cone order; hence linear cone problems are convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector-valued mapping is cone-convex when its value at a convex combination lies below the corresponding combination of its values in the cone-induced order. On a convex domain, a cone-constrained problem is convex when the objective is convex and the constraint mapping is convex in the order induced by the negative constraint cone. Affine mappings always satisfy this condition.
assumptions_latex: Q\subseteq Y\text{ is a closed convex cone}
C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is convex for the optimization-problem classification}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G(tx_1+(1-t)x_2)\preceq_Q tG(x_1)+(1-t)G(x_2);\qquad f\text{ convex and }G\text{ }(-K)\text{-convex yield a convex generalized-inequality problem on }C.

knowledge_statements.title: Intersection-of-Convex-Sets Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex feasibility represented as membership in an indexed intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a real vector space, let \(I\) be an arbitrary index set, and let \(C_i\subseteq X\) be convex for every \(i\in I\). The intersection-of-convex-sets feasibility problem is to find
\[x\in C:=\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i.\]
The system is feasible exactly when \(C\ne\varnothing\), and every feasible point belongs to every \(C_i\). The set \(C\) is convex, including when \(I\) is infinite; under the standard convention, the intersection over an empty index set is \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The problem seeks a point common to an indexed family of convex sets; the common feasible region is itself convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\) is convex, and the system is feasible if and only if \(C\ne\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological property of intersection feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a topological vector space and let every \(C_i\subseteq X\) be closed and convex. Then \[\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\] is closed and convex for an arbitrary index set \(I\). The closedness hypotheses cannot be omitted in general: an intersection of convex sets need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arbitrary intersection of closed convex sets is closed and convex; convexity alone does not ensure closedness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\text{ is closed and convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Closedness of the Common Intersection

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional finite-family characterization of empty convex intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_p\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, with \(p\geq n+1\). Then \[\bigcap_{i=1}^pC_i\neq\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\bigcap_{i\in J}C_i\neq\varnothing\ \text{for every }J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}\text{ with }|J|=n+1.\] Equivalently, if the full intersection is empty, a subfamily of at most \(n+1\) sets already has empty intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite family of convex sets in n-dimensional space, emptiness is witnessed by at most n plus one members.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigcap_{i=1}^pC_i=\varnothing\Rightarrow\exists J,\ |J|\leq n+1,\ \bigcap_{i\in J}C_i=\varnothing.

notation.meaning: index set of a witnessing subfamily

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Inequality-System Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite or indexed scalar convex inequalities defining a feasibility problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex, let \(I\) be an arbitrary index set, and let \(f_i:D\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex for every \(i\in I\). The convex inequality-system feasibility problem is to find
\[x\in D\quad\text{such that}\quad f_i(x)\le0\ \text{for every }i\in I.\]
Its feasible set is \(F=D\cap\bigcap_{i\in I}\{x\in D:f_i(x)\le0\}\). Each zero sublevel set is convex, hence \(F\) is convex; the system is feasible exactly when \(F\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex inequality feasibility system seeks a point satisfying every member of a finite or indexed family of convex inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=D\cap\bigcap_{i\in I}\{x:f_i(x)\le0\}\) is convex, and feasibility is equivalent to \(F\ne\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: finite or infinite inequality index set
feasible set of the inequality system

source_refs.locator: 2.2.3 Convex Sets p. 101

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.3 Convex Sets p. 101

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-function representation of a nonempty indexed convex inequality family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty index set \(I\), define \(g(x)=\sup_{i\in I}f_i(x)\). Then \(g\) is convex and \[\{x\in D:f_i(x)\leq0\ \forall i\in I\}=\{x\in D:g(x)\leq0\}.\] Writing \(\alpha=\inf_{x\in D}g(x)\), \(\alpha<0\) implies feasibility and \(\alpha>0\) implies infeasibility. When \(\alpha=0\), feasibility holds exactly when some \(x\in D\) satisfies \(g(x)=0\); an unattained zero infimum is not sufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indexed convex inequality family is one convex supremum inequality. A zero infimum proves feasibility only when the zero level is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F=\{x\in D:g(x)\leq0\},\qquad g=\sup_{i\in I}f_i\text{ is convex}.

notation.meaning: infimum of the supremal constraint function

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-System Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional feasibility for a system of affine equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\). The affine-system feasibility problem is to find \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \[Ax=b.\] Its feasible set is \(F=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b\}\). Thus the system is feasible exactly when \(b\in\operatorname{range}(A)\), and, whenever \(x_0\in F\), one has \(F=x_0+\ker(A)\). If \(b\notin\operatorname{range}(A)\), then \(F=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine system is feasible when its right-hand side lies in the linear map’s range; its nonempty solution set is a translate of the nullspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\neq\varnothing\iff b\in\operatorname{range}(A)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pseudoinverse Feasibility Test and Minimum-Norm Solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear-algebraic solution rule for a finite affine system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A^\dagger\) be the Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse and set \(x_\dagger=A^\dagger b\) and \(r=b-AA^\dagger b\). Then \[Ax=b\text{ is feasible}\iff r=0.\] When feasible, \(x_\dagger\) is the unique solution of minimum Euclidean norm, and every solution is \(x_\dagger+z\) with \(z\in\ker(A)\). When infeasible, \(\|r\|_2=\min_x\|Ax-b\|_2>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pseudoinverse projection tests feasibility, returns the minimum-norm solution when one exists, and otherwise returns the least-squares residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax=b\text{ is feasible}\iff b-AA^\dagger b=0\)

notation.meaning: Orthogonal residual after projecting the right-hand side onto the range of A.

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudoinverse Feasibility Test and Minimum-Norm Solution

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional left-nullspace certificate for inconsistent linear equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), exactly one holds: \(\exists x:Ax=b\), or \(\exists y:A^{\mathsf T}y=0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine system is inconsistent exactly when a left-nullspace vector pairs nontrivially with its right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax=b\text{ is feasible}\iff b\perp\ker(A^{\mathsf T})\)

knowledge_statements.title: Conic-System Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional feasibility in standard equality-form conic representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\). The conic-system feasibility problem is to find \(x\) such that \[Ax=b,\qquad x\in K.\] Its feasible set is \(F=K\cap\{x:Ax=b\}\), which is convex and closed. The system is feasible exactly when \(b\in A(K)=\{Ax:x\in K\}\); the image \(A(K)\), however, need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic system asks whether an affine fiber intersects a closed convex cone, equivalently whether the right-hand side belongs to the cone’s linear image.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\neq\varnothing\iff b\in A(K)\).

children.title: Affine–Conic Intersection Systems

knowledge_statements.title: Affine–Conic Intersection Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intersection form linking affine-equation and conic feasibility descriptions, including inconsistent affine equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a closed convex cone, let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and define the affine equation set \(L=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b\}\), which may be empty. The associated affine–conic intersection system has feasible set \[F=L\cap K=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}.\] Thus it is feasible exactly when \(L\cap K\neq\varnothing\). If \(L\neq\varnothing\), then for every \(x_0\in L\), \(L=x_0+\ker(A)\). Conversely, every equality-form conic system \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), has this intersection representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An equality-form conic system is the intersection of a closed convex cone with the possibly empty solution set of affine equations, and it is feasible exactly when that intersection is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=L\cap K=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\), and \(F\neq\varnothing\iff L\cap K\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: possibly empty solution set of the affine equations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural geometry of a nonempty affine slice of a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\), where \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a closed convex cone. Then \(F\) is closed and convex. If \(F\ne\varnothing\), then \[\operatorname{rec}(F)=K\cap\ker(A).\] Consequently, \(F\) is bounded if and only if \(K\cap\ker(A)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine slice of a closed convex cone is closed and convex; its recession directions are precisely the cone directions annihilated by the affine map.

\(F\ne\varnothing\) for the recession and boundedness conclusions

children.title: Affine–Conic Consistency Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Geometric boundaries separating consistent, weakly inconsistent, and strongly inconsistent systems.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies regimes in which the weakly infeasible boundary is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), weak infeasibility is impossible whenever \(A(K)\) is closed, since then \(\overline{A(K)}\setminus A(K)=\varnothing\). In particular, if \(K\) is polyhedral, then \(A(K)\) is polyhedral and closed, so every infeasible right-hand side has positive distance from \(A(K)\) and is strongly infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed conic images have no weakly infeasible right-hand sides; linear images of polyhedral cones are closed.
assumptions_latex: For the special case, \(K\) is polyhedral
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A(K)\text{ closed}\Longrightarrow\overline{A(K)}\setminus A(K)=\varnothing\)
knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Image Exclusion of Weak Infeasibility
Affine–Conic Consistency Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between strong infeasibility and unattained, zero-distance inconsistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a closed convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), linear map \(A\), and right-hand side \(b\), consider \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\). It is feasible when \(b\in A(K)\), strongly infeasible when \(b\notin\overline{A(K)}\), and weakly infeasible when \[b\in\overline{A(K)}\setminus A(K).\] In the weakly infeasible case, no feasible point exists although \(\inf_{x\in K}\|Ax-b\|=0\). Thus weak infeasibility can occur only at a nonclosed boundary of the conic image; it is excluded when \(A(K)\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak infeasibility occurs when the right-hand side is outside a conic image but lies in its closure, giving zero residual without a feasible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b\in\overline{A(K)}\setminus A(K)\implies \inf_{x\in K}\|Ax-b\|=0\) while the system is infeasible.

notation.meaning: any norm on the finite-dimensional codomain

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum-Violation Epigraph Form of Phase I
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elimination of the common violation variable in the canonical inequality and affine-residual Phase-I model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a specified norm \(\|\cdot\|\),
\[\inf_{x\in X,t\geq0}\{t:f_i(x)\leq t,\ \|Ax-b\|\leq t\}
=\inf_{x\in X}\max\{0,f_1(x),\ldots,f_p(x),\|Ax-b\|\}.\]
Omitting the residual term gives the inequality-only specialization; omitting the \(f_i\) terms gives the affine-equality residual specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common-bound Phase-I problem is the epigraph of the maximum violation, with inequality-only and equality-residual special cases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_I=\inf_{x\in X}\max\{0,\max_i f_i(x),\|Ax-b\|\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Violation Epigraph Form of Phase I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compact-Continuous Attainment of Common-Bound Phase I
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient condition under which the canonical maximum-violation Phase-I infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and compact, let each \(f_i:X\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, and let \(x\mapsto\|Ax-b\|\) be continuous. Then
\[\phi(x)=\max\{0,f_1(x),\ldots,f_p(x),\|Ax-b\|\}\]
attains its minimum on \(X\). Hence the associated common-bound Phase-I model attains its optimal value, and that value is zero exactly when the original inequality and equality system is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compactness and continuity guarantee attainment of the common-bound Phase-I model and make zero optimal value equivalent to feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in X}\phi(x)=0\iff\exists x\in X:\ f_i(x)\leq0\ \forall i,\ Ax=b\).
knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Continuous Attainment of Common-Bound Phase I
Phase-I Feasibility Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common scalar-violation Phase-I model for convex inequalities and affine equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex, let \(f_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex for \(i=1,\ldots,p\), and consider \(f_i(x)\leq0\) and \(Ax=b\). A Phase-I model is \[\min_{x\in X,\ t\geq0} t\quad\text{subject to}\quad f_i(x)\leq t\ \text{for all }i,\qquad \|Ax-b\|\leq t.\] Every original feasible point gives a Phase-I point with \(t=0\), and any attained Phase-I solution with \(t=0\) is feasible for the original system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Phase I minimizes a common nonnegative violation bound; an attained zero value is equivalent to feasibility of the original convex constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The original system is feasible if and only if the Phase-I model attains value \(0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Phase-I formulation and attainment qualification are precise, but no inspectable authoritative source is supplied.

children.title: Elastic Feasibility Models
children.top_down_role: Relaxed models that quantify constraint violations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero Elastic Weights Destroy Feasibility Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure of the zero-value test when a constraint has no penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{0\}\), let the sole constraint be \(f_1(0)=1\leq0\), and set \(w_1=0\). The original system is infeasible, while the elastic model has optimal value \(0\), attained for every \(s_1\geq1\). Thus strict positivity of every weight is necessary for zero elastic cost to force every violation to vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infeasible unpenalized constraint can coexist with attained zero elastic cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_{\rm el}=0\) although \(\{x\in X:f_1(x)\leq0\}=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Zero Elastic Weights Destroy Feasibility Detection

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unattained Zero Elastic Infimum Is Inconclusive
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment boundary for feasibility inference from elastic cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite \(p\) and \(w_i>0\), if \(\inf_{x\in X}\sum_iw_i[f_i(x)]_+=0\), then there is a sequence \(x_k\in X\) with \([f_i(x_k)]_+\to0\) for every \(i\). This does not imply existence of a feasible point unless zero cost is attained or another hypothesis permits passage to a feasible limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero but unattained elastic infimum gives asymptotically vanishing violations, not necessarily a feasible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x_k:\ [f_i(x_k)]_+\to0\ \forall i\), while feasibility need not follow.
knowledge_statements.title: Unattained Zero Elastic Infimum Is Inconclusive

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent violation objective obtained by minimizing the elastic variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed \(x\in X\), the minimum of \(\sum_{i=1}^p w_i s_i\) subject to \(s_i\geq0\) and \(s_i\geq f_i(x)\) is attained at \(s_i=[f_i(x)]_+\). Consequently,
\[\inf_{x,s}\left\{\sum_iw_is_i:s_i\geq0,\ f_i(x)\leq s_i\right\}=\inf_{x\in X}\sum_iw_i[f_i(x)]_+.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating the elastic slacks gives the weighted sum of positive constraint violations.
assumptions_latex: The elastic constraints are \(s_i\geq0\) and \(f_i(x)\leq s_i\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_{\rm el}=\inf_{x\in X}\sum_iw_i[f_i(x)]_+\).
knowledge_statements.title: Elimination of Elastic Slacks

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compact-Continuous Attainment of an Elastic Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient condition eliminating unattained-zero ambiguity for finitely many elastic inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and compact, let \(f_1,\ldots,f_p:X\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, and let \(w_i>0\). Then \(x\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^p w_i[f_i(x)]_+\) attains its minimum on \(X\). Consequently, its optimal value is zero if and only if some \(x\in X\) satisfies \(f_i(x)\leq0\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a nonempty compact domain with continuous constraints, the weighted elastic violation objective attains its minimum, so zero value exactly characterizes feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in X}\sum_iw_i[f_i(x)]_+=0\iff\exists x\in X:\ f_i(x)\leq0\ \forall i\).
knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Continuous Attainment of an Elastic Model
Elastic Feasibility Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted slack formulation measuring separable convex-constraint violations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For convex constraints \(f_i(x)\leq0\) on a convex set \(X\), an elastic feasibility model introduces slacks \(s_i\geq0\) and solves \[\min_{x\in X,\ s\in\mathbb{R}_+^p}\ \sum_{i=1}^p w_i s_i\quad\text{subject to}\quad f_i(x)\leq s_i\ \text{for all }i,\] where \(w_i>0\). Its optimal value is nonnegative. If an optimum exists, that value equals \(0\) exactly when the original inequalities are feasible, and every zero-valued optimizer has \(s=0\) and a feasible \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An elastic model minimizes weighted nonnegative slacks. With positive weights and attainment, zero optimal cost exactly characterizes feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under attainment, \(v^*=0\iff\{x\in X:f_i(x)\leq0\ \text{for all }i\}\neq\varnothing\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-weight elastic-slack characterization is mathematically correct under attainment, but the record has no source or locator.

children.title: Feasibility Margin Models
children.top_down_role: Auxiliary models organized around distance or margin from feasibility.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp attainment qualification for interpreting a zero uniform feasibility margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[\rho^*=\sup_{x\in X}\min_i[-f_i(x)]= -\inf_{x\in X}\max_i f_i(x).\]
Then \(\rho^*>0\) yields a strictly feasible point and \(\rho^*<0\) implies infeasibility. If \(\rho^*=0\), feasibility follows when the supremum is attained, but without attainment the system may be infeasible with margins approaching zero. For example, \(X=\mathbb R\) and \(f_1(x)=e^x\) give \(\rho^*=0\) with no feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero supremal margin implies feasibility only when attained; exp(x) at most zero is a sharp counterexample.
assumptions_latex: \(\rho^*\) is the supremal uniform signed slack
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho^*=0\) without attainment does not imply feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonattained Supremal Margin Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Feasibility Margins Depend on Constraint Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation dependence of an unnormalized uniform signed margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constraints \(f_i(x)\leq0\), replacing each constraint by \(\alpha_i f_i(x)\leq0\), where \(\alpha_i>0\), preserves the feasible set but can change \(\rho^*=\sup_x\min_i[-f_i(x)]\). For example, on \(X=\{0\}\), the equivalent systems \(-1\leq0\) and \(-\alpha\leq0\) have margins \(1\) and \(\alpha\), respectively. Thus feasibility-relevant sign classifications are preserved by positive rescaling, but margin magnitude is not representation invariant without normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive constraint rescaling preserves feasibility and the sign classification but can change the magnitude of an unnormalized uniform margin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{f_i\leq0\}=\{\alpha_i f_i\leq0\}\), but the corresponding optimal uniform margins need not be equal.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Feasibility Margins Depend on Constraint Scaling
Feasibility Margin Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Max–min signed margin model for a finite family of convex inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and compact, and let each \(f_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous and convex. Define the feasibility margin by \[\rho^*=\max_{x\in X,\ \rho\in\mathbb{R}}\ \rho\quad\text{subject to}\quad f_i(x)+\rho\leq0\ \text{for all }i.\] Equivalently, \(\rho^*=\max_{x\in X}\min_i[-f_i(x)]\). A positive margin gives a point satisfying every inequality strictly by at least \(\rho^*\); a negative margin certifies infeasibility; and a zero margin is the feasibility boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The largest uniform signed slack is positive for strict feasibility, negative for infeasibility, and zero at the boundary, assuming compactness and continuity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho^*>0\) implies strict feasibility, \(\rho^*<0\) implies infeasibility, and \(\rho^*=0\) marks the attained boundary case.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compactness and continuity hypotheses make the signed-margin classification precise, but no authoritative source with an inspectable locator is provided.

children.title: Phase-I Status Interpretation
children.top_down_role: Interpretation of auxiliary-model outcomes as evidence about the original system.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unattained Zero Phase-I Value Does Not Prove Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp counterexample to interpreting a zero Phase-I infimum without attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the infeasible convex inequality \(e^x\leq0\) on \(\mathbb R\) and its Phase-I model \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb R,\ t\geq0}\{t:e^x\leq t\}.\] The Phase-I infimum is \(0\), because \(e^x\to0\) as \(x\to-\infty\), but no feasible pair has \(t=0\). Hence the original system is infeasible although its Phase-I value is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infeasible inequality exp(x) at most zero has violations tending to zero, so its Phase-I infimum is zero but unattained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v_I=0\text{ is unattained while the original system is infeasible}.
knowledge_statements.title: Unattained Zero Phase-I Value Does Not Prove Feasibility

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Small Phase-I Residual Is Only Approximate Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between exact status and tolerance-qualified residual evidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi(x)\geq0\) be a Phase-I violation function whose zero-level set is the original feasible set. A point satisfying \(\phi(x)\leq\varepsilon\) for \(\varepsilon>0\) is only an \(\varepsilon\)-feasibility witness. Unless additional error bounds or rigorous objective bounds are available, neither \(\phi(x)\leq\varepsilon\) nor a numerically reported near-zero objective proves exact feasibility, and a positive incumbent value alone does not prove infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small computed Phase-I violation provides approximate feasibility evidence, not an exact status, unless supplemented by rigorous bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi(x)\leq\varepsilon\not\Rightarrow\phi(x)=0\), and a positive incumbent alone does not imply \(\inf\phi>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Small Phase-I Residual Is Only Approximate Feasibility
Phase-I Status Interpretation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Status interpretation for exact and unattained scalar-violation Phase-I models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v_I\) be the infimum of a nonnegative Phase-I violation model whose zero-level feasible points are exactly the original feasible points. If the original system is feasible, then \(v_I=0\) and zero is attained. If \(v_I>0\), the original system is infeasible. If \(v_I=0\) and the Phase-I infimum is attained, the original system is feasible. Without attainment, \(v_I=0\) alone is inconclusive: an infeasible system may admit a sequence whose violations converge to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive Phase-I value certifies infeasibility; attained zero certifies feasibility. An unattained zero infimum may represent only asymptotic feasibility.
assumptions_latex: Its zero-level feasible points coincide with the original feasible set
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_I>0\Rightarrow\) infeasibility, while attained \(v_I=0\Rightarrow\) feasibility; unattained \(v_I=0\) is inconclusive.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between positive value, attained zero, and unattained zero is correctly stated, but the record lacks cited evidence.

children.title: Lift-Projection Feasibility Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Feasibility represented in an extended space and transferred by projection.

children.title: Lifted Feasibility Representations
children.top_down_role: Feasibility systems expressed using auxiliary variables in an extended space.

knowledge_statements.title: Lifted Feasibility Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential conic lift of a convex feasibility set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). A lifted conic feasibility representation of \(S\) consists of an auxiliary dimension \(q\), a closed convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^r\), linear maps \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^r\) and \(B:\mathbb{R}^q\to\mathbb{R}^r\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^r\) such that \[S=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^q,\ Ax+By+c\in K\}.\] The associated lifted feasible set is \(Q=\{(x,y):Ax+By+c\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted representation describes membership in a set by the existence of auxiliary variables satisfying one affine conic constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\{x:\exists y,\ (x,y)\in Q\}\).

source_refs.locator: 3.5.2 Conic quadratic representations p. 132

source_witnesses.locator: 3.5.2 Conic quadratic representations p. 132

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity of a Conic Lift and Its Represented Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic geometry of an existential affine-conic lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^r\), linear maps \(A,B\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^r\), let \[Q=\{(x,y):Ax+By+c\in K\},\qquad S=\{x:\exists y,\ (x,y)\in Q\}.\] Then \(Q\) and \(S\) are convex. If \(K\) is closed, then \(Q\) is closed; closedness of \(S\) does not follow from these assumptions alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine-conic lift and its represented projection are convex. A closed representing cone makes the lifted set closed, but does not ensure a closed projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q\text{ and }S\text{ are convex};\qquad K\text{ closed}\Rightarrow Q\text{ closed}.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity of a Conic Lift and Its Represented Set

children.title: Projected Feasibility Sets
children.top_down_role: Feasible sets obtained as projections of higher-dimensional systems.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Principal finite-dimensional classes whose geometry is preserved by coordinate projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P:\mathbb R^{n+q}\to\mathbb R^n\) be linear. If \(Q\) is compact, then \(P(Q)\) is compact. If \(Q\) is a polyhedron, then \(P(Q)\) is a polyhedron. Thus both images are closed, and the compact image is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-dimensional linear projection preserves compactness and polyhedrality, and therefore closedness in these two regimes.
assumptions_latex: Either \(Q\) is compact or \(Q\) is a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q\text{ compact}\Rightarrow P(Q)\text{ compact};\qquad Q\text{ polyhedral}\Rightarrow P(Q)\text{ polyhedral}.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact and Polyhedral Projection Preservation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fiber representation of a projected feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+q}\), define \(Q_x=\{y\in\mathbb R^q:(x,y)\in Q\}\). Then \[\operatorname{proj}_xQ=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Q_x\ne\varnothing\}.\] Projection retains only the index set of nonempty fibers; lifted sets with the same such index set have the same projection even when their fibers differ in dimension, boundedness, or topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is projected feasible exactly when its auxiliary fiber is nonempty, and projection forgets the remaining fiber geometry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_xQ=\{x:Q_x\ne\varnothing\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Projected Fibers and Witness Sets
Projected Feasibility Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate projection of a finite-dimensional lifted feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a set \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+q}\), its projection onto the original variables is \[\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^q,\ (x,y)\in Q\}.\] A set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a projected feasibility set of \(Q\) when \(S=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\). If \(Q\) is convex, then \(S\) is convex. Even in finite dimensions, closedness of \(Q\) does not by itself imply closedness of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projected feasible set contains precisely the original-variable values admitting a feasible lift. Convexity is preserved, but closedness need not be.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\{x:\exists y,\ (x,y)\in Q\}\).

source_refs.locator: 1.1. Convex Sets and Functions p. 2

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1. Convex Sets and Functions p. 2

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection definition and convexity statement are standard, but the cited introductory locator has not been confirmed to support the additional nonclosed-projection claim.

children.title: Lift–Projection Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Preservation of feasibility information across lifting and projection.

knowledge_statements.title: Lift–Projection Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact equivalence between existential lifted feasibility and projected-set membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^r\) and \(B:\mathbb{R}^q\to\mathbb{R}^r\) be linear maps, let \(c\in\mathbb{R}^r\), let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^r\) be a convex cone, and define \(Q=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+q}:Ax+By+c\in K\}\) and \(S=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\). Then, for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[x\in S\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists y\in\mathbb{R}^q\ \text{such that}\ Ax+By+c\in K.\] Consequently, \(S\neq\varnothing\) if and only if \(Q\neq\varnothing\). Every feasible lifted pair projects to a point of \(S\), and every point of \(S\) has at least one feasible lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Membership in the projected set is equivalent to the existence of a feasible auxiliary-variable lift, so the projected and lifted systems are feasible simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(x\in S\iff\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^q\text{ with }(x,y)\in Q\), and \(S\neq\varnothing\iff Q\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: projection of the lifted feasible set onto the original variables

children.title: Nonclosed Projection Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Closure failures and limiting phenomena arising under projection.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential characterization of a missing projected boundary point of a closed finite-dimensional lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+q}\) be closed, \(S=\operatorname{proj}_xQ\), and \(\bar x\in\overline S\setminus S\). If \((x_k,y_k)\in Q\) and \(x_k\to\bar x\), then \((y_k)\) has no bounded subsequence. Consequently, if for every compact \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) the auxiliary-coordinate set \(\{y:(x,y)\in Q\text{ for some }x\in C\}\) is bounded, then \(S\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A missing projected boundary point of a closed lift can only be approached through auxiliary variables escaping every bounded set. Uniform boundedness over compact base sets prevents the pathology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x_k,y_k)\in Q,\ x_k\to\bar x\Longrightarrow (y_k)\text{ has no bounded subsequence}.

notation.meaning: unattained boundary point of the projection

knowledge_statements.title: Escape-to-Infinity Boundary for Nonclosed Projections
Nonclosed Projection Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A closed spectrahedron whose one-dimensional projection is not closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the lifted set \[Q=\left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:\begin{pmatrix}x&1\\1&y\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\right\}.\] This set is closed and convex. Positive semidefiniteness requires \(x\geq0\), \(y\geq0\), and \(xy\geq1\), so its projection onto the \(x\)-coordinate is \[\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=(0,\infty).\] Hence a linear projection of a closed convex set, even a spectrahedron, need not be closed. The missing boundary point \(x=0\) is approached by feasible pairs \((x,1/x)\) as \(x\downarrow0\), but it has no finite lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed two-variable spectrahedron projects to the open ray of positive numbers, demonstrating that projection can lose closedness at an unattained boundary.
assumptions_latex: The matrix order \(\succeq0\) denotes positive semidefiniteness
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\) is closed and convex, but \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=(0,\infty)\) is not closed.
