children.title: Geometric Program Interface
children.top_down_role: Convex-reformulable geometric programs and their specialized dual structures.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specialized multiplicative dual for the standard posynomial GP, including monomial equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_i(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{K_i}c_{ik}x^{a_{ik}}\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m\), and let the monomial equalities be \(d_jx^{b_j}=1\), \(j=1,\ldots,q\). Choose \(\delta_{ik}\geq0\), set \(\lambda_i=\sum_k\delta_{ik}\) for \(i\geq1\), and choose free \(\eta_j\in\mathbb R\). If \(\sum_k\delta_{0k}=1\) and \(\sum_{i=0}^m\sum_k\delta_{ik}a_{ik}+\sum_j\eta_jb_j=0\), then, with the continuous zero-weight convention, \[D(\delta,\eta)=\prod_k\left(\frac{c_{0k}}{\delta_{0k}}\right)^{\delta_{0k}}\prod_{i=1}^m\prod_k\left(\frac{c_{ik}\lambda_i}{\delta_{ik}}\right)^{\delta_{ik}}\prod_j d_j^{\eta_j}\] is a lower bound on every feasible primal objective. If the logarithmically transformed convex problem satisfies Slater's condition and has finite optimal value, the best such bound equals the primal value and is attained by dual multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalized nonnegative term weights, exponent balance, and free monomial-equality multipliers yield multiplicative GP lower bounds; logarithmic Slater regularity makes the best bound exact.
assumptions_latex: \(c_{ik}>0\), \(d_j>0\), and all primal variables are strictly positive.
The displayed weights satisfy normalization and exponent balance.
For exactness and dual attainment, the logarithmic convex reformulation satisfies Slater's condition and has finite optimal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D(\delta,\eta)\leq p^*,\qquad\text{and under Slater regularity }\max D(\delta,\eta)=p^*.

notation.meaning: nonnegative dual weight for a posynomial term
aggregate multiplier for posynomial constraint i
free multiplier for monomial equality j

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric-Programming Dual Certificate

assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is a posynomial and each \(h_j\) is a monomial with positive coefficients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The logarithmic substitution converts the geometric program exactly into a convex program with log-sum-exp inequalities and affine equalities.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard positive-variable geometric program and logarithmic convex reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A geometric program has the form
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb R_{++}^n} f_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad f_i(x)\leq1,\quad h_j(x)=1,
\]
where every posynomial is \(f_i(x)=\sum_k c_{ik}\prod_{r=1}^n x_r^{a_{ikr}}\), and every \(h_j\) has one such term. With \(y_r=\log x_r\), it is equivalent to
\[
\min_y \log\!\left(\sum_k c_{0k}e^{a_{0k}^{\mathsf T}y}\right)
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\log\!\left(\sum_k c_{ik}e^{a_{ik}^{\mathsf T}y}\right)\leq0,
\quad \log c_j+a_j^{\mathsf T}y=0.
\]
The transformed objective and inequalities are convex, and the equalities are affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive-variable geometric programs become convex programs after taking logarithms, with posynomials becoming log-sum-exp functions and monomial equalities becoming affine.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Program Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The logarithmic convex reformulation is standard and appears correctly stated, but the record supplies no inspectable citation. An authoritative geometric-programming source with a section, theorem, definition, or page locator is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Logarithmic convex reformulation of a geometric program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent convex formulation of a classical geometric program using logarithmic variables and the strictly increasing logarithm on its positive objective and constraint functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a geometric program on \(\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\), with posynomials \(f_i(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{K_i}c_{ik}\exp(a_{ik}^T\log x)\) and monomial equalities \(h_i(x)=d_i\exp(g_i^T\log x)=1\), where \(c_{ik}>0\) and \(d_i>0\). Under the bijective substitution \(y=\log x\), let \(b_{ik}=\log c_{ik}\) and \(q_i=\log d_i\). Applying the strictly increasing logarithm to the positive objective and inequality functions yields the equivalent problem \[\begin{aligned}\operatorname*{minimize}_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}\quad & \log\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K_0}e^{a_{0k}^Ty+b_{0k}}\right)\\ \operatorname*{subject\ to}\quad & \log\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K_i}e^{a_{ik}^Ty+b_{ik}}\right)\le0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m,\\ & g_i^Ty+q_i=0,\quad i=1,\ldots,p.\end{aligned}\] The objective and inequality functions are convex log-sum-exp functions and the equality functions are affine, so this is a convex optimization problem. If every posynomial objective and inequality function has one term, the transformed problem is a linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A geometric program is generally not convex in its original positive variables. The bijection y = log x maps each monomial to the exponential of an affine function and each posynomial to a sum of exponentials of affine functions. Because these functions are positive and logarithm is strictly increasing, taking their logarithms preserves the minimizers and inequality directions, producing an equivalent convex problem with log-sum-exp objective and inequalities and affine equalities. If every posynomial objective and inequality has one term, the transformed problem is a linear program.
assumptions_latex: \log\text{ is applied only to the positive monomial and posynomial functions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The posynomial-form geometric program is equivalent to the displayed convex log-sum-exp program in }y;\text{ if }K_i=1\text{ for every posynomial objective and inequality, it reduces to a linear program.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be nonempty and compact, let \(F:X\to\mathbb R^q\) be continuous, and let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^q\) be closed, convex, pointed, and have nonempty interior. Then the vector minimization problem has a Pareto-efficient solution.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interface minimizes \(F\) under \(\leq_K\), with weak and Pareto efficiency defined by exclusion of the displayed improving sets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional cone-ordered vector minimization and efficiency notions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The vector optimization problem is
\[
\operatorname{minimize}_{x\in X}^{K} F(x),
\]
meaning that objective vectors are compared by \(u\leq_K v\) exactly when \(v-u\in K\). A feasible point \(x^*\in X\) is weakly efficient when
\[
F(X)\cap\bigl(F(x^*)-\operatorname{int}K\bigr)=\varnothing,
\]
and is Pareto efficient when
\[
F(X)\cap\bigl(F(x^*)-(K\setminus\{0\})\bigr)=\varnothing.
\]
Thus the interface consists of the feasible set, vector objective, ordering cone, and the chosen efficiency predicate; it does not assign a total ordering to incomparable objective vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vector optimization compares objective vectors using a cone and defines weak or Pareto efficiency by the absence of feasible strict improvements.
knowledge_statements.title: Vector Optimization Interface

knowledge_statements.statement_title: General and Convex Vector Optimization Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines cone-ordered vector objectives, feasible-value comparison, the convex subclass, and the possibility of incomparable objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbf R^q\) be a proper cone. A vector optimization problem has the form
\[
\operatorname{minimize}_{K}\ f_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad f_i(x)\leq0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad h_i(x)=0\ (i=1,\ldots,p),
\]
where \(x\in\mathbf R^n\), \(f_0:\mathbf R^n\to\mathbf R^q\), and the scalar constraint functions have values in \(\mathbf R\). Feasible objective values are compared by \(\preccurlyeq_K\), with \(f_0(x)\preccurlyeq_K f_0(y)\) meaning that \(x\) is at least as good as \(y\). The problem is convex precisely when \(f_0\) is \(K\)-convex, every \(f_i\) is convex, and every \(h_i\) is affine. Unlike the scalar case, two feasible objective values can be incomparable under \(\preccurlyeq_K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector optimization problem compares vector-valued objectives using the order induced by a proper cone. It is convex precisely when the vector objective is cone-convex, the inequality functions are convex, and the equality functions are affine. Two feasible objective values need not be comparable.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbf R^q\text{ is a proper cone}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The problem is convex}\iff f_0\text{ is }K\text{-convex},\ f_i\text{ is convex for every }i,\text{ and }h_i\text{ is affine for every }i.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of Minimax Equality Without Compactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noncompact bilinear example showing that convexity-concavity alone is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=Y=(0,+\infty)\) and \(L(x,y)=xy\). Then \(L\) is affine in each variable, but \[\inf_{x>0}\sup_{y>0}xy=+\infty,\qquad \sup_{y>0}\inf_{x>0}xy=0.\] Hence convexity-concavity alone implies neither minimax equality nor existence of a saddle point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On positive noncompact domains, the bilinear payoff has upper value infinity and lower value zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{y>0}\inf_{x>0}xy=0<+\infty=\inf_{x>0}\sup_{y>0}xy.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Minimax Equality Without Compactness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real-valued, one-sided-compact convex-concave minimax equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty compact convex set and \(Y\) a nonempty convex set. Let \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) satisfy: \(L(\cdot,y)\) is lower semicontinuous and convex on \(X\) for every \(y\in Y\), and \(L(x,\cdot)\) is upper semicontinuous and concave on \(Y\) for every \(x\in X\). Then \[\min_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)=\sup_{y\in Y}\min_{x\in X}L(x,y).\] The outer minimum is attained. Attainment of the outer supremum requires an additional condition, such as compactness of \(Y\) together with the stated upper semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sion's theorem equates min-max and max-min values under one-sided compactness and the appropriate semicontinuous convex-concave section assumptions.
assumptions_latex: The x-sections are lower semicontinuous and convex; the y-sections are upper semicontinuous and concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)=\sup_{y\in Y}\min_{x\in X}L(x,y).
knowledge_statements.title: Sion Minimax Theorem

assumptions_latex: The sets \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty convex subsets of finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
For every \(y\in Y\), \(L(\cdot,y)\) is convex on \(X\), and for every \(x\in X\), \(L(x,\cdot)\) is concave on \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimax interface is the convex problem \(\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\), and weak minimax inequality gives \(\sup_y\inf_xL(x,y)\leq\inf_x\sup_yL(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex-concave minimax formulation without a strong minimax hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a convex-concave payoff \(L\), define
\[
\phi(x)=\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y),
\qquad
\psi(y)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y).
\]
The convex minimax problem and its lower counterpart are
\[
 p^*=\inf_{x\in X}\phi(x)=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y),
\qquad
 d^*=\sup_{y\in Y}\psi(y)=\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y).
\]
The function \(\phi\) is convex, \(\psi\) is concave, and the elementary minimax inequality gives \(d^*\leq p^*\). Equality requires additional closedness, compactness, or constraint-qualification hypotheses not included in this interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex minimax problem minimizes the pointwise supremum of a convex-concave payoff; its lower value never exceeds its upper value.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Minimax Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weak minimax inequality and convexity/concavity of the value functions are standard, but no source is cited. Because the payoff is extended-real-valued, an authoritative source should also establish the conventions or exclusions needed for the stated value functions and extrema.

children.title: Convex–Concave Saddle Interface
children.top_down_role: Program representations based on convex–concave saddle functions.

assumptions_latex: The payoff \(L:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is convex in its first argument and concave in its second.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A pair is a saddle point exactly when it satisfies the two-sided inequality, which certifies global optimality for both one-sided problems and zero minimax gap.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global saddle-point certificate for a convex-concave payoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A feasible pair \((x^*,y^*)\in X\times Y\) is a saddle point of \(L\) when
\[
L(x^*,y)\leq L(x^*,y^*)\leq L(x,y^*)
\qquad\text{for every }x\in X,\ y\in Y.
\]
This directly certifies
\[
 x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y),

y^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y),
\]
and
\[
\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)=L(x^*,y^*)=
\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y).
\]
The inequalities themselves are the certificate; convexity-concavity is structural but is not needed to verify a proposed global saddle pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A saddle pair bounds the payoff from both sides, simultaneously certifying both players' optimality and equality of the lower and upper minimax values.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex–Concave Saddle Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-sided saddle inequality correctly acts as a global optimality and zero-gap certificate, and certificate is the appropriate knowledge kind. The claim lacks an inspectable authoritative citation.

children.title: Scalarization Links
children.top_down_role: Connections from ordered or minimax objectives to scalar convex programs.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unsupported Efficient Point in a Nonconvex Image
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of weighted-sum completeness without upper-image convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[F(X)=\{(0,2),(1,3/2),(2,0)\},\qquad K=\mathbb R_+^2,\] the point \((1,3/2)\) is Pareto efficient but minimizes no weighted sum \(w_1z_1+w_2z_2\) with \(w\in\mathbb R_+^2\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex objective image may contain efficient points unsupported by every nonnegative weighted sum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (1,3/2)\text{ is Pareto efficient but unsupported}
knowledge_statements.title: Unsupported Efficient Point in a Nonconvex Image

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate scalarization associated with a Pareto-efficient point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For componentwise minimization of \(F=(F_1,\ldots,F_q)\), every Pareto-efficient \(x^*\) solves, for each \(k\), \[\min_{x\in X}F_k(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad F_i(x)\le F_i(x^*)\ (i\ne k).\] Conversely, a unique minimizer of this scalar problem is Pareto efficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pareto points solve their associated epsilon-constraint problems; uniqueness supplies a converse.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ Pareto efficient}\Rightarrow x^*\text{ solves every displayed coordinate scalarization}
knowledge_statements.title: Epsilon-Constraint Scalarization

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supporting-Weight Recovery of Weakly Efficient Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted-sum converse under convex upper-image separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^q\) be a closed convex cone with nonempty interior, let \(P=F(X)+K\) be convex, and let \(x^*\) be weakly efficient. Then there is \(w\in K^*\setminus\{0\}\) such that \[x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\langle w,F(x)\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every weakly efficient point of a convex upper image is supported by a nonzero dual-cone weight.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R^q\text{ is closed and convex with }\operatorname{int}K\neq\varnothing
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists w\in K^*\setminus\{0\}:x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\langle w,F(x)\rangle
knowledge_statements.title: Supporting-Weight Recovery of Weakly Efficient Points

assumptions_latex: The cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^q\) is closed and convex, and its dual cone is \(K^*\).
The feasible set \(X\) is nonempty and \(F:X\to\mathbb R^q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every nonzero \(w\in K^*\) converts the vector problem into a compatible scalar problem; any scalar minimizer is weakly efficient when \(w\in\operatorname{int}K^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted-sum scalarization of cone-ordered vector minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any nonzero weight \(w\in K^*\), the weighted scalarization is
\[
\min_{x\in X}\langle w,F(x)\rangle.
\]
If \(x^*\) solves this problem, then no \(x\in X\) can satisfy \(F(x^*)-F(x)\in K\) together with \(\langle w,F(x^*)-F(x)\rangle>0\). In particular, if \(w\in\operatorname{int}K^*\), then \(x^*\) is weakly efficient because every vector in \(\operatorname{int}K\) has strictly positive pairing with \(w\). Conversely, recovery of every supported weakly efficient point by some \(w\in K^*\setminus\{0\}\) requires suitable convexity and separation assumptions on the upper image.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual-cone weights produce scalar objectives compatible with the vector order; an interior weight makes every scalar minimizer weakly efficient.
knowledge_statements.title: Scalarization Links

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The forward weighted-sum implication is plausible and properly distinguishes the converse, but no source supports either the interior-weight claim or the stated scope of the converse. A source must specify the relevant cone, upper-image convexity, and separation hypotheses.

children.title: Minimax–Saddle Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between minimax values and saddle representations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimax Equality Without a Saddle Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the converse when the common value is not attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=Y=(0,1)\) and \(L(x,y)=x-y\). Then \[\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)=0=\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y),\] but neither outer extremum is attained, and no saddle pair exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal minimax values do not yield a saddle point without attainment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p^*=d^*=0\quad\text{and no saddle pair exists}
knowledge_statements.title: Minimax Equality Without a Saddle Point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconditional order between lower and upper minimax values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty \(X,Y\) and \(L:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), \[\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)\le \inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The max-min value never exceeds the min-max value; convexity, compactness, continuity, and attainment are unnecessary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)\le \inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Minimax Inequality

assumptions_latex: The sets \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty and the payoff \(L:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is given.
The relevant infima and suprema are well-defined in the extended real line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A saddle point exists exactly when the upper and lower minimax values coincide and both outer extrema are attained by the same candidate pair.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attained minimax equality characterized by existence of a saddle pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
p^*=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y),
\qquad
d^*=\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y).
\]
A pair \((x^*,y^*)\in X\times Y\) is a saddle point if and only if
\[
\sup_{y\in Y}L(x^*,y)=L(x^*,y^*)=
\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y^*).
\]
Consequently, a saddle pair implies \(p^*=d^*=L(x^*,y^*)\) and attainment of both outer extrema. Conversely, if \(p^*=d^*=v\), \(x^*\) attains the upper problem, and \(y^*\) attains the lower problem, then \(L(x^*,y)\leq v\leq L(x,y^*)\) for all \(x,y\), so \((x^*,y^*)\) is a saddle point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Saddle points are precisely attained minimax equalities: equality alone gives a value, while attainment supplies the pair satisfying both saddle inequalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimax–Saddle Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The attained minimax-equality characterization of a saddle pair is mathematically standard, but the record has no citation. Since extended-real payoffs are allowed, the source should also state the conventions under which all displayed extrema and equalities are meaningful.

children.title: Primal Convex Program Interface
children.top_down_role: Organization of the primal feasible geometry, value, and attainment questions.

assumptions_latex: The functions \(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_m:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) are proper convex functions.
The map \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\) is linear and \(b\in\mathbb R^p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The primal interface is determined by its feasible set \(P\), value \(p^*\), solution set \(P^*\), and the associated feasibility and attainment statuses.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex program with inequalities and affine equalities.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.2. General Optimization Duality p. 138

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The primal convex program is
\[
p^*=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{f_0(x):f_i(x)\leq0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ Ax=b\}.
\]
Its feasible and solution sets are
\[
P=\{x\in\bigcap_{i=0}^m\operatorname{dom}f_i:f_i(x)\leq0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ Ax=b\},
\qquad
P^*=\{x\in P:f_0(x)=p^*\}.
\]
The interface records infeasibility when \(P=\varnothing\), unboundedness below when \(p^*=-\infty\), finite nonattainment when \(p^*\in\mathbb R\) but \(P^*=\varnothing\), and attainment when \(P^*\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal interface records the convex constraints, feasible set, optimal value, solution set, and whether the problem is infeasible, unbounded, unattained, or attained.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal Convex Program Interface

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2.2. General Optimization Duality p. 138

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General sufficient attainment condition within the primal interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and closed, and let \(f_0:P\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and lower semicontinuous. Suppose \(p^*:=\inf_{x\in P}f_0(x)>-\infty\) and some nonempty sublevel set \(\{x\in P:f_0(x)\le\alpha\}\) is compact. Then \(p^*\in\mathbb R\) and \(P^*\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper lower-semicontinuous objective attains its finite infimum when a relevant feasible sublevel set is compact.
assumptions_latex: \(f_0\) is proper and lower semicontinuous on \(P\).
\(\{x\in P:f_0(x)\le\alpha\}\) is nonempty and compact for some finite \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p^*\in\mathbb R\quad\text{and}\quad P^*\ne\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Level-Compact Primal Attainment Test

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity of Primal Feasible and Solution Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic feasible geometry of the general primal convex-program interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal program in the seed, \[P=\{x:f_i(x)\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ Ax=b\}\] is convex. If the finite value \(p^*\) is attained, then \[P^*=P\cap\{x:f_0(x)\le p^*\}\] is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex inequality sublevel sets and affine equalities make the feasible set convex; the attained solution set is convex as well.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is convex, and }P^*\text{ is convex whenever nonempty}.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity of Primal Feasible and Solution Sets

children.title: Lagrangian Dual Program Interface
children.top_down_role: Dual programs organized through Lagrangian bounds and multiplier domains.

assumptions_latex: The functions \(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_m:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) are proper convex functions.
The map \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\) is linear, \(b\in\mathbb R^p\), and the primal program minimizes \(f_0(x)\) subject to \(f_i(x)\leq0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\) and \(Ax=b\).
The multiplier domain is \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\) and \(\nu\in\mathbb R^p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Lagrangian dual maximizes the concave lower-bound function \(g\), and every multiplier pair \((\lambda,\nu)\in\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R^p\) supplies a certified extended-real lower bound on \(p^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian dual of a finite-dimensional convex inequality-affine-equality primal program.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.2. General Optimization Duality p. 138

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the Lagrangian and dual function by
\[
L(x,\lambda,\nu)=f_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i(x)+\langle\nu,Ax-b\rangle,
\qquad
g(\lambda,\nu)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}L(x,\lambda,\nu).
\]
The Lagrangian dual program is
\[
d^*=\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m,\,\nu\in\mathbb R^p}g(\lambda,\nu).
\]
For every primal-feasible \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and every \((\lambda,\nu)\in\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R^p\), one has \(g(\lambda,\nu)\leq f_0(x)\); hence \(d^*\leq p^*\). A multiplier pair is dual optimal when it attains \(d^*\); equality \(d^*=p^*\) and dual attainment require additional regularity conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Lagrangian dual maximizes the infimum of the Lagrangian over nonnegative inequality multipliers and free equality multipliers, producing certified lower bounds on the primal value.
knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Dual Program Interface

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2.2. General Optimization Duality p. 138

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concavity and Effective Domain of the Lagrange Dual Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural properties of the multiplier lower-bound function defining the Lagrangian dual program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the primal model of the immutable seed, define \[g(\lambda,
u):=\inf_x\left(f_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i(x)+\langle
u,Ax-bangleight).\] Then \(g\) is concave on \(\mathbb R^m	imes\mathbb R^p\), and \[\operatorname{dom}g:=\{(\lambda,
u):g(\lambda,
u)>-\infty\}\] is convex. The Lagrangian dual maximizes \(g\) over \(\mathbb R_+^m	imes\mathbb R^p\). A multiplier in that set with \(g=-\infty\) is formally admissible but supplies no finite lower-bound certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Lagrange dual function is concave, and its effective domain identifies the multipliers that furnish nontrivial lower bounds.
assumptions_latex: The primal objective, convex inequality constraints, affine equality constraints, and multiplier domains are those of the immutable Lagrangian Dual Program Interface seed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is concave and \(\operatorname{dom}g\) is convex; a finite lower-bound certificate requires \(g(\lambda,\nu)>-\infty\).

notation.meaning: effective domain of the concave dual function, excluding value minus infinity

knowledge_statements.title: Concavity and Effective Domain of the Lagrange Dual Function

children.title: Perturbation Value-Function Duality
children.top_down_role: Duality organized through perturbations and the geometry of optimal-value functions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Solution Sets from the Perturbation Value Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of dual optimizers at the unperturbed parameter through the perturbation value function and its biconjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the primal problem \((P)\) is convex, with perturbation value function \(v\) and dual problem \((D)\). Then: (i) if \(\operatorname{val}(D)\) is finite, \(\operatorname{Sol}(D)=\partial v^{**}(0)\); (ii) if \(v\) is subdifferentiable at \(0\), there is no duality gap and \(\operatorname{Sol}(D)=\partial v(0)\); and (iii) if \(\operatorname{val}(P)=\operatorname{val}(D)\in\mathbb R\), then the possibly empty set \(\operatorname{Sol}(D)\) equals \(\partial v(0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex primal problem, a finite dual value identifies the dual solution set with the biconjugate subdifferential at zero. Subdifferentiability at zero gives strong duality and identifies dual optimizers with the value-function subdifferential. The same identification holds under equal finite primal and dual values, although the set may be empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{val}(D)\in\mathbb R\Rightarrow\operatorname{Sol}(D)=\partial v^{**}(0);\quad \partial v(0)\neq\varnothing\Rightarrow\operatorname{val}(P)=\operatorname{val}(D)\text{ and }\operatorname{Sol}(D)=\partial v(0);\quad \operatorname{val}(P)=\operatorname{val}(D)\in\mathbb R\Rightarrow\operatorname{Sol}(D)=\partial v(0).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Value as Subvalue and the Lower-Semicontinuity Criterion for Strong Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbation-duality result requiring convexity of the optimal-value function and subconsistency of the primal problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the optimal-value function \(v\) is convex and the primal problem \((P)\) is subconsistent. Then \[\operatorname{val}(D)=\min\left\{\operatorname{val}(P),\liminf_{y\to0}v(y)\right\}=\operatorname{lsc}v(0).\] Consequently, \[\operatorname{val}(P)=\operatorname{val}(D)\iff v\text{ is lower semicontinuous at }0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex perturbation value function and a subconsistent primal problem, the dual value equals the subvalue at zero. Strong duality therefore holds exactly when the value function is lower semicontinuous at the unperturbed parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{val}(D)=\min\{\operatorname{val}(P),\liminf_{y\to0}v(y)\};\qquad \operatorname{val}(P)=\operatorname{val}(D)\iff v\text{ is lower semicontinuous at }0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subvalue and Subconsistency of a Perturbed Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines perturbation-based consistency at zero and separately records the biconjugacy consequence requiring convexity and a real-valued subvalue.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the optimal-value function \(v\), define the subvalue of \((P)\) by \[\operatorname{lsc}v(0):=\min\left\{v(0),\liminf_{y\to0}v(y)\right\}.\] The problem is subconsistent if \(\operatorname{lsc}v(0)<+\infty\). If \(v\) is convex and \(\operatorname{lsc}v(0)\in\mathbb R\), then \[v^{**}(0)=\operatorname{lsc}v(0).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subvalue is the smaller of the unperturbed value and the lower limiting value under nearby perturbations. Subconsistency means that this quantity is below positive infinity. If the value function is convex and the subvalue is finite, the biconjugate has the same value at zero.

v\text{ is convex for the biconjugacy conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{lsc}v(0)=\min\{v(0),\liminf_{y\to0}v(y)\};\qquad v^{**}(0)=\operatorname{lsc}v(0)\text{ under the stated additional assumptions}.

children.title: Perturbation Function Interface
children.top_down_role: Parameterized convex models used to organize primal sensitivity and dual construction.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation Function Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional perturbation model for a primal convex program and its value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(U\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, and let \(F:X\times U\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and convex. The perturbation value function is \[v(u):=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,u).\] The unperturbed primal value is \(p=v(0)\). With the convention \(F^*(x^*,u^*):=\sup_{x,u}\{\langle x^*,x\rangle+\langle u^*,u\rangle-F(x,u)\}\), its perturbation dual is \[d:=\sup_{y\in U^*}-F^*(0,y).\] Thus a single function \(F\) specifies the primal slice, parameterized values, and dual objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex perturbation function encodes the primal problem at zero, nearby optimal values, and a dual problem obtained from its conjugate.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(U\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugate identity intrinsic to the perturbation interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\times U\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and convex and define \(v(u):=\inf_xF(x,u)\). Then, for every \(y\in U^*\), \[v^*(y)=\sup_u\{\langle y,u\rangle-v(u)\}=F^*(0,y).\] Consequently, \[\sup_y[-F^*(0,y)]=\sup_y[-v^*(y)]=v^{**}(0).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of the marginal value function is the zero-primal-coordinate slice of the perturbation conjugate, and the perturbation dual value equals the biconjugate value at zero.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\times U\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v^*(y)=F^*(0,y)\quad\text{and}\quad \sup_y[-F^*(0,y)]=v^{**}(0).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v(u):=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,u)\), and define \[P:=\{(u,t)\in U\times\mathbb R:\text{there exists }x\in X\text{ such that }F(x,u)\le t\}.\] Then \(v\) is convex and \(P\) is the projection of \(\operatorname{epi}F\) onto \(U\times\mathbb R\). In general, \[\{(u,t):v(u)<t\}\subseteq P\subseteq\operatorname{epi}v,\qquad \overline P=\overline{\operatorname{epi}v}.\] Equality \(P=\operatorname{epi}v\) requires attainment of the defining infimum at boundary points. Thus projection preserves convexity but can lose closedness even when \(F\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The optimal-value function is convex. The projection of the perturbation epigraph contains every point strictly above its graph, but it can omit boundary points where the infimum is not attained and need not be closed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convex Perturbation with Nonclosed Marginal Domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit finite-dimensional example showing that projection can destroy closedness of a perturbation domain and its marginal epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C:=\{(x,u)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ u\ge 1/x\}\] and let \(F(x,u):=\delta_C(x,u)\). The set \(C\) is closed and convex, so \(F\) is proper closed convex. Its marginal value is \[v(u):=\inf_xF(x,u)=\begin{cases}0,&u>0,\\+\infty,&u\le0.\end{cases}\] Hence \(\operatorname{dom}v=(0,\infty)=\operatorname{proj}_U C\), which is not closed, and \(\operatorname{epi}v=(0,\infty)\times[0,\infty)\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex perturbation can have a nonclosed projected domain and a nonclosed marginal value function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is proper closed convex, but \(\operatorname{dom}v=(0,\infty)\) and \(\operatorname{epi}v\) are not closed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Domain as a Projection of the Perturbation Domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effective-domain geometry of a proper marginal optimal-value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\times U\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be proper and convex, and suppose \(v(u):=\inf_xF(x,u)\) is proper. Then \[\operatorname{dom}v=\{u\in U:\exists x\in X\text{ with }F(x,u)<+\infty\}=\operatorname{proj}_U(\operatorname{dom}F).\] Consequently, \(\operatorname{dom}v\) is convex. This projection identity does not imply that \(\operatorname{dom}v\) or \(\operatorname{epi}v\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The effective domain of a proper marginal value function is exactly the projection of the perturbation function's effective domain; convexity survives projection but closedness need not.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(U\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(F:X\times U\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and convex, and define \(v(u):=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,u)\). Assume that \(v\) is proper and \(v(0)\) is finite. For \(y\in U^*\), the support condition \[v(u)\ge v(0)+\langle y,u\rangle\quad\text{for every }u\in U\] is equivalent to \(y\in\partial v(0)\). Moreover, \(v^*(y)=F^*(0,y)\), so the Fenchel equality at zero is \[v(0)+F^*(0,y)=0.\] Hence such a \(y\) attains the perturbation dual value and certifies zero duality gap at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper perturbation value function, a subgradient at zero is exactly a supporting dual vector; Fenchel equality then shows that it attains the dual value and certifies zero duality gap.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual optimizers and first-order value-function sensitivity under Slater regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbation sensitivity for a convex semidefinite problem at the unperturbed parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the semidefinite problem is convex and Slater's condition holds. Then \(\operatorname{Sol}(D)\) is nonempty and bounded, and the optimal-value function \(v(Y)\) is convex and continuous at \(Y=0\), with \[v'(0;A)=\sup_{\Omega\in\operatorname{Sol}(D)}\Omega\bullet A.\] If \(\operatorname{Sol}(D)=\{\bar\Omega\}\), then \(v\) is differentiable at \(0\) and \(\nabla v(0)=\bar\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex semidefinite problem satisfying Slater's condition, the dual optimal set is nonempty and bounded. The perturbation value function is convex and continuous at zero, and its directional derivative is the support function of the dual optimal set. If the dual optimizer is unique, the value function is differentiable at zero and its gradient equals that optimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Sol}(D)\neq\varnothing,\quad \operatorname{Sol}(D)\text{ is bounded},\quad v\text{ is convex and continuous at }0,\quad v'(0;A)=\sup_{\Omega\in\operatorname{Sol}(D)}\Omega\bullet A;\quad \operatorname{Sol}(D)=\{\bar\Omega\}\Rightarrow \nabla v(0)=\bar\Omega.

knowledge_statements.title: Fenchel Primal Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composite finite-dimensional Fenchel primal and its perturbation representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, and let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(g:Y\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper convex functions. The Fenchel composite primal is \[p:=\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}.\] It is the zero slice of the perturbation function \(F(x,u):=f(x)+g(Ax-u)\), whose value function is \(v(u)=\inf_x\{f(x)+g(Ax-u)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Fenchel primal minimizes a sum of a convex function and a convex function composed with a linear map.

source_refs.locator: 5.3.4. Duality and Existence of Optimal Primal Solutions p. 176

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent equality-constrained representation of the finite-dimensional composite Fenchel primal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear and let \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(g:Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be proper convex functions. Then \[\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}=\inf_{x\in X,\,z\in Y}\{f(x)+g(z):Ax-z=0\}.\] Feasible pairs of the split problem are exactly \((x,Ax)\). Thus the optimal values agree, and attained minimizers correspond under \(x\mapsto(x,Ax)\) and projection onto \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Introducing a copy of the linear image converts the composite Fenchel primal into an equivalent separable objective with one linear equality constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_x\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}=\inf_{Ax=z}\{f(x)+g(z)\}\), with a bijection between attained minimizers.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, and let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(g:Y\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper convex functions. For \[p:=\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)+g(Ax)\},\] the conjugate-dual program is \[d:=\sup_{y\in Y^*}\{-f^*(-A^*y)-g^*(y)\}.\] Fenchel inequalities imply \[-f^*(-A^*y)-g^*(y)\le f(x)+g(Ax)\] for every \(x\in X\) and \(y\in Y^*\). Consequently, \(d\le p\). Equality or attainment requires an additional regularity or closure condition and is not part of the formal dual construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For proper convex functions on finite-dimensional spaces, the Fenchel dual maximizes two negative conjugates linked by the adjoint map, and weak duality always holds.

knowledge_statements.title: Fenchel–Rockafellar Duality Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional strong Fenchel duality under a continuity qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(g:Y\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper convex functions, with \(A:X\to Y\) linear. Suppose there exists \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\) such that \(g\) is finite and continuous at \(Ax_0\), and suppose \(p:=\inf_x\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}\) is finite. Then \[p=\max_{y\in Y^*}\{-f^*(-A^*y)-g^*(y)\}.\] In particular, there is no duality gap and the dual maximum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible continuity point for one composite term guarantees equality of Fenchel primal and dual values and attainment of the dual optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(f,g\) are proper convex functions on finite-dimensional spaces.
\(g\) is finite and continuous at \(Ax_0\) for some \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=d\), and the dual supremum is attained.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, and let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(g:Y\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper convex functions. Define \[v(u):=\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)+g(Ax-u)\},\] and assume that \(v\) is proper and \(v(0)\) is finite. Then \[v^*(z)=f^*(A^*z)+g^*(-z).\] For \(p:=v(0)\) and \[d:=\sup_{y\in Y^*}\{-f^*(-A^*y)-g^*(y)\},\] one has \[p=v(0)\ge v^{**}(0)=d.\] Strong duality at the origin is therefore equivalent to \(v(0)=v^{**}(0)\). Failure of epigraphical closure at \(0\) can produce strict inequality, whereas failure of a sufficient qualification alone does not imply a gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fully specified composite Fenchel pair, the duality gap equals the difference between the perturbation value and its lower-semicontinuous convex closure at zero.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Fenchel Gap from Nonclosed Data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary composite Fenchel pair whose perturbation value differs from its lower-semicontinuous convex closure at the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=Y=\mathbb R\), \(A=0\), \(f=\delta_{\{0\}}\), and define the proper convex function \[g(t)=\begin{cases}0,&t<0,\\1,&t=0,\\+\infty,&t>0.\end{cases}\] Then the primal value is \(p=\inf_x\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}=1\). Moreover, \(f^*(0)=0\), while \(g^*(y)=0\) for \(y\ge0\) and \(g^*(y)=+\infty\) for \(y<0\). Consequently, \[d=\sup_y\{-f^*(-A^*y)-g^*(y)\}=0<p.\] The associated value function satisfies \(v(0)=1\) and \(v^{**}(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonclosed proper convex term produces a strict Fenchel duality gap exactly matching the jump between the perturbation value and its closed convex hull at zero.

notation.meaning: convex indicator of the singleton zero

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Fenchel Gap from Nonclosed Data

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Qualification Failure Without a Fenchel Duality Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary example showing that failure of the standard relative-interior qualification does not imply a gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=Y=\mathbb R\), \(A=I\), \(f=\delta_{\{0\}}\), and \(g=\delta_{[0,\infty)}\). Then \(p=\inf_x\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}=0\), while \[A(\operatorname{dom}f)-\operatorname{dom}g=(-\infty,0]\] and hence \(0\notin\operatorname{ri}(A(\operatorname{dom}f)-\operatorname{dom}g)\). Nevertheless, \(f^*\equiv0\), \(g^*(y)=0\) for \(y\le0\), and \(g^*(y)=+\infty\) for \(y>0\), so \[\sup_y\{-f^*(-y)-g^*(y)\}=0.\] Thus the dual optimum is attained and there is no gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero attained Fenchel duality gap can hold even when the usual relative-interior qualification fails.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\notin\operatorname{ri}(A\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g)\), but \(p=d=0\) and the dual optimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.title: Qualification Failure Without a Fenchel Duality Gap

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, let \(K\subseteq X\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, and let \(b\in Y\) and \(c\in X\). Define \[L(x,y):=\langle c,x\rangle+\langle y,b-Ax\rangle\quad\text{for }(x,y)\in K\times Y.\] If \(p\) and \(d\) are the associated equality-form conic primal and dual values, then \[p=\inf_{x\in K}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y),\qquad d=\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in K}L(x,y).\] Moreover, \(\inf_{x\in K}L(x,y)=\langle b,y\rangle\) when \(c-A^*y\in K^*\), and it equals \(-\infty\) otherwise. Thus minimax equality is equivalent to zero duality gap for this pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For fully specified conic data, the primal and dual values are respectively the min-max and max-min values of the cone-restricted Lagrangian.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, let \(K\subseteq X\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, and let \(b\in Y\) and \(c\in X\). Define \[L(x,y):=\langle c,x\rangle+\langle y,b-Ax\rangle.\] Let \(x\in K\) and \(y\in Y\) satisfy \(Ax=b\) and \(s:=c-A^*y\in K^*\). Then the following conditions are equivalent: \[\langle s,x\rangle=0,\] \[\langle c,x\rangle=\langle b,y\rangle,\] and \[L(x,y')\le L(x,y)\le L(x',y)\quad\text{for every }x'\in K\text{ and }y'\in Y.\] Under these conditions, \(x\) and \((y,s)\) are primal-dual optimal, so feasibility and complementarity form a directly checkable optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fully specified conic pair, primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementarity are equivalent to equality of objective values and to the associated Lagrangian saddle inequalities; together they certify optimality.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces.
\(K\subseteq X\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The linear image \(M\) can be nonclosed; missing points in \(\overline M\setminus M\) encode unattained limiting data and can obstruct attainment or strong-duality separation conditions.

notation.meaning: joint constraint-objective image of the primal cone

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonclosed cone images as geometric mechanisms for conic nonattainment and duality failure.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37
2.4 Conic duality theorem p. 57

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, let \(K\subseteq X\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, and let \(c\in X\). Define the joint constraint-objective image \[M:=\{(Ax,\langle c,x\rangle):x\in K\}\subseteq Y\times\mathbb R.\] Although \(K\) is closed, its linear image \(M\) need not be closed. Points of \(\overline M\setminus M\) represent limiting right-hand-side and objective data that are not attained by any \(x\in K\). Such nonclosedness can obstruct primal or dual attainment and the closedness-based separation arguments used for strong duality; in suitable degenerate instances it can accompany a positive duality gap. Failure of a Slater condition only removes a sufficient guarantee and does not by itself establish nonattainment or a gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed cone can have a nonclosed joint constraint-objective image. Missing boundary points encode unattained limiting data and can underlie nonattainment or a duality gap, while failure of Slater's condition alone proves neither.
knowledge_statements.title: Conic Duality Failure Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37
2.4 Conic duality theorem p. 57

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero Gap Does Not Imply Primal Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A Lorentz-cone pair with equal values and attained dual optimum but unattained primal infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{(u,v,w)\in\mathbb R^3:u\ge\sqrt{v^2+w^2}\}\) and consider \[p=\inf\{u-w:(u,v,w)\in K,\ v=1\}.\] Every feasible point satisfies \(u-w\ge\sqrt{1+w^2}-w>0\), while this expression tends to \(0\) as \(w\to+\infty\). Thus \(p=0\) and the infimum is not attained. Since \(K\) is self-dual, the dual is \[d=\sup\{y:(1,-y,-1)\in K\}.\] Cone membership forces \(y=0\), so \(d=0\) and the dual optimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lorentz-cone problem can have zero gap and an attained dual optimum while its primal infimum is approached only at infinity.
assumptions_latex: The primal equality fixes the second coordinate to one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=d=0\), the dual optimum is attained at \(y=0\), and the primal infimum is not attained.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero Gap Does Not Imply Primal Attainment

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero-Gap Dual Nonattainment in a Rotated-Cone Pair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit conic pair with an attained primal optimum and an unattained dual supremum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_r=\{(a,b,z)\in\mathbb R^3:a\ge0,\ b\ge0,\ 2ab\ge z^2\}\). Consider the conic primal-dual pair \[p^*=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}\{x:(0,1,x)\in K_r\},\qquad d^*=\sup_{(u,v,w)\in K_r}\{-v:w=1\}.\] The primal feasible set is \(\{0\}\), so its value \(0\) is attained. The dual has supremum \(0\), approached with \(v\downarrow0\) and \(u\uparrow\infty\), but no dual-feasible point attains it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rotated-second-order-cone pair has zero gap and an attained primal optimum, while its dual supremum is approached only at infinity.
assumptions_latex: \(K_r\) is the three-dimensional rotated second-order cone, using a self-dual normalization.
The displayed dual follows the stated conic-pair sign convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p^*=d^*=0,\qquad X^*=\{0\},\qquad Y^*=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Gap Dual Nonattainment in a Rotated-Cone Pair

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semidefinite Pair with a Positive Duality Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit finite-dimensional SDP whose primal and dual optima are both attained but unequal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,0)\), \(A_1=\operatorname{diag}(1,0,0)\), and \[A_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\0&1&0\\1&0&0\end{pmatrix}.\] Consider \[p^*=\sup_{x_1,x_2}\{2x_2:B-x_1A_1-x_2A_2\succeq0\}\] and \[d^*=\inf_{Y\succeq0}\{\langle B,Y\rangle:\langle A_1,Y\rangle=0,\ \langle A_2,Y\rangle=2\}.\] Their attained optimal values are \(p^*=0\) and \(d^*=2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A three-by-three semidefinite primal and dual can both attain their optima while having a positive gap of two.
assumptions_latex: The displayed pair uses the trace inner product on \(\mathbb S^3\).
Positive-semidefinite inequalities are interpreted in \(\mathbb S_+^3\).

notation.meaning: Trace inner product on symmetric matrices.
Primal maximization and dual minimization values.

knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Pair with a Positive Duality Gap

children.title: Weak-Duality Value Ordering
children.top_down_role: Value comparison structure common to convex primal-dual pairs.

assumptions_latex: \(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_m:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) are proper convex functions.
\(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^q\) is linear and \(b\in\mathbb R^q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in F\) and \((\lambda,\nu)\in\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R^q\), \(g(\lambda,\nu)\le f_0(x)\), and consequently \(d^*\le p^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real weak duality for a convex minimization problem and its Lagrange dual.

source_refs.locator: 5.3. Convex Programming Duality p. 167

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the primal feasible set \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:f_i(x)\le 0	ext{ for }i=1,\ldots,m,\ Ax=b\}\) and the primal value \[p^*=\inf_{x\in F}f_0(x).\] For \((\lambda,
u)\in\mathbb R_+^m	imes\mathbb R^q\), define \[g(\lambda,
u)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\left(f_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i(x)+
u^{\mathsf T}(Ax-b)ight),\qquad d^*=\sup_{(\lambda,
u)\in\mathbb R_+^m	imes\mathbb R^q}g(\lambda,
u).\] For every \(x\in F\) and every \((\lambda,
u)\in\mathbb R_+^m	imes\mathbb R^q\), one has \(g(\lambda,
u)\le f_0(x)\). Consequently, in the extended-real order, \(d^*\le p^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every value furnished by nonnegative inequality multipliers and unrestricted equality multipliers is no larger than every primal-feasible objective value; hence the dual optimal value does not exceed the primal optimal value.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak duality is algebraic but depends on the multiplier sign compatible with the displayed minimization convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\inf\{f_0(x):f_i(x)\le0,\ Ax=b\}\), define \(g(\lambda,
u)=\inf_x igl(f_0(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i f_i(x)+
u^{\mathsf T}(Ax-b) igr)\), with all extended-real expressions well-defined. If \(\lambda\ge0\), then \(g(\lambda,
u)\le f_0(x)\) for every feasible \(x\), without convexity, a constraint qualification, or attainment. The sign restriction is essential: for \(\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}0\) with redundant constraint \(-1\le0\), \(\lambda=-1\) gives \(g(-1)=1>p^*=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak duality needs no convexity or regularity, but the inequality multipliers must have the sign dictated by the Lagrangian convention; a wrong sign can destroy the bound.
assumptions_latex: The convention is minimization with constraints \(f_i(x)\le0\) and Lagrangian terms \(\lambda_i f_i(x)\).
The displayed extended-real sums are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda\ge0\Longrightarrow g(\lambda,\nu)\le p^*\); without the compatible sign restriction, this implication can fail.

children.title: Primal Upper-Bound Interface
children.top_down_role: Primal feasible values interpreted as bounds relative to the dual problem.

assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the primal feasible set and \(p^*=\inf_{x\in F}f_0(x)\).
\(g:\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R^q\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is a Lagrange dual function satisfying weak duality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: With \(u=f_0(\widehat x)\), \(p^*\le u\); moreover, every \((\lambda,\nu)\in\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R^q\) satisfies \(g(\lambda,\nu)\le p^*\le u\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A feasible primal point with finite objective value certifies an upper bound for a minimization problem.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be the primal feasible set and let \(p^*=\inf_{x\in F}f_0(x)\). If \(\widehat x\in F\) and \(f_0(\widehat x)\in\mathbb R\), then \((\widehat x,u)\), where \(u=f_0(\widehat x)\), is a primal upper-bound certificate because \[p^*\le u.\] If \(g:\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R^q\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is the associated Lagrange dual function, then weak duality also gives, for every \((\lambda,\nu)\in\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R^q\), \[g(\lambda,\nu)\le p^*\le f_0(\widehat x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal-feasible point with finite objective value certifies that value as an upper bound on the primal infimum. Together with any Lagrange-dual value, it brackets the primal optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal Upper-Bound Interface

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Best Feasible-Point Upper Bound and Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structure and exactness of upper bounds furnished by primal-feasible points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_0:F\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), \(p^*=\inf_{x\in F}f_0(x)\), and \(U=\{f_0(x):x\in F,\ f_0(x)<+\infty\}\). Then every \(u\in U\) satisfies \(p^*\le u\), and \(\inf U=p^*\) under \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). If \(p^*\in\mathbb R\), then \(p^*\in U\) exactly when the infimum is attained. Among finitely many incumbent values, their minimum is the strongest resulting upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite feasible objective values are upper bounds whose infimum is the primal value. A finite exact feasible-point bound exists exactly when the minimum is attained, and the best incumbent is the one with smallest objective value.
assumptions_latex: \(p^*=\inf_{x\in F}f_0(x)\) is interpreted in the extended-real sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf U=p^*\), and if \(p^*\in\mathbb R\), then \(p^*\in U\iff\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f_0(x)\ne\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: finite objective values furnished by primal-feasible points

children.title: Infinite-Value Bound Regimes
children.top_down_role: Bound interpretation when primal or dual optimal values are extended-valued.

knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Value Bound Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-duality implications when primal or dual optimal values are infinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Adopt 
\(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\) and 
\(\sup\varnothing=-\infty\). Weak duality 
\(d^*\le p^*\) remains meaningful in the extended reals. If 
\(d^*=+\infty\), then necessarily 
\(p^*=+\infty\); thus no primal-feasible point can have finite objective value. If 
\(p^*=-\infty\), then necessarily 
\(d^*=-\infty\). In contrast, 
\(p^*=+\infty\) alone does not determine 
\(d^*\), and 
\(d^*=-\infty\) alone does not determine 
\(p^*\). Expressions such as 
\(p^*-d^*\) are left undefined when they involve 
\(+\infty-(+\infty)\) or 
\((-\infty)-(-\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extended-real weak duality forces a positive-infinite dual value to imply a positive-infinite primal value, and a negative-infinite primal value to imply a negative-infinite dual value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^*=+\infty\Rightarrow p^*=+\infty\) and \(p^*=-\infty\Rightarrow d^*=-\infty\).

children.title: Strong-Duality Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes supporting equality of primal and dual optimal values.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Duality as Finite Value Equality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of strong duality independently of optimizer existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a primal minimization problem with value \(p^*\) and a dual maximization problem with value \(d^*\), finite strong duality holds when \[p^*=d^*\in\mathbb R.\] This is a statement about optimal values and, without a separate existence conclusion, does not assert that either extremum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong duality means equality of the finite primal and dual values; optimizer existence is a separate property.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual values \(p^*\) and \(d^*\) are defined in the extended reals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Finite strong duality}\iff p^*=d^*\in\mathbb R.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Duality as Finite Value Equality
Strong-Duality Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Slater-type sufficient regime for equality of finite primal and dual values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a finite-dimensional convex program minimizing 
\(f_0(x)\) subject to 
\(f_i(x)\le 0\) and 
\(Ax=b\), where all objective and inequality functions are proper, closed, and convex. If the primal value is finite and there exists 
\(\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}(\bigcap_{i=0}^m\operatorname{dom}f_i)\) satisfying 
\(A\bar x=b\) and 
\(f_i(\bar x)<0\) for every inequality constraint, then the Lagrange dual has no value gap:
\[d^*=p^*\in\mathbb R.\]
Under this constraint qualification, the dual supremum is also attained whenever the standard finite-dimensional multiplier conclusion applies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relative-interior strictly feasible point, together with a finite primal value, is a standard sufficient regime for equal primal and dual values and dual attainment.
assumptions_latex: \(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_m\) are proper closed convex functions on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^*=p^*\in\mathbb R\), with attainment of the dual supremum under the stated finite-dimensional Slater regime.

source_refs.locator: 5.3.1. Strong Duality Theorem - Inequality Constraints p. 168

source_witnesses.locator: 5.3.1. Strong Duality Theorem - Inequality Constraints p. 168

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-gap conclusion is a recognizable finite-dimensional Slater-type result, and the condition kind fits the regime container. However, the exact relative-interior formulation over the intersection of all effective domains and the asserted dual attainment require inspection of the cited theorem. The phrase about attainment whenever a standard multiplier conclusion applies is not itself a precise hypothesis. Source uncertainty therefore affects the theorem's hypotheses and conclusion.

children.title: Primal Attainment
children.top_down_role: Existence of primal optimal solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment of the primal infimum by a feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let 
\(F\) be the primal feasible set and define 
\(p^*=\inf_{x\in F}f_0(x)\) in the extended reals. The primal problem attains its optimal value if there exists 
\(x^*\in F\) such that 
\[f_0(x^*)=p^*.\]
When 
\(p^*\in\mathbb R\), this is equivalent to the primal solution set 
\(X^*=\{x\in F:f_0(x)=p^*\}\) being nonempty. Primal feasibility and finiteness of 
\(p^*\) alone do not imply attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal attainment means that some feasible point realizes the primal infimum; for a finite value, equivalently the primal solution set is nonempty.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the primal feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X^*\ne\varnothing\), equivalently \(\exists x^*\in F\) with \(f_0(x^*)=p^*\).

F(x,0)=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in X,\ g(x)\leq0,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\text{ has compact level sets}

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment of the Lagrange-dual supremum by feasible multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let 
\(D\) be the dual feasible set and define 
\(d^*=\sup_{(\lambda,\nu)\in D}g(\lambda,\nu)\). The dual problem attains its optimal value if there exists 
\((\lambda^*,\nu^*)\in D\) such that 
\[g(\lambda^*,\nu^*)=d^*.\]
When 
\(d^*\in\mathbb R\), this is equivalent to the dual solution set 
\(Y^*=\{(\lambda,\nu)\in D:g(\lambda,\nu)=d^*\}\) being nonempty. Equality 
\(d^*=p^*\) does not by itself imply dual attainment.

children.top_down_role: Simultaneous existence of compatible primal and dual optimizers.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) and \(D\) are the primal and dual feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
Joint attainment is equivalent to \(X^*
e\varnothing\) and \(Y^*
e\varnothing\); if additionally \(p^*=d^*\), then every \(x^*\in X^*\) and \((\lambda^*,
u^*)\in Y^*\) satisfy \(f_0(x^*)-g(\lambda^*,
u^*)=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of simultaneous realization of finite primal and dual optimal values.

source_refs.locator: 5.3. Convex Programming Duality p. 167

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) and \(D\) be the primal and dual feasible sets, let \(p^*=\inf_{x\in F}f_0(x)\in\mathbb R\), and let \(d^*=\sup_{(\lambda,
u)\in D}g(\lambda,
u)\in\mathbb R\). Define \[X^*=\{x\in F:f_0(x)=p^*\},\qquad Y^*=\{(\lambda,
u)\in D:g(\lambda,
u)=d^*\}.\] The primal and dual problems are jointly attained when \[X^*
e\varnothing\qquad	ext{and}\qquad Y^*
e\varnothing.\] Equivalently, there exist \(x^*\in F\) and \((\lambda^*,
u^*)\in D\) satisfying \(f_0(x^*)=p^*\) and \(g(\lambda^*,
u^*)=d^*\). If strong duality also holds, then \[f_0(x^*)-g(\lambda^*,
u^*)=p^*-d^*=0.\] Joint attainment alone does not imply \(p^*=d^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint primal-dual attainment means that both the primal infimum and the dual supremum are realized. If strong duality also holds, the attained objective values coincide; joint attainment alone does not assert value equality.

children.title: One-Sided Attainment Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cases where an optimizer exists on only one side of a primal-dual pair.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical classification of primal-only and dual-only attainment without asserting value equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X^*\) and \(Y^*\) be the primal and dual solution sets. One-sided attainment holds exactly when one, but not both, of these sets is nonempty: \[(X^*\ne\varnothing\ \wedge\ Y^*=\varnothing)\ \vee\ (X^*=\varnothing\ \wedge\ Y^*\ne\varnothing).\] The first alternative is primal-only attainment and the second is dual-only attainment. This status condition alone imposes no equality or inequality beyond the weak-duality relation between \(p^*\) and \(d^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One-sided attainment means exactly one of the primal and dual solution sets is nonempty; it is logically separate from the size of the duality gap.
assumptions_latex: \(X^*\) and \(Y^*\) are the primal and dual solution sets.
The associated primal and dual values obey their usual weak-duality ordering.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (X^*\ne\varnothing)\mathbin{\oplus}(Y^*\ne\varnothing).
knowledge_statements.title: Exclusive One-Sided Attainment Status
One-Sided Attainment Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal and dual attainment are logically independent, even under zero value gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For finite optimal values, primal-only attainment means 
\(X^*\ne\varnothing\) and 
\(Y^*=\varnothing\), while dual-only attainment means 
\(X^*=\varnothing\) and 
\(Y^*\ne\varnothing\). These regimes are distinct from a value gap: either can occur while 
\(p^*=d^*\). Thus strong duality, primal attainment, and dual attainment are separate predicates unless an existence theorem or constraint qualification links them. In a primal-only zero-gap regime, an optimal primal point exists but no dual multiplier realizes the common value; the dual-only case is symmetric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exactly one side may attain even when primal and dual values coincide; value equality and existence of optimizers are separate properties.
assumptions_latex: \(X^*\) and \(Y^*\) are the primal and dual solution sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((X^*\ne\varnothing,\,Y^*=\varnothing)\) or \((X^*=\varnothing,\,Y^*\ne\varnothing)\) may coexist with \(p^*=d^*\).

source_refs.locator: 5.3.4. Duality and Existence of Optimal Primal Solutions p. 176

source_witnesses.locator: 5.3.4. Duality and Existence of Optimal Primal Solutions p. 176

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The logical definitions of primal-only and dual-only attainment are clear, but the substantive claim that each one-sided regime can occur with a zero duality gap requires examples or a source explicitly supporting both directions. The cited existence section may support only particular primal-existence implications, and the available inventory does not establish the asserted symmetry.

children.title: Positive Duality Gaps
children.top_down_role: Finite primal-dual value separation.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Duality Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite strict separation between primal and dual optimal values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose the primal and dual optimal values are finite. Their duality gap is
\[\Delta=p^*-d^*.\]
Weak duality gives 
\(\Delta\ge 0\). The primal-dual pair has a positive duality gap precisely when
\[0<\Delta<+\infty,\]
equivalently when 
\(d^*<p^*\) with both values real. In this regime no primal-feasible point and dual-feasible point can have equal objective and dual values, and strong duality fails regardless of whether either optimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive duality gap is the finite strict difference between the primal infimum and dual supremum; it rules out strong duality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta=p^*-d^*>0\), equivalently \(d^*<p^*\).

children.title: Infinite Duality Gaps
children.top_down_role: Value separation involving extended optimal values.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact extended-real value pairs for which the primal-minus-dual gap is well-defined and positive infinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p^*,d^*\in\overline{\mathbb R}\) satisfy weak duality \(d^*\le p^*\). Under the convention that the duality gap is \(\Delta=p^*-d^*\) only when this extended-real subtraction is defined, \[\Delta=+\infty\] exactly when either \(p^*=+\infty\) and \(d^*<+\infty\), or \(d^*=-\infty\) and \(p^*>-\infty\). The pairs \((+\infty,+\infty)\) and \((-\infty,-\infty)\) do not define a gap by subtraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A well-defined infinite duality gap occurs exactly when the ordered primal and dual values are infinitely separated; equal infinities yield an undefined difference, not an infinite gap.
assumptions_latex: The gap is defined by extended-real subtraction only when that subtraction is defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta=+\infty\iff[(p^*=+\infty\land d^*<+\infty)\lor(d^*=-\infty\land p^*>-\infty)].
knowledge_statements.title: Classification of Well-Defined Infinite Separation
Infinite Duality Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-value regimes in which primal and dual bounds are infinitely separated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under weak duality, an infinite duality gap is present when the optimal values are ordered but infinitely separated, namely when
\[(p^*,d^*)\in\bigl(\{+\infty\}\times(\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\})\bigr)\cup\bigl((\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\})\times\{-\infty\}\bigr),\]
excluding the indeterminate pairs 
\((+\infty,+\infty)\) and 
\((-\infty,-\infty)\). Equivalently, the extended gap 
\(p^*-d^*\) is well-defined and equals 
\(+\infty\). This can arise from primal infeasibility, primal unbounded separation from the dual bound, dual infeasibility, or failure of regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infinite gap occurs when the ordered extended-real optimal values are infinitely separated and their difference is well-defined as positive infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^*-d^*=+\infty\) whenever this extended-real difference is defined.

children.title: Primal Nonattainment
children.top_down_role: Finite or limiting primal values without a primal optimizer.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Nonattainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite primal infimum approached by feasible points but realized by none.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let 
\(F\ne\varnothing\) and suppose 
\(p^*=\inf_{x\in F}f_0(x)\in\mathbb R\). Primal nonattainment means
\[\{x\in F:f_0(x)=p^*\}=\varnothing.\]
Equivalently, for every 
\(x\in F\), one has 
\(f_0(x)>p^*\), while for every 
\(\varepsilon>0\) there exists 
\(x_\varepsilon\in F\) satisfying 
\(f_0(x_\varepsilon)<p^*+\varepsilon\). Thus minimizing sequences exist, but no feasible limit point realizes the infimum. Nonattainment may coexist with the zero-gap equality 
\(p^*=d^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal nonattainment means a finite infimum is approached arbitrarily closely by feasible points but is achieved by no feasible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in F:f_0(x)=p^*\}=\varnothing\), although \(\forall\varepsilon>0\;\exists x_\varepsilon\in F\) with \(f_0(x_\varepsilon)<p^*+\varepsilon\).

source_refs.locator: 5.3.4. Duality and Existence of Optimal Primal Solutions p. 176

source_witnesses.locator: 5.3.4. Duality and Existence of Optimal Primal Solutions p. 176

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convex Objective with Unattained Infimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal unconstrained example showing that closed convexity alone does not ensure primal attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}e^x.\] The objective is finite, continuous, closed, and strictly convex. Its infimum is \(p^*=0\), approached as \(x\to-\infty\), but \(e^x>0\) for every real \(x\). Hence \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R}e^x=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The continuous strictly convex exponential objective has infimum zero, approached only at minus infinity, and has no minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in\mathbb R}e^x=0\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R}e^x=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Objective with Unattained Infimum

children.title: Dual Nonattainment
children.top_down_role: Finite or limiting dual values without a dual optimizer.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary sufficient condition ruling out finite dual nonattainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the dual feasible set \(D\) is nonempty and compact and the proper objective \(g:D\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\) is upper semicontinuous, then \(g\) attains its supremum on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper upper-semicontinuous dual objective on a nonempty compact feasible set attains its supremum.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is proper and upper semicontinuous on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in D}g(y)\ne\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Compactness Boundary Excluding Dual Nonattainment

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic finite-valued dual nonattainment independent of a specialized dual representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\ne\varnothing\), let \(g:D\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\), and suppose \(d^*:=\sup_{y\in D}g(y)\in\mathbb R\). Dual nonattainment means \[\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in D}g(y)=\varnothing.\] Equivalently, \(g(y)<d^*\) for every \(y\in D\), while for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(y_\varepsilon\in D\) with \(g(y_\varepsilon)>d^*-\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite dual supremum is unattained exactly when every dual-feasible point falls strictly below it although epsilon-optimal dual points exist at every tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in D}g(y)=\varnothing\iff(\forall y\in D,\ g(y)<d^*)\land(\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists y_\varepsilon\in D,\ g(y_\varepsilon)>d^*-\varepsilon).
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Characterization of Dual Nonattainment
Dual Nonattainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value equality does not imply existence of an optimal dual multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the convex program 
\[p^\star=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}\{x:x^2\le 0\},\]
the feasible set is \(\{0\}\), so \(p^\star=0\) is attained. Its Lagrange dual function is
\[q(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}(x+\lambda x^2)=\begin{cases}-1/(4\lambda),&\lambda>0,\\-\infty,&\lambda=0,\end{cases}\]
for \(\lambda\ge0\). Consequently \(d^\star=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}q(\lambda)=0=p^\star\), but no \(\lambda\ge0\) attains the dual supremum. Thus dual nonattainment can occur even with primal attainment and zero duality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-dimensional convex program attains its primal optimum and has zero duality gap, yet its dual supremum is approached only as the multiplier diverges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^\star=d^\star=0\), \(p^\star\) is attained, and \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{\lambda\ge0}q(\lambda)=\varnothing\).

children.title: Zero-Gap Nonattainment
children.top_down_role: Equal primal-dual values without complete optimizer existence.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhaustive optimizer-existence regimes when the primal and dual values coincide finitely.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a primal-dual pair satisfy weak duality and \(p^*=d^*\in\mathbb R\). Exactly one of the following holds: both optima are attained; only the primal optimum is attained; only the dual optimum is attained; or neither optimum is attained. Zero-gap nonattainment comprises the latter three cases. In any such case, value equality alone does not provide an attained primal-dual certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a common finite value, primal and dual attainment are separate questions; zero-gap nonattainment means that at least one optimizer set is empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Zero-gap nonattainment}\iff P^*=\varnothing\ \lor\ D^*=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Zero-Gap Attainment-Status Partition
Zero-Gap Nonattainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero value gap can coexist with failure of primal or dual attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p^\star=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\) and \(d^\star=\sup_{y\in Y}g(y)\) be a primal-dual convex pair satisfying weak duality. A zero-gap nonattainment regime is characterized by
\[p^\star=d^\star\in\mathbb R,\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x)=\varnothing\quad\text{or}\quad \operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in Y}g(y)=\varnothing.\]
Hence equality of optimal values alone supplies neither a primal optimizer nor a dual certificate; attainment must be established separately by compactness, coercivity, closedness, or a suitable constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal and dual values may coincide finitely even though at least one side has no optimizer; value equality alone is not an attainment certificate.
assumptions_latex: Weak duality holds: \(g(y)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\) and \(y\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^\star=d^\star\) does not imply nonemptiness of both optimal-solution sets.
