children.title: Slater-Type Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Strict-feasibility qualification families for convex inequality systems.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Slater Regularity Depends on the Constraint Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent feasible sets can have different Slater status.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The feasible set \(\{0\}\subset\mathbb R\) has the affine representation \(x=0\), which satisfies the Slater condition because affine equalities require exact feasibility but no strict inequality. The equivalent convex-inequality representation \(x^2\leq0\) has no point satisfying \(x^2<0\), so Slater's condition fails. Hence Slater regularity is a property of a chosen constraint representation, not only of its feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same singleton feasible set satisfies Slater when represented by an affine equality but fails Slater when represented by x squared at most zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:x=0\}=\{x:x^2\leq0\}=\{0\}\), but only the affine-equality representation is Slater regular.
knowledge_statements.title: Slater Regularity Depends on the Constraint Representation
Slater-Type Qualifications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional strict-feasibility condition for convex inequalities and affine equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider minimizing a proper convex function \(f_0\) over \(x\in D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), subject to convex inequalities \(f_i(x)\le0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\) and affine equalities \(Ax=b\), where \(D\) is convex. The Slater condition holds if there exists \(\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}D\) such that
\[f_i(\bar x)<0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad A\bar x=b,\]
and every \(f_i(\bar x)\) is finite. The point \(\bar x\) is a Slater point; the relative interior permits \(D\) to lie in a proper affine subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Slater regularity requires a relative-interior feasible point satisfying every convex inequality strictly and every affine equality exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}D\) with \(f_i(\bar x)<0\) for all \(i\) and \(A\bar x=b\).

children.title: Relative-Interior Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Regularity conditions expressed within affine hulls of convex domains or feasible sets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional perturbation-set formulation of a relative-interior constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:D\to\mathbb R\) be convex, and let \(x\mapsto Ax-b\) be affine. Define the convex upper perturbation set \[C=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^p:\exists x\in D,\ f_i(x)\le u_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ v=Ax-b\}.\] The nominal-perturbation relative-interior qualification is \[(0,0)\in\operatorname{ri}C.\] Relative interior is taken in \(\operatorname{aff}C\), so redundant or lower-dimensional perturbation coordinates do not by themselves invalidate the condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative-interior qualification holds when the nominal zero perturbation lies in the relative interior of the achievable upper perturbation set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (0,0)\in\operatorname{ri}C.

notation.meaning: Upper perturbation set for inequality bounds and equality residuals
Interior relative to the affine hull of C

knowledge_statements.title: Nominal-Perturbation Relative-Interior Qualification
Relative-Interior Qualifications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric qualification expressed through the relative interior of the convex perturbation set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For convex \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), convex finite-valued constraint functions \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\) on \(D\), and an affine residual \(Ax-b\), define
\[C=\{(u,v):\exists x\in D,\ f_i(x)\le u_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ v=Ax-b\}.\]
The relative-interior qualification at the unperturbed problem is
\[(0,0)\in\operatorname{ri}C.\]
It requires the zero perturbation to be interior relative to \(\operatorname{aff}C\), rather than interior in the full ambient perturbation space, and therefore accommodates redundant equalities and lower-dimensional perturbation geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The qualification holds when the zero right-hand-side perturbation lies in the relative interior of the convex achievable-perturbation set.
assumptions_latex: The equality residual \(x\mapsto Ax-b\) is affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((0,0)\in\operatorname{ri}C\).

relative interior in the affine hull of the perturbation set

children.title: Core Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Algebraic-interior regularity conditions for convex program geometry.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixes the algebraic-interior convention used for core-based perturbation regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a real vector space \(X\), and let \(c_0\in C\). Under the convention used here, \[c_0\in\operatorname{core}C\iff \forall d\in X\ \exists\varepsilon_d>0\ \forall |t|<\varepsilon_d:\ c_0+td\in C,\] whereas \[c_0\in\operatorname{icr}C\iff \forall d\in\operatorname{span}(C-C)\ \exists\varepsilon_d>0\ \forall |t|<\varepsilon_d:\ c_0+td\in C.\] A core-based qualification must specify which membership condition is imposed; the intrinsic-core version tests only directions generated by the perturbation set and invokes no topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Core regularity permits small two-sided motion in every ambient direction, while intrinsic-core regularity tests only directions generated by the convex perturbation set.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space and \(c_0\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c_0\in\operatorname{core}C\ \text{or}\ c_0\in\operatorname{icr}C\ \text{according to the explicitly selected qualification}.

notation.meaning: Algebraic interior with respect to all ambient directions
Intrinsic algebraic core with respect to span(C-C)

knowledge_statements.title: Core and Intrinsic-Core Qualifications
Core Qualifications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic regularity condition suitable when topological interior is unavailable or too restrictive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a convex perturbation set in a real vector space and let \(c_0\in C\) represent the unperturbed problem. The intrinsic-core qualification is
\[c_0\in\operatorname{icr}C,\]
meaning that for every \(d\in\operatorname{span}(C-C)\) there exists \(\varepsilon_d>0\) such that
\[c_0+t d\in C\qquad\text{for every }t\in[0,\varepsilon_d].\]
This condition is algebraic: it tests feasible motion in every direction of the linear hull generated by \(C-C\), without invoking a topology on the perturbation space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A core qualification requires locally feasible motion from the nominal perturbation in every direction intrinsic to the convex perturbation set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c_0\in\operatorname{icr}C\).

notation.meaning: intrinsic algebraic core of the convex set
space of intrinsic directions of the set

children.title: Lower-Dimensional Feasible Geometry

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Dimensional Feasible Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative interior detects regularity inside the feasible affine hull when ambient interior is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and convex, then \(\operatorname{ri}F\ne\varnothing\). If additionally \(\dim(\operatorname{aff}F)<n\), then
\[\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^n}F=\varnothing,\qquad \operatorname{ri}F=\operatorname{int}_{\operatorname{aff}F}F\ne\varnothing.\]
Thus an ambient-interior qualification necessarily fails for every lower-dimensional feasible set, whereas a relative-interior qualification can remain valid after affine equalities, redundant coordinates, or facial restrictions reduce the effective dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty finite-dimensional convex set has relative-interior points, even when lying in a proper affine subspace and having empty ambient interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^n}F=\varnothing\) while \(\operatorname{ri}F=\operatorname{int}_{\operatorname{aff}F}F\ne\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: affine hull of the feasible set
interior relative to the affine hull

children.title: Relative-Interior–Core Comparison
children.top_down_role: Relationships between topological and algebraic interior-based qualifications.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Intrinsic Core Can Exceed Relative Interior in Infinite Dimensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional boundary for the finite-dimensional relative-interior–core equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be an infinite-dimensional normed real vector space admitting a discontinuous linear functional \(\varphi:X\to\mathbb R\), and set \(C=\{x\in X:\varphi(x)\leq1\}\). Then \(C\) is convex and \(\operatorname{aff}C=X\). Its intrinsic algebraic core is
\[\operatorname{icr}C=\{x:\varphi(x)<1\},\]
which is nonempty, whereas its norm-topological relative interior is empty. Thus \(\operatorname{icr}C=\operatorname{ri}C\) is not an unrestricted infinite-dimensional identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A halfspace defined by a discontinuous linear functional has nonempty intrinsic core but empty norm-topological relative interior.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an infinite-dimensional normed real vector space
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{icr}C=\{\varphi<1\}\neq\varnothing\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{ri}C=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Intrinsic Core Can Exceed Relative Interior in Infinite Dimensions
Relative-Interior–Core Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional equivalence between relative interior and intrinsic algebraic core.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex. Define its intrinsic core using directions in \(L=\operatorname{span}(C-C)\). Then
\[\operatorname{icr}C=\operatorname{ri}C.\]
Equivalently, \(x\in C\) belongs to \(\operatorname{ri}C\) exactly when, for every \(d\in L\), some \(\varepsilon_d>0\) satisfies \(x+t d\in C\) for all sufficiently small \(t\in[0,\varepsilon_d]\). This equivalence is finite-dimensional; in general infinite-dimensional spaces, algebraic-core and topological relative-interior conditions need not coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonempty finite-dimensional convex sets, intrinsic core and relative interior coincide; this equivalence can fail in infinite-dimensional spaces.
assumptions_latex: Core directions are taken relative to \(\operatorname{span}(C-C)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{icr}C=\operatorname{ri}C\).

notation.meaning: intrinsic direction space of the convex set

children.title: Polyhedral Constraint Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Regularity regimes for programs whose relevant constraint geometry is polyhedral.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Constraint Qualifications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualification separating polyhedral constraints from constraints requiring strict feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a convex program over a nonempty polyhedral set \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), with proper convex inequality functions \(f_i\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Let \(P\) index the polyhedral convex functions and let \(N\) index the remaining functions. A polyhedral constraint qualification holds when there exists
\[\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}X\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_i)\]
such that
\[f_i(\bar x)\le 0\quad(i\in P),\qquad f_i(\bar x)<0\quad(i\in N).\]
Thus strict feasibility is imposed only on the nonpolyhedral inequalities; active polyhedral inequalities are permitted at the qualifying point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a common relative-domain point, polyhedral inequalities need only be feasible, while nonpolyhedral convex inequalities must hold strictly.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is proper convex, and \(f_i\) is polyhedral for every \(i\in P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}X\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_i)\) satisfying \(f_i(\bar x)\le0\) for \(i\in P\) and \(f_i(\bar x)<0\) for \(i\in N\).

children.title: Partially Polyhedral Qualifications

knowledge_statements.title: Partially Polyhedral Qualifications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized Slater condition for programs containing both polyhedral and nonpolyhedral components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be the nonempty polyhedral feasible set determined by affine equalities, a polyhedral domain, and polyhedral convex inequalities. Suppose additional proper convex functions \(g_1,\ldots,g_r\) impose \(g_j(x)\le0\). The partially polyhedral qualification holds if there exists \(\bar x\) such that
\[\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}F\cap\bigcap_{j=1}^r\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g_j),\qquad g_j(\bar x)<0\quad(j=1,\ldots,r).\]
No strict slack is required for the polyhedral constraints already incorporated into \(F\); strict feasibility is reserved for the nonpolyhedral block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Build the polyhedral feasible set first, then require a point in its relative interior and in the relative domains of the remaining functions that strictly satisfies every nonpolyhedral inequality.
assumptions_latex: All nonpolyhedral restrictions are represented by \(g_j(x)\le0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}F\cap\bigcap_{j=1}^r\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g_j)\) such that \(g_j(\bar x)<0\) for every \(j=1,\ldots,r\).

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Automatic-Regularity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility replaces strict feasibility for finite-dimensional polyhedral convex programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[p^\star=\inf_{x\in X} f_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad f_i(x)\le0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m,\]
where \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is polyhedral and every \(f_i\), including \(f_0\), is a proper closed polyhedral convex function. If the problem is feasible and \(p^\star\in\mathbb R\), then its perturbation value function is polyhedral and closed at the origin. Consequently, the Lagrange dual satisfies \(d^\star=p^\star\) and admits an optimal nonnegative multiplier. No Slater point with strict slack is required in this fully polyhedral regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible finite-dimensional polyhedral convex program with finite value has strong Lagrange duality and an optimal nonnegative multiplier without requiring strict feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_m\) are proper closed polyhedral convex functions.
The primal problem is feasible and \(p^\star\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^\star=p^\star\), and the Lagrange-dual optimal-multiplier set is nonempty.

children.title: Mixed-Geometry Qualification Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits of polyhedral regularity when nonpolyhedral components remain active.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of Automatic Regularity in Mixed Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit of fully polyhedral automatic regularity after adding an unqualified nonpolyhedral constraint block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron and let additional constraints \(g_j(x)\le0\) be imposed by proper convex functions that need not be polyhedral. Feasibility of
\[
x\in F,\qquad g_j(x)\le0
\]
alone does not guarantee Lagrange-multiplier existence, dual attainment, or KKT necessity. Such conclusions require an applicable qualification for the nonpolyhedral block, for example a common relative-domain point satisfying \(g_j(x)<0\) for every nonpolyhedral inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Automatic regularity of a polyhedral block does not survive the addition of an arbitrary active nonpolyhedral block; feasibility alone no longer guarantees multipliers or dual attainment.
assumptions_latex: No strict-feasibility or other qualification is assumed for the nonpolyhedral block.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Multiplier existence, dual attainment, and KKT necessity are not guaranteed by feasibility alone.

notation.meaning: feasible set supplied by the polyhedral constraint block

knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Automatic Regularity in Mixed Geometry
Mixed-Geometry Qualification Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral automatic regularity does not extend to an active nonpolyhedral constraint without qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The implication from feasibility to multiplier existence fails when a nonpolyhedral constraint is added without strict feasibility. Indeed,
\[\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}\{x:x^2\le0\}\]
has the polyhedral objective \(x\mapsto x\) and the nonpolyhedral convex constraint \(x^2\le0\). Its only feasible point is \(0\), at which the constraint has no strict slack. For \(\lambda>0\), the dual function equals \(-1/(4\lambda)\); hence its supremum is \(0\), but no finite \(\lambda\ge0\) attains it. The nonpolyhedral block therefore requires an additional qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding one active nonpolyhedral constraint can destroy automatic multiplier existence: a simple quadratic constraint yields zero gap but dual nonattainment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^\star=d^\star=0\), but the dual optimum is not attained because the nonpolyhedral constraint lacks strict feasibility.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perturbation Closure and Subgradient Consequence Bridge
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract finite-dimensional mechanism separating value equality from dual attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(v:\mathbb R^k\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be the proper convex perturbation value function of a convex primal problem, with \(p^\star=v(0)\in\mathbb R\), and define
\[
d^\star=\sup_{y\in\mathbb R^k}\{-v^*(y)\}=v^{**}(0).
\]
If \(v\) is lower semicontinuous at \(0\), then \(d^\star=p^\star\). If \(\partial v(0)\ne\varnothing\), every \(y^\star\in\partial v(0)\) satisfies
\[
v(0)+v^*(y^\star)=0,
\]
and therefore attains the perturbation dual. Thus closure at the reference parameter yields value equality, while a subgradient supplies an attained dual multiplier; value equality alone does not imply attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower semicontinuity of the perturbation value function gives zero duality gap, while a subgradient at the reference parameter gives an attaining dual multiplier. The two conclusions are distinct.
assumptions_latex: \(v\) is a proper convex perturbation value function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Lower semicontinuity at \(0\) implies \(d^\star=p^\star\); nonempty \(\partial v(0)\) implies dual attainment.

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate of the value function

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation Closure and Subgradient Consequence Bridge
Qualification Consequence Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional route from convex constraint qualification to value equality and multiplier existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a finite-dimensional convex program with proper closed convex objective, convex inequalities, affine equalities, and finite optimal value \(p^\star\). If an applicable Slater, relative-interior, or partially polyhedral qualification holds, then the perturbation value function is closed and subdifferentiable at the unperturbed parameter. Consequently
\[d^\star=p^\star\]
and the Lagrange dual admits an optimal multiplier. If a primal optimizer \(x^\star\) also exists, some optimal multiplier together with \(x^\star\) satisfies primal feasibility, dual feasibility, complementary slackness, and Lagrangian stationarity; these conditions form an optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A suitable convex constraint qualification yields zero duality gap and an optimal multiplier; with primal attainment, the pair supplies a KKT certificate.
assumptions_latex: The convex program is finite-dimensional and has \(p^\star\in\mathbb R\).
The objective and constraint functions are proper and closed on their common domain.
A Slater, relative-interior, or applicable partially polyhedral qualification holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^\star=p^\star\) and the dual optimum is attained; if \(x^\star\) exists, a primal-dual KKT certificate exists.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Qualification Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional failure of a relative-interior Slater condition; other constraint qualifications may still hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the convex program \(\inf\{f_0(x):f_i(x)\le 0,\ i=1,\ldots,m,\ Ax=b\}\), the relative-interior Slater condition fails precisely when \[\left\{x\in\bigcap_{i=0}^m\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_i):Ax=b,\ f_i(x)<0\ \text{for every }i=1,\ldots,m\right\}=\varnothing.\] This condition does not assert primal infeasibility and does not by itself imply a duality gap or nonexistence of multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative-interior Slater condition fails when no point lying in every individual domain's relative interior satisfies the affine equations and all inequalities strictly; feasible points may nevertheless exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in\bigcap_{i=0}^m\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_i):Ax=b,\ f_i(x)<0\ \forall i=1,\ldots,m\}=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp nonimplication example for failure of strict feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R}x^2\) subject to \(x^2\le0\). The unique feasible point is \(x^*=0\), and strict feasibility fails. For \(L(x,\lambda)=(1+\lambda)x^2\), however, \(q(\lambda)=0\) for every \(\lambda\ge0\). Thus \(p^*=d^*=0\), the dual optimum is attained, and \((x^*,\lambda)=(0,0)\) satisfies KKT.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Slater failure can coexist with attained strong duality and a valid KKT multiplier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p^*=d^*=0,\quad 0\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{\lambda\ge0}q(\lambda),\quad (x^*,\lambda)=(0,0)\text{ satisfies KKT}.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unique optimum is \(x^*=0\), but no \(\lambda\ge 0\) satisfies \(0=1+2\lambda x^*\).

source_refs.locator: 5.3. Convex Programming Duality p. 167

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the convex program \[\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}} x\quad\text{subject to}\quad x^2\le 0,\] the feasible set is \(\{0\}\), so \(x^*=0\) is the unique optimum. Slater qualification fails because no point satisfies \(x^2<0\). A KKT multiplier would have to satisfy \(\lambda\ge 0\), complementary slackness, and stationarity \(0=1+2\lambda x^*\). At \(x^*=0\), stationarity becomes \(0=1\), which is impossible. Hence primal optimality need not admit any finite Lagrange-multiplier certificate after constraint qualification is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without constraint qualification, a convex optimum may exist but admit no finite KKT multiplier; minimizing x subject to x-squared at most zero is an example.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar family demonstrating multiplier instability near a qualification-failing limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\varepsilon>0\), consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R}x\) subject to \(x^2\le\varepsilon\). Its optimizer is \(x_\varepsilon=-\sqrt\varepsilon\). Stationarity for the active constraint gives \(1+2\lambda_\varepsilon x_\varepsilon=0\), hence \(\lambda_\varepsilon=(2\sqrt\varepsilon)^{-1}\). Therefore \(\lambda_\varepsilon\to+\infty\) as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), while the limiting problem has optimizer zero and no finite KKT multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multipliers of strictly feasible relaxations can diverge as they approach a qualification-failing problem with no finite multiplier.
assumptions_latex: The inequality uses the standard nonnegative multiplier convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_\varepsilon=-\sqrt\varepsilon,\qquad \lambda_\varepsilon=\frac{1}{2\sqrt\varepsilon}\longrightarrow+\infty\quad(\varepsilon\downarrow0).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(L(x,\lambda)=x+\lambda x^2\), the dual function is \[q(\lambda)=\inf_x L(x,\lambda)=\begin{cases}-1/(4\lambda),&\lambda>0,\\-\infty,&\lambda=0.\end{cases}\] Therefore \(\sup_{\lambda\ge 0}q(\lambda)=0\), equal to the primal value, but no finite \(\lambda\) attains this supremum. Thus failure of constraint qualification can destroy dual attainment even when the primal optimum exists and the duality gap is zero. More generally, absent a suitable qualification, strong duality and dual attainment are guarantees that may both be lost, not conclusions whose failure is automatic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint-qualification failure can cause dual nonattainment even with zero duality gap, as the scalar constraint x-squared at most zero demonstrates.

knowledge_statements.title: Facial-Reduction Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One facial-reduction step for a finite-dimensional conic feasibility system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z=A^*y\in K^*\setminus K^\perp\) satisfy \(\langle b,y\rangle=0\). Then \[S\subseteq F:=K\cap z^\perp,\] and \(F\) is a proper exposed face of \(K\). Thus \(y\) certifies a feasible-set-preserving replacement of \(K\) by the smaller face \(F\). Repeated valid reductions may be used to reach the minimal face containing \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual exposing vector that is orthogonal to the affine right-hand side but not to the whole cone certifies that all feasible points lie in a proper exposed face.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a closed convex cone, \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^p\) is linear, \(b\in\mathbb{R}^p\), and \(S=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\ne\varnothing\).
There exists \(y\in\mathbb{R}^p\) such that \(z=A^*y\in K^*\setminus K^\perp\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\subseteq F:=K\cap z^\perp\), where \(F\) is a proper exposed face of \(K\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(F_0=K\). If \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}F_j=\varnothing\), choose \(y_j\) with \(z_j=A^*y_j\in F_j^*\setminus F_j^\perp\) and \(\langle b,y_j\rangle=0\), and set \(F_{j+1}=F_j\cap z_j^\perp\). Then \(S\subseteq F_{j+1}\subsetneq F_j\). Repeating valid steps terminates at the minimal face \(F_r\) containing \(S\), where \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}F_r\ne\varnothing\), after at most \(\dim(\operatorname{span}K)\) strict dimension reductions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The minimal-face representation of the conic system is \[S=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}=\{x\in F_{\min}:Ax=b\}.\] Because \(S\) is a nonempty convex set and \(F_{\min}\) is its minimal containing face in \(K\), there exists \(\bar x\in S\cap\operatorname{ri}F_{\min}\). Thus the reformulated system is relatively strictly feasible in its natural cone. Replacing \(K\) by \(F_{\min}\) removes directions responsible for the original Slater failure without changing feasible points or primal objective values; corresponding dual constructions must use the dual of the reduced cone within its linear span.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing the original cone by the minimal face containing the feasible set preserves feasibility and yields a relatively strictly feasible constraint representation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(x^*\in\operatorname{dom}f\) globally minimizes \(f\) over \(\mathbb{R}^n\) if and only if \[0\in\partial f(x^*).\] Indeed, the inclusion means exactly that \(f(x)\ge f(x^*)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x^*\), then \(\partial f(x^*)=\{\nabla f(x^*)\}\), so the condition reduces to \(\nabla f(x^*)=0\). Convexity makes these first-order conditions sufficient as well as necessary; no coercivity or strict convexity is required for the equivalence at a given point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point minimizes a proper closed convex function exactly when zero is a subgradient there; in the differentiable case, its gradient is zero.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set-constrained minimization is unconstrained minimization of the extended-valued function \(f+\delta_C\). Consequently, \[x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in\partial(f+\delta_C)(x^*).\] If \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{ri}C\ne\varnothing\), the convex subdifferential sum rule gives \(\partial(f+\delta_C)(x^*)=\partial f(x^*)+N_C(x^*)\). Under this qualification, optimality is therefore equivalent to \[0\in\partial f(x^*)+N_C(x^*).\] The undecomposed condition remains exact even when the stated sum-rule qualification is unavailable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient variational-inequality condition for minimizing a differentiable convex term plus a possibly nonsmooth convex term over a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex, let \(f:Q\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and differentiable on \(Q\), and let \(\Psi:Q\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex. Then \(x^*\in Q\) minimizes \(f+\Psi\) over \(Q\) if and only if
\[
\langle\nabla f(x^*),x-x^*\rangle+\Psi(x)\geq\Psi(x^*)\qquad\forall x\in Q.
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[N_C(x^*)=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle v,x-x^*\rangle\le 0\ \text{for every }x\in C\}.\] Then \(-g\in N_C(x^*)\) is equivalent to the variational inequality \[\langle g,x-x^*\rangle\ge 0\quad\text{for every }x\in C.\] Since \(g\in\partial f(x^*)\), the subgradient inequality yields \(f(x)\ge f(x^*)+\langle g,x-x^*\rangle\ge f(x^*)\) for every \(x\in C\). Hence the pair \((g,-g)\), with \(g\in\partial f(x^*)\) and \(-g\in N_C(x^*)\), is a directly checkable certificate that \(x^*\) minimizes \(f\) over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subgradient whose negative is normal to the feasible set certifies constrained optimality and is equivalent to a variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Optimality Interface

Let \(L=\operatorname{par}(C)\). If \(x^*\in\operatorname{ri}C\), then \(N_C(x^*)=L^\perp\), so constrained optimality is equivalent to \(-
abla f(x^*)\in L^\perp\), or equivalently to vanishing of the gradient component tangent to \(\operatorname{aff}C\). In particular, when \(C\) is full-dimensional and \(x^*\in\operatorname{int}C\), this reduces to \(

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable finite-dimensional convex KKT theorem under Slater qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \[\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} f_0(x)\quad	ext{subject to}\quad f_i(x)\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\quad Ax=b,\] a feasible point \(x^*\) is optimal if and only if there exist \(\lambda^*\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\) and \(
u^*\in\mathbb{R}^p\) such that \[
abla f_0(x^*)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i^*
abla f_i(x^*)+A^*
u^*=0,\qquad \lambda_i^*f_i(x^*)=0\quad	ext{for every }i=1,\ldots,m.\] Together with primal feasibility and \(\lambda^*\ge0\), these are the smooth convex KKT conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under Slater qualification, a feasible point solves the smooth convex program exactly when explicitly dimensioned inequality and equality multipliers satisfy stationarity and complementary slackness.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad f_i(x)\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\quad Ax=b,\] a feasible point \(x^*\) is optimal if and only if there exist \(\lambda^*\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\), \(\nu^*\in\mathbb{R}^p\), \(s_0\in\partial f_0(x^*)\), and \(s_i\in\partial f_i(x^*)\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\) such that \[0=s_0+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i^*s_i+A^*\nu^*,\qquad \lambda_i^*f_i(x^*)=0\quad\text{for every }i=1,\ldots,m.\] These conditions, together with primal feasibility and \(\lambda^*\ge0\), form the nonsmooth convex KKT family.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Calculus Qualification Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex subdifferential sum calculus and its relative-interior qualification boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r\ge 2\) and let \(h_j:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(j=1,\ldots,r\), be proper convex functions. If \(\bigcap_{j=1}^r\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}h_j)\ne\varnothing\), then, at every \(x\in\bigcap_{j=1}^r\operatorname{dom}h_j\), \[\partial\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^r h_j\right)(x)=\sum_{j=1}^r\partial h_j(x).\] Without an applicable qualification, only \[\sum_{j=1}^r\partial h_j(x)\subseteq\partial\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^r h_j\right)(x)\] is automatic, and equality may fail. Consequently, a nonsmooth KKT-necessity argument that decomposes a subdifferential into objective and constraint terms must separately verify the relevant qualification; its conclusion is not guaranteed when that qualification fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common relative-interior domain point makes the convex subdifferential sum rule exact. Without an applicable qualification, only one inclusion is automatic, so a KKT-necessity derivation based on exact subdifferential decomposition may fail.
assumptions_latex: For \(j=1,\ldots,r\), \(h_j:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is a proper convex function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relative-interior condition guarantees the exact finite-dimensional convex subdifferential sum rule; without an applicable qualification, exact decomposition and the associated KKT-necessity argument are not guaranteed.

notation.meaning: Convex subdifferential of a function at a point.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_x f(x)\) subject to \(G(x)\in-K\). A pair \((x^*,\lambda^*)\) is a generalized-inequality KKT certificate when \(G(x^*)\in-K\), \(\lambda^*\in K^*\), \(\nabla f(x^*)+DG(x^*)^*\lambda^*=0\), and \(\langle\lambda^*,G(x^*)\rangle=0\). Cone convexity implies \(G(z)-G(x^*)-DG(x^*)(z-x^*)\in K\) for every \(z\). Consequently, every feasible \(z\) satisfies \(f(z)\ge f(x^*)\), so \(x^*\) is globally optimal. A suitable constraint qualification is needed for the converse assertion that every optimizer has such a multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized-inequality KKT conditions combine cone feasibility, a dual-cone multiplier, stationarity, and zero pairing; in a convex problem they certify global optimality.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad x^2\le0.\] The unique feasible and optimal point is \(x^*=0\), but no \(\lambda\ge0\) satisfies stationarity because \[1+\lambda(2x^*)=1\ne0.\] There is no strictly feasible point, so KKT necessity fails although the problem is convex.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimizer \(x^*=0\) admits no \(\lambda\in K^*\) satisfying generalized KKT stationarity.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Program KKT Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard finite-dimensional primal-dual conic linear programming form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal-dual pair \(P\) and \(D\), a triple \((x^*,y^*,s^*)\) satisfies the conic KKT conditions when \(Ax^*=b\), \(x^*\in K\), \(c-A^*y^*=s^*\in K^*\), and \(\langle x^*,s^*\rangle=0\). Weak duality gives \[\langle c,x^*\rangle-\langle b,y^*\rangle=\langle s^*,x^*\rangle=0.\] Hence \(x^*\) and \((y^*,s^*)\) are globally optimal and have equal objective values. Conversely, attained primal and dual optima having zero duality gap satisfy these conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible primal point and feasible dual point are both optimal when their cone variables are complementary; the zero pairing equals the duality gap.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementary slackness form a verifiable global optimality certificate for the conic primal-dual pair.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(g\in-K\), the normal cone to the feasible cone has the representation \[N_{-K}(g)=K^*\cap g^\perp=\{\lambda\in K^*:\langle\lambda,g\rangle=0\}.\] Thus a generalized-inequality multiplier is geometrically an outward normal to \(-K\) at the constraint value. knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cone-feasible pair \((x,s)\in K\times K^*\) is complementary exactly when \(\langle x,s\rangle=0\). Equivalently, \(s\in K^*\cap x^\perp\) and \(x\in K\cap s^\perp\). Hence each member lies in the exposed face complementary to the other. For \(K=\mathbb{R}_+^n\), this becomes the componentwise regime \(x_i s_i=0\) for every \(i\). For the positive-semidefinite cone, it becomes \(\operatorname{tr}(XS)=0\), equivalently \(XS=0\), for \(X\succeq0\) and \(S\succeq0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone, \(x\in K\), and \(s\in K^*\). A complementary pair \(\langle x,s\rangle=0\) is strictly complementary if there is a face \(F\unlhd K\) such that \[x\in\operatorname{ri}F,\qquad s\in\operatorname{ri}F^\triangle,\qquad F^\triangle:=K^*\cap F^\perp.\] Weak complementarity does not imply strict complementarity: for \(K=\mathbb R_+\), \((x,s)=(0,0)\) is complementary but not strictly complementary.

knowledge_statements.title: KKT Sufficiency for Convex Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global sufficiency of nonsmooth convex KKT conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing \(f_0(x)\) subject to \(f_i(x)\le 0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\) and \(Ax=b\). Let \(x^*\) be feasible. Suppose that there exist \(u_i\in\partial f_i(x^*)\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m\), multipliers \(\lambda_i\ge 0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and \(\nu\in\mathbb{R}^p\) such that \[0=u_0+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i u_i+A^*\nu,\qquad \lambda_i f_i(x^*)=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).\] Then \(f_0(x)\ge f_0(x^*)\) for every feasible \(x\), so \(x^*\) is a global minimizer. This sufficiency direction requires no constraint qualification.

\(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^p\) is linear, \(b\in\mathbb{R}^p\), and \(A^*:\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is its adjoint.
\(x^*\) is feasible, and the displayed subgradients and multipliers exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The convex KKT relations imply that \(x^*\) is a global minimizer, without requiring a constraint qualification.

knowledge_statements.title: KKT Necessity Under Qualification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonsmooth convex KKT necessity under relative-interior Slater qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^*\) minimize \(f_0(x)\) subject to \(f_i(x)\le 0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\) and \(Ax=b\), with \(f_0(x^*)<+\infty\). Under the stated relative-interior Slater condition, there exist \(u_i\in\partial f_i(x^*)\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m\), multipliers \(\lambda_i\ge 0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and \(\nu\in\mathbb{R}^p\) such that \[0=u_0+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i u_i+A^*\nu,\qquad \lambda_i f_i(x^*)=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).\] Thus the KKT conditions are necessary at every finite-valued optimizer. Together with convex KKT sufficiency, they characterize optimality under this qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative-interior Slater feasibility guarantees that every finite-valued convex optimizer has nonnegative inequality multipliers, an equality multiplier, subgradient stationarity, and complementary slackness.
assumptions_latex: For \(i=0,\ldots,m\), \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is a proper closed convex function.
\(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^p\) is linear, \(b\in\mathbb{R}^p\), and \(A^*:\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is its adjoint.
There exists \(\bar x\in\bigcap_{i=0}^m\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_i)\) such that \(A\bar x=b\) and \(f_i(\bar x)<0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every finite-valued optimizer admits KKT multipliers under the stated relative-interior Slater qualification.

children.title: Necessity Without Standard Qualification
children.top_down_role: Exceptional structures where multiplier necessity persists beyond common qualifications.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordinary KKT necessity for a differentiable convex objective over a polyhedron, without strict feasibility or another standard constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}\) be convex and differentiable, and let \(P=\{x:Bx\le d,\ Ax=b\}\) be nonempty. If \(x^*\in P\) minimizes \(f\) over \(P\), then there exist \(\lambda\ge0\) and \(
u\) such that \[
abla f(x^*)+B^*\lambda+A^*
u=0,\qquad \lambda_i((Bx^*)_i-d_i)=0\quad	ext{for every }i.\] No strict-feasibility assumption is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a differentiable convex objective over a polyhedron, every optimizer admits ordinary KKT multipliers even when the polyhedron has no strictly feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Bx\le d,\ Ax=b\}\) is a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(\lambda\ge0\) and \(\nu\) satisfying ordinary KKT stationarity and complementary slackness, without Slater strict feasibility.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative multipliers for the affine inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral-Constraint KKT Necessity Without Slater

assumptions_latex: \(x^*\) is a local minimizer subject to \(g_i(x)\le0\) and \(Ax=b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Even without a constraint qualification, a local minimizer satisfies Fritz John stationarity with a possibly zero objective multiplier.

notation.meaning: Fritz John multiplier on the objective.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional Fritz John necessity without a constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exist multipliers \(\lambda_0\ge0\), \(\lambda_i\ge0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and \(
u\), not all zero, such that \[\lambda_0
abla f(x^*)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i
abla g_i(x^*)+A^*
u=0,\qquad \lambda_i g_i(x^*)=0.\] These Fritz John conditions require no standard constraint qualification. If \(\lambda_0>0\), normalization by \(\lambda_0\) gives ordinary KKT conditions. If every admissible multiplier system has \(\lambda_0=0\), stationarity is abnormal and does not yield a normalized KKT multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a constraint qualification, Fritz John multipliers still exist, but their objective multiplier may vanish, preventing normalization to ordinary KKT conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Necessity Without Standard Qualification

children.title: Sufficient but Nonnnecessary KKT Regimes
children.top_down_role: Convex settings where KKT conditions retain certificate value but fail to capture every optimizer.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Separation of KKT Sufficiency and Necessity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex regimes without a constraint qualification or automatic regularity, where KKT points remain sufficient but need not include every optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex program, let \(\mathcal K\) be the set of feasible points admitting multipliers and subgradients satisfying the convex KKT relations, and let \(X^*\) be its set of global minimizers. Always \(\mathcal K\subseteq X^*\). Without a constraint qualification or another multiplier-existence condition, the inclusion can be strict: \(\mathcal K\subsetneq X^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex KKT points are always globally optimal, but without multiplier regularity some optimizers may have no KKT multipliers, so the KKT set can be a strict subset of the solution set.
assumptions_latex: The objective and inequality functions are convex and the equality constraints are affine.
No constraint qualification or alternative multiplier-existence condition is assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The KKT-point set is contained in the optimizer set, and this containment may be strict.

notation.meaning: Set of feasible points admitting a convex KKT system.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Separation of KKT Sufficiency and Necessity

assumptions_latex: The optimization problem is \(\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}}x\) subject to \(x^2\le0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unique optimizer has no KKT multiplier, although any KKT point of a convex program would be sufficient for optimality.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete convex failure of KKT necessity when Slater's condition fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The feasible set of \(\min x\) subject to \(x^2\le0\) is the singleton \(\{0\}\), so \(x^*=0\) is the unique global minimizer. Both the objective and constraint are convex and differentiable. KKT stationarity would require \[0=1+\lambda(2x^*)=1\] for some \(\lambda\ge0\), which is impossible. Thus the convex KKT conditions remain sufficient whenever they hold, but they are not necessary here. The missing hypothesis is a constraint qualification: no point satisfies \(x^2<0\), and the active constraint gradient vanishes at \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing x subject to x squared at most zero has the unique optimizer zero, but stationarity is impossible; KKT is sufficient yet not necessary.
knowledge_statements.title: Sufficient but Nonnnecessary KKT Regimes

children.title: Saddle-Point Optimality Certificates
children.top_down_role: Global primal-dual optimality represented through convex-concave saddle structure.

assumptions_latex: \(L:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is convex in its first argument and concave in its second.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A saddle pair simultaneously certifies primal and dual optimality and equality of their values.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global convex-concave saddle certificate and zero-gap representation.

source_refs.locator: 3.4. Saddle Point and Minimax Theory p. 127
5.5.2. Saddle Point Theorems p. 204

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pair \((x^*,y^*)\in X\times Y\) is a saddle-point certificate when \[L(x^*,y)\le L(x^*,y^*)\le L(x,y^*)\qquad\text{for all }x\in X,\ y\in Y.\] These inequalities imply \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}p(x)\), \(y^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in Y}d(y)\), and \[\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)=L(x^*,y^*)=\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y).\] Therefore the pair is directly verifiable evidence of primal optimality, dual optimality, and zero duality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex-concave saddle pair certifies both primal and dual optimality and makes the min-max and max-min values equal.
knowledge_statements.title: Saddle-Point Optimality Certificates

children.title: Multiplier Degeneracy Regimes

children.title: Abnormal Multiplier Regimes
children.top_down_role: Multiplier systems lacking the usual objective normalization.

assumptions_latex: \(x^*\) is feasible for a differentiable program with inequalities \(g_i(x)\le0\) and affine equalities \(Ax=b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An abnormal multiplier is a nonzero Fritz John constraint multiplier system whose objective coefficient is zero.

notation.meaning: Objective multiplier in Fritz John conditions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fritz John sense of abnormality for smooth finite-dimensional programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A Fritz John multiplier system \((\lambda_0,\lambda,
u)\) at \(x^*\) is abnormal when \(\lambda_0=0\) and \((\lambda,
u)
e0\), while \(\lambda_i\ge0\), \(\lambda_i=0\) for \(i
otin I(x^*)\), and \[\sum_{i\in I(x^*)}\lambda_i
abla g_i(x^*)+A^*
u=0.\] An abnormal regime is one in which such a system exists. Because the objective gradient disappears, abnormal stationarity expresses constraint degeneracy rather than a normalized KKT balance. Constraint qualifications such as Mangasarian-Fromovitz exclude nonzero abnormal systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An abnormal Fritz John system has zero objective multiplier but nonzero constraint multipliers; it records constraint geometry alone and is excluded by standard regularity conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Abnormal Multiplier Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selected Fritz John meaning of abnormality is coherent, but the terminology and the claim that Mangasarian-Fromovitz excludes such systems require an authoritative, specifically located source.

children.title: Degenerate Multiplier Regimes
children.top_down_role: Multiplier structures affected by redundant or singular active geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(x^*\) is a KKT point of a differentiable inequality-and-equality constrained problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Linear dependence among active constraint gradients defines the selected degenerate regime and permits, but does not force, multiplier nonuniqueness.

notation.meaning: Perturbation of a KKT multiplier pair.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: LICQ-based local sense of smooth constraint-multiplier degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In the selected smooth local sense, the multiplier regime at \(x^*\) is degenerate when the active inequality gradients together with the equality gradients are linearly dependent: there exists \((\delta\lambda,\delta
u)
e0\), supported on \(I(x^*)\), such that \[\sum_{i\in I(x^*)}\delta\lambda_i
abla g_i(x^*)+A^*\delta
u=0.\] Equivalently, the linear independence constraint qualification fails at \(x^*\). If a KKT multiplier \((\lambda,
u)\) can be perturbed to \((\lambda+t\delta\lambda,
u+t\delta
u)\) while preserving nonnegativity for sufficiently small nonzero \(t\), then the KKT multiplier is nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This local smooth notion calls a multiplier regime degenerate when active constraint gradients are dependent; feasible null-direction perturbations then produce multiple KKT multipliers.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Multiplier Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: LICQ failure is precisely described, but calling every such situation a degenerate multiplier regime is terminology-dependent across nonlinear and conic optimization. A source fixing this local definition and its relation to multiplier nonuniqueness is required.

children.title: Multiplier Nonuniqueness
children.top_down_role: Optimality systems admitting multiple inequivalent multiplier representations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multiplier-Set Geometry at a KKT Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex geometry of all KKT multipliers for a fixed smooth feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a fixed feasible point \(x^*\), the KKT multiplier set is \[\Lambda(x^*)=\{(\lambda,
u):\lambda\ge0,\ \lambda_i g_i(x^*)=0,\ 
abla f(x^*)+\sum_i\lambda_i
abla g_i(x^*)+Dh(x^*)^*
u=0\}.\] It is the intersection of an affine subspace with a coordinate face of the nonnegative orthant times the unrestricted equality-multiplier space. Hence it is closed and convex, and the multiplier is unique exactly when \(\Lambda(x^*)\) is a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a fixed KKT point, the multipliers form a closed convex affine-orthant intersection; uniqueness means that this set is a singleton.
assumptions_latex: \(x^*\) is feasible for differentiable inequality constraints \(g_i\le0\) and equality constraints \(h=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Lambda(x^*)\) is closed and convex, and the multiplier is unique if and only if \(\Lambda(x^*)\) is a singleton.

notation.meaning: Set of all KKT multiplier pairs at the fixed primal point.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier-Set Geometry at a KKT Point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient, but not necessary, condition for uniqueness of smooth KKT multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^*\) admit a KKT multiplier. If the equality gradients and active inequality gradients are linearly independent at \(x^*\), then the KKT multiplier pair is unique. The converse fails: active-gradient dependence need not provide a sign-compatible perturbation of the multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LICQ makes a KKT multiplier unique, but failure of LICQ alone does not establish nonuniqueness.
assumptions_latex: The equality gradients and active inequality gradients are linearly independent at \(x^*\).

notation.meaning: KKT multiplier set at the primal point.

knowledge_statements.title: LICQ Implies Multiplier Uniqueness

assumptions_latex: The problem is \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R} x\) subject to \(-x\le 0\) imposed twice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Lambda(0)=\{(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)\in\mathbb R_+^2:\lambda_1+\lambda_2=1\}\), so the primal optimizer is unique but its multiplier is not.

notation.meaning: Set of KKT multiplier vectors at the optimizer
Multipliers of the two duplicated inequalities

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A duplicated-constraint convex program exhibiting nonunique KKT multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R} x\) subject to \(g_1(x)=g_2(x)=-x\le 0\). The unique optimizer is \(x^*=0\). For multipliers \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2\ge 0\), complementary slackness holds automatically at \(x^*\), while stationarity is \(1-\lambda_1-\lambda_2=0\). Hence every point of \(\{(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)\in\mathbb R_+^2:\lambda_1+\lambda_2=1\}\) is a KKT multiplier. Thus uniqueness of a primal solution does not imply uniqueness of its multipliers when active constraint gradients are linearly dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicating an active inequality leaves the unique primal solution unchanged but creates a continuum of KKT multipliers whose components sum to one.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier Nonuniqueness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is mathematically correct and the counterexample kind fits the nonuniqueness leaf, but no inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Multiplier Instability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity and limiting behavior of multipliers near regularity failure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential boundedness of smooth KKT multipliers near a feasible point satisfying MFCQ.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^k\to x^*\) be feasible points for fixed continuously differentiable constraints \(g_i(x)\le0\) and \(h(x)=0\), and let \((\lambda^k,\nu^k)\) be KKT multipliers at \(x^k\). If the objective gradients remain bounded along the sequence and MFCQ holds at \(x^*\), then \(\{(\lambda^k,\nu^k)\}\) is bounded. Thus multiplier blow-up along a convergent KKT sequence requires loss of MFCQ or failure of the bounded first-order-data assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: MFCQ and bounded first-order data keep nearby KKT multipliers bounded; blow-up signals a regularity or data boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(x^k\to x^*\), with each \(x^k\) feasible and admitting the KKT multiplier \((\lambda^k,\nu^k)\).
The fixed constraint functions are continuously differentiable near \(x^*\), and \(\{\nabla f(x^k)\}\) is bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_k\|(\lambda^k,\nu^k)\|<+\infty\).

notation.meaning: Inequality-multiplier vector at the kth point.
Equality-multiplier vector at the kth point.

knowledge_statements.title: MFCQ Prevents Local Multiplier Blow-Up

assumptions_latex: For each \(t>0\), consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R}x\) subject to \(x^2\le t\).
The parameter approaches the degenerate value through \(t\downarrow 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_t=-\sqrt t\) and \(\lambda_t=(2\sqrt t)^{-1}\to+\infty\); at \(t=0\), no finite KKT multiplier exists.

notation.meaning: Optimal multiplier for the quadratic inequality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A parametric convex example locating multiplier blow-up at constraint-qualification failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(t>0\), the convex problem \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R}x\) subject to \(x^2-t\le 0\) has optimizer \(x_t=-\sqrt t\). Its active-constraint stationarity equation is \(1+2\lambda_t x_t=0\), giving \(\lambda_t=(2\sqrt t)^{-1}\). Consequently \(\lambda_t\to+\infty\) as \(t\downarrow0\). At \(t=0\), the only feasible point is \(x=0\), the active constraint gradient vanishes, and \(1+\lambda\,0=0\) has no finite solution. Multiplier boundedness therefore fails at this degenerate boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: As a quadratic feasible interval collapses to one point, its optimal multiplier diverges; at the limiting degenerate problem no finite KKT multiplier exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier Instability Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The parametric calculation correctly exhibits multiplier blow-up and failure of finite KKT multipliers at the degenerate limit, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. An inspectable source with a specific locator is still required.

children.title: Convex Feasibility Certificate Interface
children.top_down_role: Witness families supporting exact, numerical, lifted, or strict-feasibility claims.

children.title: Exact Feasible-Point Witnesses
children.top_down_role: Point-based witnesses checked directly against the mathematical model.

assumptions_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(g_i:X\to\mathbb R\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and let \(A\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A supplied \(\bar x\) certifies feasibility exactly iff \(\bar x\in X\), \(g_i(\bar x)\le0\) for every \(i\), and \(A\bar x=b\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct exact-arithmetic certification for an inequality-and-equality convex model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the feasibility system \(x\in X\), \(g_i(x)\le0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and \(Ax=b\), an exact feasible-point witness is a point \(\bar x\) represented in an arithmetic domain where membership, inequalities, and equalities are decidable without tolerance. Verification consists of checking \(\bar x\in X\), evaluating every \(g_i(\bar x)\le0\), and verifying \(A\bar x=b\). Acceptance of all checks certifies that the mathematical feasible set is nonempty; failure of any check rejects this witness but does not certify infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exactly represented point certifies nonemptiness when every domain, inequality, and equality constraint can be checked without tolerance and is satisfied.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Feasible-Point Witnesses

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact point-checking interface is precise, distinguishes rejection of a witness from certification of infeasibility, and is correctly classified as a certificate. No source or standard-field rationale is supplied.

children.title: Numerical Feasibility Witnesses
children.top_down_role: Point-based witnesses interpreted through scaled residual and tolerance conventions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Small Residual Need Not Imply Geometric Near-Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling and conditioning boundary for absolute equality-residual tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a>0\), consider \(ax=0\), whose feasible set is \(C=\{0\}\). Under the absolute rule \(|ax|\le\tau\), with \(\tau>0\), the point \(\hat x=\tau/(2a)\) is accepted, yet \[d_C(\hat x)=\frac{\tau}{2a}.\] Thus accepted residual is at most \(\tau\), while distance from feasibility becomes arbitrarily large as \(a\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Across ill-scaled equivalent constraints, a small absolute residual can coexist with arbitrarily large distance from the exact feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |a\hat x|=\tau/2\le\tau\quad\text{but}\quad d_{\{0\}}(\hat x)=\tau/(2a)\to\infty\text{ as }a\downarrow0.

notation.meaning: distance to the exact feasible set

knowledge_statements.title: Small Residual Need Not Imply Geometric Near-Feasibility

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constraint-Scale Invariance of Normalized Residual Tests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariance under consistent positive rescaling of a constraint and its declared residual scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an inequality residual be tested through \([g(x)]_+/s\), where \(s>0\). For every \(\alpha>0\), replacing \(g\) by \(\widetilde g=\alpha g\) and \(s\) by \(\widetilde s=\alpha s\) gives \[\frac{[\widetilde g(x)]_+}{\widetilde s}=\frac{[g(x)]_+}{s}.\] Likewise, replacing an equality residual \(r(x)\) and scale \(s_e\) by \(\alpha r(x)\) and \(\alpha s_e\) leaves \(\|r(x)\|/s_e\) unchanged. Therefore an aggregate rule formed from these normalized residuals is invariant under consistent positive rescaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized residual test is unchanged when each constraint and its declared scale are multiplied by the same positive factor.
assumptions_latex: All affected residual scales are positive and rescaled consistently.
The norm and acceptance tolerance are unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widetilde\rho(x)=\rho(x)\quad\text{for every }x.

notation.meaning: declared inequality and equality residual scales

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Scale Invariance of Normalized Residual Tests

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact feasibility of a nearby constraint system induced by measured residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a candidate \(\hat x\), define \(r_e=A\hat x-b\) and \(r_i=[g_i(\hat x)]_+\). Then \(\hat x\) is exactly feasible for the perturbed system \[Ax=b+r_e,\qquad g_i(x)\le r_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).\] If a declared numerical test gives \(\|r_e\|/s_e\le\tau\) and \(r_i/s_i\le\tau\), then \(\|r_e\|\le\tau s_e\) and \(0\le r_i\le\tau s_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual witness exactly solves a nearby system whose equality and inequality right-hand sides are displaced by the measured residuals.
assumptions_latex: The equality and inequality residuals are evaluated at \(\hat x\).
The scales \(s_e,s_i\) are positive and \(\tau\ge0\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \hat x\in\{x:Ax=b+r_e,\ g_i(x)\le r_i\ \forall i\},\quad \|r_e\|\le\tau s_e,\quad 0\le r_i\le\tau s_i.

notation.meaning: nonnegative inequality relaxation required by the candidate

knowledge_statements.title: Backward-Error Interpretation of Residual Feasibility

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Error-Bound Conversion from Residual Acceptance to Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric interpretation of an accepted scaled residual under a declared error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be the exact feasible set and let \(\rho:X\to[0,+\infty]\) be the aggregate residual used by a numerical acceptance rule. Suppose \(d_F(x)\le\kappa\rho(x)\) for every \(x\) in a region \(S\), with \(\kappa<+\infty\). Then every \(\hat x\in S\) satisfying \(\rho(\hat x)\le\tau\) obeys \[d_F(\hat x)\le\kappa\tau.\] Without such an error bound, residual acceptance alone supplies no uniform distance-to-feasibility guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual tolerance yields geometric near-feasibility only when a quantitative error bound relates residual to distance from the exact feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_F(\hat x)\le\kappa\tau.

notation.meaning: distance to the exact feasible set

knowledge_statements.title: Error-Bound Conversion from Residual Acceptance to Distance

assumptions_latex: Let \(s_i>0\), \(s_e>0\), and tolerance \(\tau\ge0\) be fixed before verification.
The candidate \(\hat x\) and all residual evaluations use a declared numerical precision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The witness is accepted precisely when \(\rho(\hat x)\le\tau\), which certifies only tolerance-relative numerical feasibility.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-relative certification under an explicitly fixed residual scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constraints \(g_i(x)\le0\) and \(Ax=b\), fix positive scales \(s_i\), \(s_e\), a norm \(\|\cdot\|\), and tolerance \(\tau\ge0\). Define \(\rho(\hat x)=\max\{\max_i [g_i(\hat x)]_+/s_i,\,\|A\hat x-b\|/s_e\}\), where \([u]_+=\max\{u,0\}\). A numerical feasibility witness is accepted exactly when \(\rho(\hat x)\le\tau\), together with any separately specified domain-membership test. This conclusion is relative to the declared scaling, precision, and tolerance and is not an exact certificate that all mathematical constraints hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A numerical point is accepted when its largest scaled inequality or equality residual is below a declared tolerance; this does not establish exact feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Feasibility Witnesses

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual-based acceptance rule is internally consistent and correctly limits its conclusion to tolerance-relative feasibility. The certificate kind fits the leaf, but the particular residual convention has no cited source or standard-field rationale.

children.title: Lifted Feasibility Witnesses
children.top_down_role: Witnesses requiring consistency between original and extended model spaces.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Sided Projection Soundness for a Lifted Witness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal condition under which a verified extended-space point certifies its projected original point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(F^{\mathrm{lift}}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^q\), and let \(\pi_x(x,z)=x\). If \(\pi_x(F^{\mathrm{lift}})\subseteq F\), then every verified pair \((\bar x,\bar z)\in F^{\mathrm{lift}}\) certifies \(\bar x\in F\). Equality \(\pi_x(F^{\mathrm{lift}})=F\) is unnecessary for soundness of supplied witnesses: for example, \(F=[0,1]\) and \(F^{\mathrm{lift}}=\{(0,0)\}\) define a sound but incomplete lifted witness system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted point is a sound positive witness whenever every feasible lifted point projects into the original set; surjectivity is needed for representation completeness, not for soundness of a supplied witness.
assumptions_latex: Membership of \((\bar x,\bar z)\) in \(F^{\mathrm{lift}}\) is verified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\bar x,\bar z)\in F^{\mathrm{lift}}\Longrightarrow \bar x\in F.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Projection Soundness for a Lifted Witness

assumptions_latex: Let \(F^{\mathrm{lift}}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^q\) be an extended feasible set.
Assume the original feasible set is exactly \(F=\{x:\exists z,\ (x,z)\in F^{\mathrm{lift}}\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A pair \((\bar x,\bar z)\in F^{\mathrm{lift}}\) certifies \(\bar x\in F\).

notation.meaning: Feasible set in the extended space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection-based certification for an exact extended formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an original feasible set satisfies \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists z\in\mathbb R^q,\ (x,z)\in F^{\mathrm{lift}}\}\). A lifted feasibility witness is a pair \((\bar x,\bar z)\) for which every constraint defining \(F^{\mathrm{lift}}\) is verified. The projection consistency check identifies the original component as \(\bar x\). If \((\bar x,\bar z)\in F^{\mathrm{lift}}\), then the defining projection equality implies \(\bar x\in F\). The certificate is unsound if the extended formulation only relaxes, rather than exactly projects onto, the original feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible original point is certified by an extended-space pair only when all lifted constraints hold and the lifted formulation projects exactly onto the original model.
knowledge_statements.title: Lifted Feasibility Witnesses

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection argument is correct under the explicitly assumed exact extended formulation, and certificate is the appropriate kind. No inspectable source or standard-field rationale supports the formulation.

children.title: Regularity-Qualified Feasibility Witnesses
children.top_down_role: Witnesses that additionally establish a regularity or robust-solvability regime.

children.title: Strict Feasibility Witnesses
children.top_down_role: Feasible witnesses exhibiting strict satisfaction of relevant convex constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional strict-feasibility witness distinguishing affine from nonaffine inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_i\) be proper convex functions with common domain \(D=\bigcap_i\operatorname{dom}g_i\), and partition the inequalities into affine indices \(I_{\rm aff}\) and nonaffine indices \(I_{\rm na}\). A refined Slater witness is a point \(\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}D\) satisfying \(A\bar x=b\), \(g_i(\bar x)\le0\) for \(i\in I_{\rm aff}\), and \(g_i(\bar x)<0\) for \(i\in I_{\rm na}\). These checks certify ordinary feasibility and the stated strict-feasibility qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A refined Slater witness lies in the relative common domain, satisfies equalities and affine inequalities feasibly, and satisfies nonaffine inequalities strictly.
assumptions_latex: The inequality family is finite and each \(g_i\) is proper convex.
The affine and nonaffine inequality indices are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}D,\ A\bar x=b,\ g_i(\bar x)\le0\ (i\in I_{\rm aff}),\ g_i(\bar x)<0\ (i\in I_{\rm na})\) is a strict-feasibility witness.
knowledge_statements.title: Refined Slater Strict-Feasibility Witness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strictness Preserved Toward a Strict Witness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex interpolation property of a strict-feasibility witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x^{\mathrm s}\) strictly satisfies a convex inequality family, \(x^{\mathrm f}\) satisfies it non-strictly, both points lie in a common convex domain and satisfy \(Ax=b\), then \(x_t=(1-t)x^{\mathrm f}+t x^{\mathrm s}\) strictly satisfies that family for every \(t\in(0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nontrivial interpolation from a feasible point toward a strict witness remains strictly feasible.
assumptions_latex: The relevant inequality functions are convex on a common convex domain.
\(x^{\mathrm s}\) satisfies them strictly and \(x^{\mathrm f}\) non-strictly.
Both points satisfy the same affine equalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\in(0,1]\Longrightarrow Ax_t=b\) and \(g_i(x_t)<0\) for every relevant index.
knowledge_statements.title: Strictness Preserved Toward a Strict Witness

assumptions_latex: Each \(g_i:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper convex, and \(A x=b\) gives the affine constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A point \(\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}D\) with \(A\bar x=b\) and \(g_i(\bar x)<0\) for all nonaffine inequalities is a strict-feasibility witness.

notation.meaning: Common effective domain of the inequalities

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Slater witness with affine equalities retained exactly.

source_refs.locator: 1.3. Relative Interior and Closure p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex system \(g_i(x)\le0\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and \(Ax=b\), let \(D=\bigcap_i\operatorname{dom}g_i\). A strict-feasibility witness is a point \(\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}D\) satisfying \(A\bar x=b\) and \(g_i(\bar x)<0\) for every inequality that is not required to be affine. Direct verification of these relations certifies both ordinary feasibility and the stated Slater-type regularity. Equalities are not made strict, and relative-domain membership prevents artificial failure caused solely by a lower-dimensional effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Slater witness lies in the relative interior of the common domain, satisfies equalities exactly, and satisfies every relevant convex inequality strictly.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Feasibility Witnesses

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3. Relative Interior and Closure p. 23

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited relative-interior section does not support the full Slater-type predicate. Moreover, the statement requires strict satisfaction only for nonaffine inequalities but does not separately require affine inequalities to satisfy their non-strict constraints, so the claimed certification of ordinary feasibility is not justified as written. A source for the intended refined Slater condition and an explicit feasibility condition for affine inequalities are required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict feasibility of primal and dual conic quadratic programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specializes strict-feasibility witnesses to the explicit primal and dual second-order-cone standard forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal conic quadratic program \[\min_x\left\{c^Tx:\|D_ix-d_i\|_2\le p_i^Tx-q_i,\quad i=1,\ldots,k\right\},\] strict feasibility means \[\exists\bar x\quad\forall i=1,\ldots,k:\quad\|D_i\bar x-d_i\|_2<p_i^T\bar x-q_i.\] For its dual, strict feasibility means that there exist \(\{\bar\mu_i,\bar v_i\}_{i=1}^k\) satisfying \[\sum_{i=1}^k(D_i^T\bar\mu_i+\bar v_ip_i)=c,\qquad\|\bar\mu_i\|_2<\bar v_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,k).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal conic quadratic program is strictly feasible when one point satisfies every second-order-cone inequality strictly. Its dual is strictly feasible when a collection satisfying the dual equality lies in the interior of every Lorentz-cone block.
assumptions_latex: \text{The primal and dual have the displayed conic quadratic standard forms.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{StrictFeas}(QP)\Longleftrightarrow\exists\bar x\ \forall i:\|D_i\bar x-d_i\|_2<p_i^T\bar x-q_i,\qquad \operatorname{StrictFeas}(QD)\Longleftrightarrow\exists\{\bar\mu_i,\bar v_i\}_{i=1}^k:\sum_i(D_i^T\bar\mu_i+\bar v_ip_i)=c,\ \|\bar\mu_i\|_2<\bar v_i\ \forall i.

children.title: Relative-Interior Feasibility Witnesses
children.top_down_role: Feasible witnesses located in the relative interior of relevant domains or constraint sets.

assumptions_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex.
Let \(L=\operatorname{aff}F\) carry the Euclidean topology induced from \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\) is a relative-interior witness iff \(\bar x\in F\) and some \(\varepsilon>0\) satisfies \(B(\bar x,\varepsilon)\cap L\subseteq F\).

notation.meaning: Affine hull of the feasible set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional relative-interior witness expressed by a ball in the affine hull.

source_refs.locator: 1.3. Relative Interior and Closure p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty convex feasible set and \(L=\operatorname{aff}F\). A relative-interior feasibility witness consists of \(\bar x\in F\) and a radius \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(B(\bar x,\varepsilon)\cap L\subseteq F\). Equivalently, \(\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}F\). The ball is taken only along the affine hull, so this certificate remains meaningful when \(F\) has empty interior in \(\mathbb R^n\). Verification must establish both feasibility and the stated neighborhood inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point lies in the relative interior when a positive-radius neighborhood within the feasible set's affine hull remains feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Feasibility Witnesses
