children.title: Robust Feasibility Margins
children.top_down_role: Witness information describing separation from feasibility boundaries.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unscaled common slack for a nonempty finite inequality family at an equality-feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\ge1\), let \(g_i:D\to\mathbb R\), and let \(\bar x\in D\) satisfy \(A\bar x=b\). Define \(\mu(\bar x)=\min_{1\le i\le m}(-g_i(\bar x))\). Then \(\mu(\bar x)>0\) if and only if there exists \(\delta>0\) such that \(g_i(\bar x)\le-\delta\) for every \(i\). Any \(0<\delta\le\mu(\bar x)\), together with the equality and domain checks, is a common-margin feasibility certificate. The numerical margin changes if the constraint functions are positively rescaled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The robust feasibility margin is the smallest slack among a nonempty finite family; positivity is equivalent to a common strictly positive slack.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu(\bar x)>0\iff\exists\delta>0\ \forall i:\ g_i(\bar x)\le-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Family Common Feasibility Margin

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converts a common positive slack and local Lipschitz bounds into an affine-relative feasible neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose each \(g_i\) is \(L_i\)-Lipschitz on \(D\cap B(\bar x,r)\), \(g_i(\bar x)\le-\delta\) for all \(i\), and \(A\bar x=b\), where \(\delta>0\). Put \(L=\max_iL_i\). If \(L>0\), every \(x\in D\) with \(Ax=b\) and \(\|x-\bar x\|\le\min\{r,\delta/L\}\) satisfies every inequality. If \(L=0\), the same holds throughout \(D\cap B(\bar x,r)\) on the equality affine space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive slack plus local Lipschitz bounds certifies a feasible neighborhood within the equality affine space.
assumptions_latex: \(A\bar x=b\) and \(g_i(\bar x)\le-\delta\) for all \(i\), with \(\delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax=b,\ \|x-\bar x\|\le\min\{r,\delta/L\}\Longrightarrow g_i(x)\le0\ \forall i\), when \(L>0\).

notation.meaning: Closed norm ball around the witness

knowledge_statements.title: Margin-to-Neighborhood Robustness

assumptions_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be the declared domain and let \(g_i:D\to\mathbb R\).
Fix a candidate \(\bar x\in D\) satisfying \(A\bar x=b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu(\bar x)>0\) iff every inequality has a common positive slack at \(\bar x\); any \(0<\delta\le\mu(\bar x)\) certifies \(g_i(\bar x)\le-\delta\) for all \(i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A common unscaled slack margin for finitely many convex inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a point \(\bar x\in D\) satisfying the equality constraints \(A\bar x=b\), define its inequality feasibility margin by \(\mu(\bar x)=\min_{1\le i\le m}\{-g_i(\bar x)\}\). The point has a positive robust feasibility margin when \(\mu(\bar x)>0\). Equivalently, there exists \(\delta>0\) such that \(g_i(\bar x)\le-\delta\) for every \(i\). A reported \(\delta\) is a verifiable margin certificate when the equalities, domain membership, and all strengthened inequalities are checked. The numerical value depends on the chosen scaling of the constraint functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The robust feasibility margin is the smallest inequality slack at a feasible point; a positive reported lower bound certifies uniform strict slack.
knowledge_statements.title: Robust Feasibility Margins

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and its equivalence are correct for a nonempty finite inequality family, and definition fits the margin leaf. However, the record does not explicitly assume an integer m at least one, and no source or standard-field rationale is supplied for the chosen unscaled margin convention.

children.title: Lower-Dimensional Witness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regularity witnesses for feasible geometry contained in a proper affine subspace.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^2}F=\varnothing\), while \(\operatorname{ri}F=\{(u,0):u>0\}\); hence \((1,0)\) is a relative-interior witness despite absent ambient interior.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A convex ray showing why ambient-interior witnesses fail in lower-dimensional models.

source_refs.locator: 1.3. Relative Interior and Closure p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(F=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2:u\ge0,\ v=0\}\). Its affine hull is \(L=\{(u,0):u\in\mathbb R\}\). Because every ambient ball around a point of \(F\) contains points with \(v\ne0\), one has \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^2}F=\varnothing\). Nevertheless, \(\operatorname{ri}F=\{(u,0):u>0\}\), and \((1,0)\) admits a positive-radius feasible neighborhood relative to \(L\). Thus requiring an ambient-interior witness incorrectly rejects regular feasible points in lower-dimensional regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible ray has empty interior in the ambient plane but nonempty relative interior, so ambient-interior regularity is too strong for lower-dimensional models.
knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Dimensional Witness Regimes

children.title: Farkas Alternative Family
children.top_down_role: Linear and polyhedral feasibility alternatives and their certificate interpretations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier characterization of valid affine inequalities for a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\neq\varnothing\). Then \[c^{\mathsf T}x\le d\quad\forall x\in P\] if and only if there exists \(\lambda\ge0\) such that \[A^{\mathsf T}\lambda=c,\qquad b^{\mathsf T}\lambda\le d.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine inequality is valid on a nonempty polyhedron exactly when it is dominated by a nonnegative combination of the defining inequalities.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(d\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\forall x\in P,\ c^{\mathsf T}x\le d\bigr]\iff\bigl[\exists\lambda\ge0:\ A^{\mathsf T}\lambda=c,\ b^{\mathsf T}\lambda\le d\bigr].

notation.meaning: Polyhedron defined by the antecedent inequalities

knowledge_statements.title: Farkas Valid-Inequality Characterization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional inequality-feasibility form of Farkas' alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), exactly one of the following systems is feasible: \[\exists x\in\mathbb R^n:\ Ax\le b,\] \[\exists y\in\mathbb R^m:\ y\ge0,\quad A^{\mathsf T}y=0,\quad b^{\mathsf T}y<0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Either a finite system of linear inequalities is feasible or a nonnegative combination yields a strict contradiction, but not both.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of \(\exists x:Ax\le b\) and \(\exists y\ge0:A^{\mathsf T}y=0,\ b^{\mathsf T}y<0\) holds.
knowledge_statements.title: Inequality-System Farkas Alternative

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of \(\exists x\ge0:Ax=b\) and \(\exists y:A^\mathsf{T}y\ge0,\ b^\mathsf{T}y<0\) holds.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional equality-form Farkas alternative with a nonnegative primal variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), exactly one of the following systems is solvable: \(\mathrm{(P)}\) there exists \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) with \(x\ge0\) and \(Ax=b\); or \(\mathrm{(D)}\) there exists \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(A^\mathsf{T}y\ge0\) and \(b^\mathsf{T}y<0\). A vector satisfying \(\mathrm{(D)}\) is an infeasibility certificate for \(\mathrm{(P)}\). The two systems cannot both hold, and failure of \(\mathrm{(P)}\) guarantees such a certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Either a nonnegative solution of the linear equations exists, or a separating vector gives a strictly negative contradiction, but never both.
knowledge_statements.title: Farkas Alternative Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated equality-form Farkas alternative has consistent signs and dimensions, and theorem is the correct kind for this leaf. A named theorem requires an authoritative source with a theorem, section, or page locator.

children.title: Gordan-Stiemke Homogeneous Alternative Family
children.top_down_role: Homogeneous linear alternatives connecting strict positivity, null spaces, and cone separation.

children.title: Gordan Alternative Family
children.top_down_role: Homogeneous linear alternatives organized around strict positivity and null-space witnesses.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of \(\exists x:A x<0\) and \(\exists y\ge0:y\ne0,\ A^\mathsf{T}y=0\) holds.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict homogeneous inequality form of Gordan's theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). Exactly one of the following homogeneous systems has a solution: \(\mathrm{(G1)}\) there exists \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \(Ax<0\) componentwise; or \(\mathrm{(G2)}\) there exists \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) such that \(y\ge0\), \(y\ne0\), and \(A^\mathsf{T}y=0\). Thus a nonzero nonnegative vector annihilated by \(A^\mathsf{T}\) is a certificate that no direction makes every row product strictly negative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Either one direction makes every row product strictly negative, or a nonzero nonnegative combination of the rows vanishes, but not both.
knowledge_statements.title: Gordan Alternative Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strict homogeneous alternative is mathematically coherent and theorem fits the Gordan-family leaf. Because naming conventions and sign variants differ across sources, an authoritative locator confirming this exact formulation is required.

children.title: Stiemke Alternative Family
children.top_down_role: Homogeneous alternatives organized around nonnegative dependence and strict separating witnesses.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of \(\exists x>0:A x=0\) and \(\exists y:A^\mathsf{T}y\ge0,\ A^\mathsf{T}y\ne0\) holds.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictly positive null-vector form of Stiemke's theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). Exactly one of the following systems has a solution: \(\mathrm{(S1)}\) there exists \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) with \(x>0\) and \(Ax=0\); or \(\mathrm{(S2)}\) there exists \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) such that \(A^\mathsf{T}y\ge0\) and \(A^\mathsf{T}y\ne0\). Hence a vector whose transpose image is nonnegative and nonzero certifies that the null space of \(A\) contains no componentwise strictly positive vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Either the matrix has a strictly positive null vector, or a transpose image is nonnegative and nonzero, but the two alternatives cannot coexist.
knowledge_statements.title: Stiemke Alternative Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strictly positive null-vector alternative is mathematically coherent and theorem fits the Stiemke-family leaf. An authoritative locator is required to confirm this exact named variant and its strictness conventions.

children.title: Homogeneous Cone Alternatives

knowledge_statements.title: Homogeneous Cone Alternatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Gordan-Stiemke alternative for a cone with nonempty interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exactly one of the following systems is feasible: \[\text{(P)}\quad Ax=0,\qquad x\in\operatorname{int}K;\] \[\text{(D)}\quad y\in F,\qquad A^*y\in K^*\setminus\{0\}.\] Equivalently, \[\ker A\cap\operatorname{int}K\neq\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{range}A^*\cap(K^*\setminus\{0\})=\varnothing.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear kernel meets the cone interior exactly when its orthogonal range contains no nonzero dual-cone separator.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(F\) are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone with \(\operatorname{int}K\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ker A\cap\operatorname{int}K\neq\varnothing\) if and only if \(\operatorname{range}A^*\cap(K^*\setminus\{0\})=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing \(x\in\operatorname{int}K\) by \(x\in K\setminus\{0\}\) destroys exclusivity of the homogeneous alternative.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary example showing why the primal cone condition must be strict.

source_refs.locator: 1.4.3 Proof of the homogeneous Farkas lemma p. 35

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The nonzero boundary point \(x=(1,0)\) satisfies \(x\in K\setminus\{0\}\) and \(Ax=0\). Simultaneously, for \(y=1\), one has \(A^*y=(0,1)\in K^*\setminus\{0\}\). Hence both modified systems are feasible. The interior requirement in the Gordan-Stiemke primal system cannot generally be weakened to nonzero cone membership while retaining mutual exclusivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a simple orthant map, a nonzero boundary kernel point and a nonzero dual certificate coexist, so strict cone membership is essential.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Farkas Alternative Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-image finite-dimensional conic Farkas alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exactly one of the following systems is feasible: \[\text{(P)}\quad Ax=b,\qquad x\in K;\] \[\text{(D)}\quad y\in F,\qquad A^*y\in K^*,\qquad \langle b,y\rangle<0.\] Closedness of \(A(K)\) ensures exhaustiveness; without it, primal infeasibility need not yield a strict dual certificate.

assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(F\) are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, and \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone.
\(A:E\to F\) is linear and \(A(K)\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of \(\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing\) and \(\{y\in F:A^*y\in K^*,\ \langle b,y\rangle<0\}\neq\varnothing\) holds.

children.title: Nonlinear Convex Alternative Family
children.top_down_role: Alternatives for convex inequality systems under appropriate regularity.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and convex, and \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:X\to\mathbb{R}\) are convex.
\(U=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^m:\exists x\in X,\ f_i(x)\leq u_i\ \forall i\}\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of \(\exists x\in X:\ f_i(x)\leq0\ \forall i\) and \(\exists\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\setminus\{0\}:\inf_{x\in X}\sum_i\lambda_i f_i(x)>0\) holds.

notation.meaning: Convex upper image of the vector-valued constraint map

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonlinear Farkas alternative under closedness of the convex upper image.

source_refs.locator: 5.1. Nonlinear Farkas' Lemma p. 160

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Exactly one of the following assertions holds: \[\exists x\in X\quad f_i(x)\leq0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\] or \[\exists\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\setminus\{0\}\quad
\inf_{x\in X}\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i(x)>0.\] The multiplier assertion supplies a scalar convex inequality that is positive throughout \(X\), and therefore certifies infeasibility of the simultaneous inequality system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a closed-upper-image condition, either all convex inequalities are jointly feasible or a nonnegative weighted sum is uniformly positive.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Convex Alternative Family

source_witnesses.locator: 5.1. Nonlinear Farkas' Lemma p. 160

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the nonstrict alternative when the convex upper image is not closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=(0,\infty)\) and \(f(x)=x\). The system \(f(x)\le0\) is infeasible, but for every \(\lambda>0\), \(\inf_{x\in X}\lambda f(x)=0\), so no multiplier has strictly positive infimum. The upper image is \(U=(0,\infty)\), which is not closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without upper-image closedness, infeasibility need not admit a nonnegative weighted sum with strictly positive infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nexists x\in X:\ f(x)\le0,\qquad \nexists\lambda>0:\ \inf_{x\in X}\lambda f(x)>0.

notation.meaning: Upper image of the scalar constraint

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Upper-Image Failure for Nonstrict Feasibility

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict-feasibility nonlinear alternative requiring convexity but no closed-upper-image assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:X\to\mathbb R\) be convex. Exactly one of the following holds: \[\exists x\in X:\ f_i(x)<0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\] or \[\exists\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\setminus\{0\}:\ \inf_{x\in X}\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i(x)\ge0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Either all convex inequalities are simultaneously strict somewhere, or a nonzero nonnegative weighted sum is everywhere nonnegative, but not both.
assumptions_latex: X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty and convex}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\exists x\in X:\ f(x)<0\bigr)\ \dot\vee\ \bigl(\exists\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\setminus\{0\}:\inf_X\lambda^\mathsf{T}f\ge0\bigr).
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Nonlinear Convex Alternative

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong alternatives for convex systems under constraint qualification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A conditional upgrade of an associated weak-alternative pair. The extract does not identify the particular constraint qualification, so no specific regularity condition is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal S_p\) and \(\mathcal S_a\) be the associated weak-alternative systems. Suppose every primal inequality function \(f_i\) is convex, every equality function \(h_i\) is affine, and the relevant constraint qualification holds. Then exactly one of \(\mathcal S_p\) and \(\mathcal S_a\) is feasible; equivalently, each is feasible if and only if the other is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the original system has convex inequality functions and affine equality functions, and the relevant constraint qualification holds, its weak-alternative pair becomes a strong-alternative pair: exactly one system is feasible. The extract does not specify which constraint qualification is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Alternative Exclusivity

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) denote \(\exists x\in K\) such that \(Ax=b\), and let \(D\) denote \(\exists y\in F\) such that \(A^*y\in K^*\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\). Then \[P\Longrightarrow\neg D.\] This exclusivity property requires no closedness assumption on \(A(K)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal conic solution and a strict dual infeasibility witness cannot coexist; this needs no closed-image assumption.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(F\) are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a convex cone, \(A:E\to F\) is linear, and \(b\in F\).
\(P\) denotes \(\exists x\in K\) with \(Ax=b\), and \(D\) denotes \(\exists y\in F\) with \(A^*y\in K^*\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\Longrightarrow\neg D\), independently of any closed-image or regularity assumption.

knowledge_statements.title: Alternative Exhaustiveness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-image condition ensuring exhaustive conic alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the conic primal system \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), closedness of \(A(K)\) is a sufficient exhaustiveness condition: \[b\notin A(K)\Longrightarrow\exists y\in F:\quad A^*y\in K^*,\quad\langle b,y\rangle<0.\] Together with exclusivity, this makes primal feasibility and strict dual certification an exact alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closedness of the conic image ensures that every infeasible right-hand side has a strict dual-cone separator.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(F\) are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone, \(A:E\to F\) is linear, and \(b\in F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(b\notin A(K)\), then \(\exists y\in F\) such that \(A^*y\in K^*\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Exhaustiveness Characterizes Closed Conic Images
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact condition for strict-certificate exhaustiveness over all right-hand sides.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=A(K)\). Then \[C\text{ is closed}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \forall b\notin C\;\exists y\in F:\ A^*y\in K^*,\ \langle b,y\rangle<0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict conic infeasibility certificates exist for every infeasible right-hand side exactly when the conic image is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(F\) are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone and \(A:E\to F\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A(K)\text{ is closed}\iff \bigl[\forall b\notin A(K),\ \exists y:\ A^*y\in K^*,\ \langle b,y\rangle<0\bigr].
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Exhaustiveness Characterizes Closed Conic Images

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Failure of Strong Alternatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite example where a nonclosed image defeats strict-certificate exhaustiveness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With the trace inner product on \(\mathbb{S}^2\), \[A(K)=\{(a,c)\in\mathbb{R}^2:a>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\},\] so \(A(K)\) is not closed and \(b=(0,1)\) belongs to \(\operatorname{cl}A(K)\setminus A(K)\). For every \(y=(y_1,y_2)\in\mathbb{R}^2\), \[A^*y\succeq0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y_2=0\text{ and }y_1\geq0,\] and consequently \(\langle b,y\rangle=0\). Thus the primal system is infeasible but has no strict dual certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonclosed semidefinite image excludes the target while admitting no strict separating dual certificate at that boundary limit.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb{S}^2\) carries the trace inner product, \(\mathbb{R}^2\) carries its Euclidean inner product, and \(K=\mathbb{S}_+^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The system \(\{X\in\mathbb{S}_+^2:A(X)=b\}\) is empty, yet no \(y\in\mathbb{R}^2\) satisfies \(A^*y\succeq0\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infeasible conic system lacks a strict separating certificate exactly when its right-hand side is a missing closure point of the conic image.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(F\) are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone, \(A:E\to F\) is linear, and \(b\in F\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A separating-hyperplane certificate for \(b\notin C\) is a pair \((a,\beta)\) with \(a\neq0\) satisfying \[\langle a,x\rangle\leq\beta<\langle a,b\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.\] Equivalently, \(\sigma_C(a)\leq\beta<\langle a,b\rangle\), where \(\sigma_C\) is the support function. The displayed strict gap directly verifies that \(b\) cannot belong to \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hyperplane whose support bound on the feasible set lies strictly below its value at the target certifies exclusion.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Missing Boundary Point Without Strict Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary failure of strict separation for a point excluded only from a nonclosed set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=(-\infty,0)\subset\mathbb R\) and \(b=0\), one has \(b\notin C\) but \(b\in\overline C\). No scalar \(a\) satisfies \(\sigma_C(a)<ab\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A missing boundary point of an open half-line is infeasible for membership but has no strict separator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: b\notin C\quad\text{and}\quad\nexists a:\sigma_C(a)<ab.
knowledge_statements.title: Missing Boundary Point Without Strict Separation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact existence boundary for strict point-exclusion separators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), there exists \(a\) with \(\sigma_C(a)<\langle a,b\rangle\) if and only if \(b\notin\overline C\). Thus an excluded point in \(\overline C\setminus C\) has no strict separating-hyperplane certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict separation detects exclusion from the closure, not a missing point of a nonclosed convex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\exists a:\sigma_C(a)<\langle a,b\rangle)\iff b\notin\overline C.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Boundary for Strict Separation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distance as the Maximum Separation Margin
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection construction and optimal normalized margin for point separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex and let \(b\notin C\). With \(p=P_C(b)\) and \(u=(b-p)/\|b-p\|\), \(\sigma_C(u)=\langle u,p\rangle<\langle u,b\rangle\), and \[\operatorname{dist}(b,C)=\langle u,b\rangle-\sigma_C(u)=\max_{\|a\|\le1}\bigl(\langle a,b\rangle-\sigma_C(a)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection produces an optimal unit-normal separator whose gap equals the distance to the closed convex set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{\|a\|\le1}(\langle a,b\rangle-\sigma_C(a))=\operatorname{dist}(b,C)>0.

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection of b onto C

knowledge_statements.title: Distance as the Maximum Separation Margin

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Separation of Two Convex Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-versus-set variant with an attained positive distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let nonempty convex sets \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) have positive distance attained at \((p,q)\in C\times D\). For \(a=(q-p)/\|q-p\|\), \[\sup_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle\le\langle a,p\rangle<\langle a,q\rangle\le\inf_{y\in D}\langle a,y\rangle.\] The normalized separation gap equals \(\operatorname{dist}(C,D)\). Attainment is guaranteed when both sets are closed and one is compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two convex sets at attained positive distance admit a strong separator whose normalized gap equals their distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{x\in C}\langle a,x\rangle<\inf_{y\in D}\langle a,y\rangle.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Separation of Two Convex Sets

knowledge_statements.title: Alternative-System Certificates

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An alternative-system certificate is a vector \(y\in F\) satisfying \[A^*y\in K^*,\qquad \langle b,y\rangle<0.\] The displayed cone membership and strict scalar inequality certify that no \(x\in K\) can satisfy \(Ax=b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual vector whose adjoint image lies in the dual cone and pairs negatively with the right-hand side certifies infeasibility.

\(K\subseteq E\) is a convex cone, \(A:E\to F\) is linear, and \(b\in F\).
The primal feasibility system is \(Ax=b\) with \(x\in K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any \(y\in F\) with \(A^*y\in K^*\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\) certifies primal infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pair \((\bar x,d)\) is a recession-direction certificate of unboundedness below when \(\bar x\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\), \(d\in\operatorname{rec}C\setminus\{0\}\), and \(f^{\infty}(d)<0\). children.title: Conflict Certificates
children.top_down_role: Localized evidence identifying mutually incompatible model components.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Localized infeasibility certificate for finite convex inequalities and affine equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multipliers whose aggregate has a positive global lower bound certify inconsistency of their supported constraints.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is convex and each \(g_j\) is affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in X}(\sum_i\lambda_if_i(x)+\sum_j\nu_jg_j(x))>0\Longrightarrow\) the supported subsystem is infeasible.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conflict Support Does Not Certify Minimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes an arbitrary conflict certificate from IIS and minimal-conflict certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A certificate establishing \(\bigcap_{i\in S}C_i=\varnothing\) proves only that \(S\) is a conflict. It does not prove inclusion minimality. For finite \(S\), deletion minimality additionally requires \(\bigcap_{i\in S\setminus\{j\}}C_i\ne\varnothing\) for every \(j\in S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certificate support proves inconsistency, not that every supported constraint is necessary.
assumptions_latex: A valid certificate establishes infeasibility of the subsystem indexed by \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\text{ conflict}\not\Longrightarrow S\text{ inclusion-minimal conflict}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Conflict Support Does Not Certify Minimality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upward-closed structure of inconsistent constraint subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constraint feasible sets \(C_i\), call \(S\) a conflict when \(\bigcap_{i\in S}C_i=\varnothing\). If \(S\subseteq T\) and \(S\) is a conflict, then \(T\) is a conflict. A subset of a conflict need not itself be a conflict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding constraints preserves a conflict, while deleting constraints may remove it.
assumptions_latex: Each \(C_i\) is the feasible set of one indexed constraint.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Infeasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric definition for robust infeasibility of an affine-conic intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine-conic system \(L\cap K\neq\varnothing\) is strongly infeasible when \(L\cap K=\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(L,K)=\inf\{\|u-v\|:u\in L,\ v\in K\}>0\). Thus strong infeasibility requires positive separation, not merely an empty intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong infeasibility means the affine constraints and cone are disjoint and separated by a positive distance.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The system is strongly infeasible exactly when \(L\cap K=\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(L,K)>0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential notion for infeasible conic systems with vanishing residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The system \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), is asymptotically feasible but not feasible when no \(x\in K\) satisfies \(Ax=b\), yet there exists a sequence \((x_k)\subseteq K\) such that \(\|Ax_k-b\|\to0\). Equivalently, \(b\in\overline{A(K)}\setminus A(K)\).

\(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\).

children.title: Closure-Based Feasibility Status
children.top_down_role: Status distinctions between a feasible set, its image, and its closure.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Based Feasibility Status
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies conic feasibility through membership in the linear image of the cone and its closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, and set \(C=A(K)\). The system \(Ax=b,\ x\in K\) is feasible when \(b\in C\), weakly infeasible when \(b\in\overline C\setminus C\), and strongly infeasible when \(b\notin\overline C\). In finite dimensions, strong infeasibility is equivalently \(\operatorname{dist}(b,C)>0\), whereas weak infeasibility has \(\operatorname{dist}(b,C)=0\) without an attainable feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasibility is membership in the cone image; weak infeasibility lies only in its closure, while strong infeasibility has positive distance from it.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b\in C\), \(b\in\overline C\setminus C\), and \(b\notin\overline C\) define the feasible, weakly infeasible, and strongly infeasible statuses, respectively.

children.title: Ill-Posed Feasibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Models whose feasibility classification is unstable under arbitrarily small perturbations.

knowledge_statements.title: Ill-Posed Feasibility Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies right-hand sides where arbitrarily small perturbations change conic feasibility status.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(A\) and \(K\), let \(C=A(K)\). A right-hand side \(b\) lies on the ill-posed feasibility boundary when \(b\in\partial\overline C\). For every \(\varepsilon>0\), there then exist \(b_F\in C\) and \(b_I\notin\overline C\) satisfying \(\lVert b_F-b\rVert<\varepsilon\) and \(\lVert b_I-b\rVert<\varepsilon\). Thus arbitrarily small right-hand-side perturbations can produce a feasible system or a strongly infeasible system, so the closure-based classification has zero perturbation margin at \(b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the boundary of the closed cone image, arbitrarily small right-hand-side perturbations can produce either feasibility or strong infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b\in\partial\overline{A(K)}\) implies zero distance to both feasible and strongly infeasible right-hand sides.

notation.meaning: Boundary of the closed cone image

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restriction of the boundary characterization to right-hand-side perturbations of a fixed conic representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The condition \(b\in\partial\overline{A(K)}\) characterizes ill-posedness for perturbations of \(b\) with \(A\), \(K\), the norm, and the ambient perturbation space fixed. Perturbing the map, cone, scaling, lifted representation, or perturbation subspace defines a different instance space and may change the relevant boundary and distance to ill-posedness. If \(A(K)\) has empty ambient interior, no feasible right-hand side is robust to arbitrary ambient perturbations, although relative perturbations within \(\operatorname{span}A(K)\) may be stable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed-image boundary is a fixed-formulation, right-hand-side notion whose meaning depends on the perturbation model.
assumptions_latex: The data norm and permitted perturbations are part of the instance specification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial\overline{A(K)}\text{ is not a representation-independent boundary for arbitrary data perturbations}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Status-preserving perturbation margins for fixed cone and linear map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(C=A(K)\). If \(b\notin\overline C\), every perturbation \(d\) with \(\|d\|<\operatorname{dist}(b,\overline C)\) remains strongly infeasible. If \(b\in\operatorname{int}C\), every perturbation with \(\|d\|<\operatorname{dist}(b,\mathbb R^m\setminus C)\) remains feasible. At \(b\in\partial\overline C\), the closure-based right-hand-side status margin is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to the opposite status region is a right-hand-side stability radius, and it vanishes on the closed-image boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: b\in\partial\overline C\text{ implies zero closure-based right-hand-side status margin}.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Infeasibility Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies infeasibility of a finite-dimensional conic primal constraint system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the primal conic system \(Ax=b,\ x\in K\), where \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone. Writing \(C=A(K)\), exactly one of the following holds: primal feasibility, \(b\in C\); weak primal infeasibility, \(b\in\overline C\setminus C\); or strong primal infeasibility, \(b\notin\overline C\). Strong primal infeasibility admits strict separation from \(C\), while weak primal infeasibility does not admit a strict separating functional despite the absence of a feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic primal system is feasible, weakly infeasible, or strongly infeasible according to the right-hand side's position relative to the cone image.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The three sets \(C\), \(\overline C\setminus C\), and \(\mathbb R^m\setminus\overline C\) form the primal feasibility-status partition.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Recession Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines homogeneous directions preserving the dual conic constraints and improving the dual objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the dual conic program \(\sup\{\langle b,y\rangle:A^*y+s=c,\ s\in K^*\}\), a dual recession direction is a pair \((h,r)\in\mathbb R^m\times K^*\) satisfying \(A^*h+r=0\). If \((y,s)\) is dual feasible, then \((y+th,s+tr)\) is dual feasible for every \(t\geq0\). The direction is improving when \(\langle b,h\rangle>0\); in that case the dual objective tends to \(+\infty\) along the ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual recession direction satisfies the homogeneous dual constraints; a positive objective slope makes its feasible ray unbounded above.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A^*h+r=0\), \(r\in K^*\), and \(\langle b,h\rangle>0\) define an improving dual recession direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Ray Infeasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives a directly verifiable dual ray certifying strong primal conic infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, and let \(b\in\mathbb R^m\). For the primal system \(Ax=b,\ x\in K\), a dual-ray certificate of strong infeasibility is a pair \((h,r)\in\mathbb R^m\times K^*\) satisfying \(A^*h+r=0\) and \(\langle b,h\rangle>0\). Its existence implies \(b\notin\overline{A(K)}\), so the primal system is strongly infeasible. The certificate is checked by one linear equality, membership in \(K^*\), and one strict scalar inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogeneous dual ray with positive objective slope certifies that the primal conic system is strongly infeasible.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Existence of \((h,r)\in\mathbb R^m\times K^*\) with \(A^*h+r=0\) and \(\langle b,h\rangle>0\) certifies \(b\notin\overline{A(K)}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic alternative linking strong primal infeasibility to an improving dual recession ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty closed convex cone and \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear. knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b\notin\overline{A(K)}\iff\exists(h,r):r\in K^*,\ A^*h+r=0,\ \langle b,h\rangle>0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies feasibility of the dual affine conic constraint through its slack-image closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the dual constraint system \(A^*y+s=c,\ s\in K^*\), define \(S=\operatorname{range}(A^*)+K^*\). Exactly one of the following holds: dual feasibility, \(c\in S\); weak dual infeasibility, \(c\in\overline S\setminus S\); or strong dual infeasibility, \(c\notin\overline S\). Equivalently, weak dual infeasibility has zero distance from \(c\) to \(S\) without attainment, whereas strong dual infeasibility has strictly positive distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual feasibility and its weak or strong failure are determined by the objective vector's membership in the dual slack image and its closure.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sets \(S\), \(\overline S\setminus S\), and \(\mathbb R^n\setminus\overline S\) partition the dual feasibility statuses.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Recession Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines homogeneous feasible directions of a primal conic program and identifies objective-improving rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal conic program \(\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\), a primal recession direction is a vector \(d\in K\) satisfying \(Ad=0\). If \(x\) is primal feasible, then \(x+td\) is primal feasible for every \(t\geq0\). The direction is improving when \(\langle c,d\rangle<0\); along the resulting ray, \(\langle c,x+td\rangle\to-\infty\) as \(t\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal recession direction lies in the cone and nullspace of the constraints; negative objective slope yields an unbounded feasible ray.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\in K\), \(Ad=0\), and \(\langle c,d\rangle<0\) define an improving primal recession direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Ray Unboundedness Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies a feasible base point and improving primal ray certifying unboundedness below.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A primal-ray unboundedness certificate for \(\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\) is a pair \((x_0,d)\) satisfying \(x_0\in K\), \(Ax_0=b\), \(d\in K\), \(Ad=0\), and \(\langle c,d\rangle<0\). The points \(x_0+td\) are feasible for all \(t\geq0\), and their objective values tend to \(-\infty\). The direction \(d\) alone also certifies infeasibility of the dual constraint \(A^*y+s=c,\ s\in K^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point plus a negative-cost recession direction certifies primal unboundedness and consequently dual infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The verifiable pair \((x_0,d)\) implies that the primal optimal value is \(-\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ray Certificates Are Sufficient but Not Necessary for Conic Unboundedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp limitation of feasible-base-point plus improving-direction certificates for nonpolyhedral conic programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\inf\{X_{12}:X\succeq0,\ X_{22}=1\}\) over \(X\in\mathbb S^2\). The feasible matrices \(X(t)=\begin{pmatrix}t^2&t\\t&1\end{pmatrix}\) have objective \(t\to-\infty\). Nevertheless, every recession matrix \(D\succeq0\) satisfies \(D_{22}=0\), which forces \(D_{12}=0\); hence no recession direction has strictly negative objective slope. Thus a primal-ray certificate is sufficient but not necessary for unboundedness in general. A converse does hold under additional hypotheses, including polyhedral feasible geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonpolyhedral conic program can be unbounded below without possessing a strictly improving recession ray.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf\{X_{12}:X\succeq0,\ X_{22}=1\}=-\infty\), but every \(D\in\operatorname{rec}(F)\) satisfies \(D_{12}=0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Simultaneous Status Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes conic instances in which primal and dual constraint systems are simultaneously infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal-dual pair \(Ax=b,\ x\in K\) and \(A^*y+s=c,\ s\in K^*\), simultaneous infeasibility means \(b\notin A(K)\) and \(c\notin\operatorname{range}(A^*)+K^*\). It is simultaneously strongly infeasible when, additionally, there exist \((h,r)\) and \(d\) satisfying \(r\in K^*\), \(A^*h+r=0\), \(\langle b,h\rangle>0\), \(d\in K\), \(Ad=0\), and \(\langle c,d\rangle<0\). Simultaneous primal and dual infeasibility is not excluded by weak duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Both conic constraint systems may be infeasible; simultaneous strong infeasibility is witnessed by strict dual and primal recession certificates.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Simultaneous strong infeasibility holds exactly when both a strict dual ray and a strict primal recession certificate exist.

knowledge_statements.title: Indeterminate Status Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies infeasible conic systems for which strict ray certificates are absent because the relevant image is nonclosed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=A(K)\) and \(S=\operatorname{range}(A^*)+K^*\). A primal-dual instance is certificate-indeterminate whenever \(b\in\overline C\setminus C\) or \(c\in\overline S\setminus S\). In the first case the primal system is infeasible but admits no strict dual-ray certificate; in the second case the dual system is infeasible but admits no strict primal-recession certificate. If both inclusions hold, both sides are infeasible and neither standard strict ray resolves the status. The failure arises from nonclosedness of the corresponding linear cone image.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak infeasibility creates certificate indeterminacy: an infeasible side lies in an image closure but has no strict recession-ray certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b\in\overline C\setminus C\) or \(c\in\overline S\setminus S\) prevents the corresponding strict-ray infeasibility certificate.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between genuine unboundedness and recession evidence lacking primal feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimizing \(\langle c,x\rangle\) over a convex set \(F\), a direction \(d\in\operatorname{rec}F\) with \(\langle c,d\rangle<0\), together with a point \(x_0\in F\), implies \(x_0+td\in F\) and \(\langle c,x_0+td\rangle\to-\infty\) as \(t\to\infty\). A direction satisfying only the homogeneous recession conditions is not an unboundedness certificate when no feasible base point is supplied. Consequently, apparent overlap between infeasible and unbounded labels occurs at certificate conventions that omit feasibility; under the value-based definition, one problem cannot be both infeasible and unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative-cost recession direction proves unboundedness only when paired with a feasible point; omitting that witness creates apparent status overlap.

children.title: Primal-Dual Value-Matching Certificates
children.top_down_role: Optimality evidence combining compatible primal and dual feasible witnesses.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(D\) form a weak-duality pair: \(d(y)\le p(x)\) for every primal-feasible \(x\) and dual-feasible \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility of \((\bar x,\bar y)\) and \(p(\bar x)=d(\bar y)\) certify that both witnesses are optimal and that the common value equals both optimal values.

dual objective value at a feasible point

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a primal minimization problem with feasible set \(X_P\) and value function \(p\), and a dual maximization problem with feasible set \(Y_D\) and value function \(d\). Assume weak duality: \(d(y)\le p(x)\) for all \(x\in X_P\) and \(y\in Y_D\). A pair \((\bar x,\bar y)\in X_P\times Y_D\) satisfying \(p(\bar x)=d(\bar y)\) is a value-matching certificate. It verifies \(p(\bar x)=\inf_{x\in X_P}p(x)=\sup_{y\in Y_D}d(y)=d(\bar y)\), so \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\) are respectively primal and dual optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal-feasible and dual-feasible pair with equal objective values certifies optimality of both points by weak duality.

u\) such that \( ar x\in C\), \(g_i( ar x)\le0\), \(A ar x=b\), \(\lambda_i g_i( ar x)=0\), and \[0\in\partial f( ar x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\partial g_i( ar x)+A^*
u+N_C( ar x).\] These conditions imply that \( ar x\) globally minimizes the primal objective; when the corresponding Lagrangian dual value is proper, \((\lambda,
u)\) is dual optimal and the gap is zero.

children.title: Subgradient Certificates
children.top_down_role: Global optimality evidence expressed through objective or Lagrangian subgradients.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The witness \(0\in\partial h(\bar x)\) is equivalent to global minimality of \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of h at x

review_flags: authoritative locator for the Fermat subgradient rule is missing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained certificate, including extended-valued objectives that encode constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper convex function \(h:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), a vector \(g\) belongs to \(\partial h(\bar x)\) exactly when \(h(z)\ge h(\bar x)+\langle g,z-\bar x\rangle\) for every \(z\in X\). Hence \(g=0\) is a subgradient certificate precisely when \(h(z)\ge h(\bar x)\) for every \(z\in X\). Equivalently, \[0\in\partial h(\bar x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}h(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero subgradient at a point is an exact certificate that the point globally minimizes a proper convex function.
knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-subgradient Fermat certificate is standard and fits the leaf, but the record supplies no inspectable authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subgradient Certificate for Constrained Convex Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient global optimality condition over a convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} be convex, let X\subset\mathbb{R}^n be convex, and let x\in X. Then x minimizes f over X if and only if there exists g\in\partial f(x) such that g^\top(z-x)\ge 0 for every z\in X.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point globally minimizes a convex function over a convex set exactly when it has a subgradient whose inner product with every feasible displacement is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in X}f(z)\iff\exists g\in\partial f(x)\ \text{such that}\ g^\top(z-x)\ge 0\ \forall z\in X.

children.title: Normal-Cone Certificates
children.top_down_role: Global optimality evidence expressed through feasible-set normal geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient constrained convex optimality certificate under the stated normal-cone convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty and convex, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex, and let \(\bar x\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\). Define \(N_C(\bar x)=\{v\in X^*: \langle v,z-\bar x\rangle\le 0\text{ for all }z\in C\}\). If there exists \(g\in\partial f(\bar x)\) such that \(-g\in N_C(\bar x)\), equivalently \(0\in\partial f(\bar x)+N_C(\bar x)\), then \(\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subgradient whose negative is normal to the feasible set certifies constrained global optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty and convex, \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper convex, and \(\bar x\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A pair \(g\in\partial f(\bar x)\) and \(-g\in N_C(\bar x)\) certifies that \(\bar x\) minimizes \(f\) over \(C\).

notation.meaning: normal cone defined by nonpositive displacement pairings
a subgradient of f at the candidate

review_flags: authoritative locator for the normal-cone optimality condition is missing

children.title: Subgradient–Normal-Cone Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Translation between the two certificate representations in compatible convex formulations.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper convex, \(C\) is nonempty closed convex, and a subdifferential sum-rule qualification holds at \(\bar x\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Constrained optimality, zero subgradient of \(f+\delta_C\), and cancellation between a subgradient and a normal vector are equivalent.
review_flags: exact source and ambient-space qualification are missing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence under a valid subdifferential sum rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex and let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty closed convex. At \(\bar x\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\), suppose the exact sum rule \(\partial(f+\delta_C)(\bar x)=\partial f(\bar x)+N_C(\bar x)\) holds. Then \[\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ 0\in\partial(f+\delta_C)(\bar x)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \exists g\in\partial f(\bar x)\text{ with }-g\in N_C(\bar x).\] Thus zero-subgradient and normal-cone certificates are two representations of the same first-order certificate under the sum-rule qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the exact subdifferential sum rule holds, constrained optimality is equivalent to cancellation of a subgradient by a feasible-set normal.
knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient–Normal-Cone Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional equivalence is correct when the displayed exact sum rule holds and the property kind fits the correspondence leaf. A source and an explicit ambient-space framework are still required.

children.title: Convex-Analytic Certificate Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on certificate interpretation caused by domain, closure, or qualification issues.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of Decomposed Stationarity without a Sum Rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite-dimensional closed-convex example where constrained optimality has no subgradient-plus-normal decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \mathbb R^2, let C=\{(u,v):v\ge u^2\}, D=\{(u,v):v\le-u^2\}, and f(u,v)=u+\delta_D(u,v). Both C and D are closed convex and C\cap D=\{(0,0)\}, so \bar x=(0,0) minimizes f over C. At \bar x, N_C(\bar x)=\{(0,-a):a\ge0\}, N_D(\bar x)=\{(0,b):b\ge0\}, and \partial f(\bar x)=(1,0)+N_D(\bar x). Consequently \partial f(\bar x)+N_C(\bar x)=\{(1,t):t\in\mathbb R\}, which excludes zero, although 0\in\partial(f+\delta_C)(\bar x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two tangent convex sets can leave a singleton feasible domain while decomposed subgradient-normal stationarity fails at its optimizer.
assumptions_latex: Subdifferentials and normal cones are taken in the ambient space \(\mathbb R^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x),\qquad 0\notin\partial f(\bar x)+N_C(\bar x).

notation.meaning: ambient-space convex normal cone to C at the origin

knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Decomposed Stationarity without a Sum Rule

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper convex and \(C\) is nonempty closed convex.
No subdifferential sum-rule qualification is assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The condition \(0\in\partial f(ar x)+N_C(ar x)\) remains sufficient, but it need not be necessary for minimizing \(f\) over \(C\).
review_flags: concrete counterexample and authoritative source are needed
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between validity and necessity of decomposed convex-analytic certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every proper convex \(f\) and closed convex \(C\), \(0\in\partial f(\bar x)+N_C(\bar x)\) is sufficient for \(\bar x\) to minimize \(f\) over \(C\). Necessity requires an exact sum rule at \(\bar x\). Without an appropriate relative-interior, continuity, or other qualification, only \(\partial f(\bar x)+N_C(\bar x)\subseteq\partial(f+\delta_C)(\bar x)\) is generally available. Therefore \(0\in\partial(f+\delta_C)(\bar x)\) may hold while \(0\notin\partial f(\bar x)+N_C(\bar x)\), so optimality need not admit a decomposed subgradient-normal certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a sum-rule qualification, decomposed subgradient-normal conditions remain sufficient for optimality but may cease to be necessary.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Analytic Certificate Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary claim depends on the ambient-space subdifferential calculus and needs a sourced counterexample showing failure of necessity. The conclusion also contains the malformed variable text 'ar x'.

children.title: Saddle-Point Certificates
children.top_down_role: Primal-dual optimality evidence supplied by a saddle representation.

assumptions_latex: \(L:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is the saddle function of a primal minimization and dual maximization pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The saddle inequalities certify primal and dual optimality and equality of the associated values.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global saddle inequality for a convex-concave primal-dual representation.

source_refs.locator: 5.5.2. Saddle Point Theorems p. 204

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pair \((\bar x,\bar y)\in X\times Y\) is a saddle-point certificate for \(L\) if \[L(\bar x,y)\le L(\bar x,\bar y)\le L(x,\bar y)\qquad\text{for all }x\in X, y\in Y.\] For the primal value \(\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\) and dual value \(\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)\), these inequalities certify that \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\) attain their respective optima and that both values equal \(L(\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pair satisfying the global saddle inequalities certifies attainment and equal optimal values for the represented primal and dual problems.
knowledge_statements.title: Saddle-Point Certificates

children.title: Zero-Gap Certificates
children.top_down_role: Exact value-matching certificates in an attained duality regime.

assumptions_latex: Weak duality holds: \(d(y)\le p(x)\) for all primal-feasible \(x\) and dual-feasible \(y\).
The supplied primal and dual witnesses are feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A zero primal-dual gap certifies exact optimality and attainment on both sides.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact certificate in an attained weak-duality pair.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be primal feasible and \(y\) dual feasible for a weak-duality pair, and define \(G(x,y)=p(x)-d(y)\ge0\). If \(G(\bar x,\bar y)=0\), then for every primal-feasible \(x\) and dual-feasible \(y\), \[d(y)\le d(\bar y)=p(\bar x)\le p(x).\] Hence \(\bar x\) is primal optimal, \(\bar y\) is dual optimal, both optima are attained, and their common value is \(p(\bar x)=d(\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible primal and dual witnesses with zero gap certify exact attained optimality on both sides.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Gap Certificates

children.title: Absolute Gap Certificates
children.top_down_role: Approximate value evidence measured on the original objective scale.

knowledge_statements.title: Absolute Gap Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive objective-accuracy certificate for feasible primal-dual witnesses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a primal-feasible \(x\) and dual-feasible \(y\), define the absolute gap by \(G_{\mathrm{abs}}(x,y)=p(x)-d(y)\). Weak duality gives \(G_{\mathrm{abs}}(x,y)\ge0\). If \(G_{\mathrm{abs}}(x,y)\le\varepsilon\), then, writing \(p^*\) and \(d^*\) for the primal and dual optimal values, \[0\le p(x)-p^*\le\varepsilon,\qquad 0\le d^*-d(y)\le\varepsilon,\] whenever these values are finite. Thus feasibility and the displayed gap bound form an additive \(\varepsilon\)-optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible pair whose primal value exceeds its dual value by at most epsilon certifies additive epsilon-optimality on both sides.
assumptions_latex: Weak duality holds and \((x,y)\) is a primal-dual feasible pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequality \(p(x)-d(y)\le\varepsilon\) certifies primal and dual objective errors of at most \(\varepsilon\).

source_refs.locator: 3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191

source_witnesses.locator: 3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Translation Invariance and Positive Scaling of the Absolute Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural behavior of an absolute primal-dual gap under a common affine change of objective units.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p,d\in\mathbb R\) with \(d\le p\), and let \(G_{\mathrm{abs}}=p-d\). Under \(p'=ap+b\) and \(d'=ad+b\), where \(a>0\), one has \[G'_{\mathrm{abs}}=p'-d'=a(p-d)=aG_{\mathrm{abs}}.\] Thus a common additive shift leaves the absolute gap unchanged, while a positive change of objective units scales the gap and the corresponding additive tolerance by \(a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common objective shift leaves the absolute gap unchanged; positive rescaling multiplies the gap and its additive tolerance by the same factor.

notation.meaning: primal upper bound and dual lower bound
positive scale factor and common additive shift

knowledge_statements.title: Translation Invariance and Positive Scaling of the Absolute Gap

children.title: Relative Gap Certificates
children.top_down_role: Approximate value evidence normalized by a problem-dependent reference scale.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scaled Additive Error Consequence of a Relative-Gap Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interpretation of a relative-gap threshold as an additive error bound measured in the declared scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be primal feasible and \(y\) dual feasible with finite values \(p(x)\) and \(d(y)\), and let \(0<M(x,y)<\infty\). If weak duality holds and \[(p(x)-d(y))/M(x,y)\le\varepsilon,\] then \[0\le p(x)-p^\star\le\varepsilon M(x,y),\qquad 0\le d^\star-d(y)\le\varepsilon M(x,y),\] whenever \(p^\star,d^\star\) are finite. This is a scale-relative additive bound, not automatically a multiplicative error bound relative to \(|p^\star|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relative-gap threshold yields additive primal and dual error bounds equal to the tolerance times the declared scale, but not automatically a multiplicative error bound relative to the optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) and \(y\) are feasible and have finite objective values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(x)-p^\star\le\varepsilon M(x,y)\) and \(d^\star-d(y)\le\varepsilon M(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Scaled Additive Error Consequence of a Relative-Gap Bound

assumptions_latex: Weak duality holds and \((x,y)\) is primal-dual feasible with finite objective values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequality \((p(x)-d(y))/M(x,y)\le\varepsilon\) certifies a scale-normalized primal-dual gap under the stated convention.
review_flags: normalization convention is one explicit standard choice
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scale-normalized certificate with a denominator protected against zero and small objective values.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite objective values at a primal-dual feasible pair \((x,y)\), set \(M(x,y)=\max\{1,|p(x)|,|d(y)|\}\) and \[G_{\mathrm{rel}}(x,y)=\frac{p(x)-d(y)}{M(x,y)}.\] Weak duality ensures \(G_{\mathrm{rel}}(x,y)\ge0\). The bound \(G_{\mathrm{rel}}(x,y)\le\varepsilon\) is equivalent to \(p(x)-d(y)\le\varepsilon M(x,y)\), and therefore certifies a scale-normalized gap no larger than \(\varepsilon\). The denominator convention is part of the certificate and prevents division by zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relative-gap certificate divides the nonnegative feasible primal-dual gap by an explicit, nonzero objective scale.
knowledge_statements.title: Relative Gap Certificates

source_witnesses.locator: 3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191

Let \(\phi_\star>0\) and \(\delta>0\). A value \(\bar\phi\) is a \(\delta\)-approximation of \(\phi_\star\) in relative scale if

\phi_\star\geq\bar\phi\geq\phi_\star e^{-\delta}.

children.title: Gap Normalization Conventions
children.top_down_role: Alternative scale choices governing the interpretation of relative gap values.

knowledge_statements.title: Gap Normalization Conventions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines absolute and scale-relative normalization of a finite nonnegative primal–dual gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\in\mathbb R\) be a primal upper bound, let \(d\in\mathbb R\) be a dual lower bound, and suppose \(g=p-d\ge 0\). Given a finite scale \(s(p,d)>0\), the normalized gap is \(\eta=g/s(p,d)\). The absolute convention uses \(s(p,d)=1\); a standard relative convention uses \(s(p,d)=\max\{1,|p|,|d|\}\). Thus an \(\varepsilon\)-normalized-gap certificate is the verifiable inequality \(\eta\le\varepsilon\), equivalently \(p-d\le\varepsilon s(p,d)\). The scale function and its floor must be reported with the certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized certificate divides the nonnegative primal–dual gap by a declared positive scale; absolute and relative conventions differ only in that scale.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\eta\le\varepsilon\iff p-d\le\varepsilon s(p,d)\)

notation.meaning: Primal upper bound and dual lower bound.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of absolute and scale-relative primal-dual gaps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the leaf, but no citation supports the asserted standard relative normalization convention.

children.title: Degenerate Normalization Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where zero, tiny, signed, or unstable reference values undermine normalized certificates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexample showing that objective-magnitude normalization is not invariant under an equivalent additive shift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p=1\), \(d=0\), and define \(\eta(p,d)=(p-d)/\max\{1,|p|,|d|\}\). Then \(\eta(1,0)=1\). After adding the same constant \(T\ge0\) to both bounds, the absolute gap remains one but \[\eta(1+T,T)=\frac{1}{1+T}\longrightarrow0.\] Thus an arbitrarily small reported relative gap can result from an equivalent additive objective shift without reducing the primal-dual separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Magnitude-normalized gaps can be made arbitrarily small by adding a large common constant to both objective bounds.

notation.meaning: magnitude-normalized gap under the stated convention

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Shift Instability of Magnitude-Normalized Gaps
Degenerate Normalization Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies zero, infinite, and unstable scales that invalidate normalized-gap conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A normalized gap \(g/s\) is not a valid certificate when \(s=0\), \(s=+\infty\), or \(s\) is undefined. For example, the unfloored scale \(s(p,d)=\max\{|p|,|d|\}\) gives \(s(0,0)=0\), so even the exact gap \(g=0\) produces the indeterminate ratio \(0/0\). If either bound is infinite, the corresponding relative ratio may likewise be undefined. Moreover, when \(s\downarrow0\), fixed absolute perturbations are amplified without bound. A positive floor, such as \(s(p,d)=\max\{1,|p|,|d|\}\), removes these degeneracies for finite \(p,d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalized gaps fail at zero, infinite, or undefined scales; an unfloored relative scale is already indeterminate when both bounds equal zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s\notin(0,\infty)\Longrightarrow g/s\text{ is not a valid finite normalized-gap certificate}\)
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary boundary analysis of quotient-based gap normalization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but the treatment of infinite scales and undefined extended-real ratios depends on conventions that require an inspectable source.

children.title: Problem-Dependent Gap Certificate Family
children.top_down_role: Problem-dependent gap constructions used when a full dual objective is unavailable or inconvenient.

children.title: Restricted Gap Certificates
children.top_down_role: Gap evidence evaluated over a restricted comparison set or bounded test region.

knowledge_statements.title: Restricted Gap Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses a saddle gap restricted to selected primal and dual comparison domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be convex in its first argument and concave in its second. For nonempty sets \(X_R\subseteq X\) and \(Y_R\subseteq Y\), define
\[G_R(x,y)=\sup_{v\in Y_R}L(x,v)-\inf_{u\in X_R}L(u,y).\]
If \(x\in X_R\), \(y\in Y_R\), and a saddle point \((x^\star,y^\star)\in X_R\times Y_R\) exists, then \(G_R(x,y)\ge L(x,y^\star)-L(x^\star,y)\ge0\). Consequently, a verified bound \(G_R(x,y)\le\varepsilon\) certifies that this saddle residual is at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A restricted gap compares a candidate only against declared domains. It certifies saddle accuracy when those domains contain a saddle point.
assumptions_latex: \((x^\star,y^\star)\in X_R\times Y_R\) is a saddle point
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_R(x,y)\le\varepsilon\Longrightarrow 0\le L(x,y^\star)-L(x^\star,y)\le\varepsilon\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate construction is plausible, but with an extended-real saddle function the difference of extrema can be undefined. A source is needed to establish the intended finiteness and domain hypotheses.

children.title: Surrogate Gap Certificates
children.top_down_role: Proxy value evidence used when the full primal-dual objective comparison is unavailable.

knowledge_statements.title: Surrogate Gap Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certifies a target error through a computable dominating surrogate gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E:Z\to[0,+\infty]\) be the target optimality error and let \(\widehat G:Z\to[0,+\infty]\) be computable from the candidate and validated problem data. If
\[E(z)\le \widehat G(z)\quad\text{for every }z\in D,\]
then, for any \(z\in D\), the inequality \(\widehat G(z)\le\varepsilon\) is a surrogate-gap certificate for \(E(z)\le\varepsilon\). The certificate must specify the domain \(D\), the target error \(E\), and the established domination inequality; nonnegativity of \(\widehat G\) alone is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A computable surrogate certifies optimality only when it is known to upper-bound the stated target error throughout the declared domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\in D\text{ and }\widehat G(z)\le\varepsilon\Longrightarrow E(z)\le\varepsilon\)

notation.meaning: Domain on which domination is valid.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The domination implication is correct and the certificate kind fits, but no source specifies the formal surrogate-gap convention, including the relation between D and Z and the tolerance domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Surrogate Duality Gap for Primal–Dual Interior-Point Iterates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the complementarity-based surrogate gap used when intermediate primal–dual interior-point iterates are not necessarily feasible, and states precisely when it equals an actual duality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\) satisfying \(f(x)\prec0\) and \(\lambda\succeq0\), define
\[
\widehat\eta(x,\lambda)=-f(x)^T\lambda.
\]
At a generally infeasible iterate this is only a surrogate. In the standard convex-program setting, if additionally
\[
r_{\mathrm{pri}}=Ax-b=0,\qquad r_{\mathrm{dual}}=\nabla f_0(x)+Df(x)^T\lambda+A^T\nu=0,
\]
then \(\widehat\eta\) is the primal–dual duality gap. When \(\widehat\eta>0\), the associated centrality parameter is
\[
t=\frac{m}{\widehat\eta}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a strictly inequality-feasible point and nonnegative inequality multipliers, the surrogate gap is minus the inner product of the constraint values and multipliers. It is merely a proxy when the iterate is infeasible. It equals the actual primal–dual gap when both the equality-feasibility and dual-stationarity residuals vanish. A positive surrogate gap corresponds to the centrality parameter m divided by that gap.
assumptions_latex: \text{The gap-identification statement uses the standard differentiable convex-program setting.}
r_{\mathrm{pri}}=0\ \text{and}\ r_{\mathrm{dual}}=0\ \text{when identifying }\widehat\eta\text{ with the actual duality gap}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat\eta(x,\lambda)=-f(x)^T\lambda;\qquad r_{\mathrm{pri}}=r_{\mathrm{dual}}=0\Longrightarrow\widehat\eta=\operatorname{gap};\qquad \widehat\eta>0\Longrightarrow t=m/\widehat\eta.
