children.title: Restricted-Gap Domain Selection
children.top_down_role: Structural choices of comparison domains that determine certificate strength.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares restricted gaps for nested comparison domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_1\subseteq X_2\) and \(Y_1\subseteq Y_2\), and suppose the displayed extrema are finite. If \(G_i(x,y)=\sup_{v\in Y_i}L(x,v)-\inf_{u\in X_i}L(u,y)\), then \[G_1(x,y)\le G_2(x,y).\] Thus enlarging either comparison domain cannot decrease the restricted gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested larger comparison domains produce a restricted gap at least as large as that produced by smaller domains.
assumptions_latex: All displayed suprema and infima are finite real numbers
knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity Under Domain Enlargement
Restricted-Gap Domain Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the containment and finiteness conditions required of restricted comparison domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the restricted saddle gap
\[G_R(x,y)=\sup_{v\in Y_R}L(x,v)-\inf_{u\in X_R}L(u,y),\]
a domain pair \((X_R,Y_R)\) is certificate-valid for a candidate \((x,y)\) and comparator saddle point \((x^\star,y^\star)\) when \(x,x^\star\in X_R\), \(y,y^\star\in Y_R\), and both displayed extrema are finite. Containment of \((x^\star,y^\star)\) ensures that \(G_R\) dominates the corresponding saddle residual; finiteness makes its numerical upper bound meaningful. If the comparator is not known, a sufficient selection rule is to use certified sets containing the entire primal and dual solution sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricted domains must contain the candidate and a valid saddle comparator, while producing finite extrema; otherwise the restricted gap need not certify the desired error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x,x^\star\in X_R,\ y,y^\star\in Y_R\text{ and }G_R(x,y)\in\mathbb R\)
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: containment and finiteness requirements follow from the restricted-gap definition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits, but the asserted certificate-valid domain rule and the sufficient rule involving entire solution sets require a source and explicit finite-extrema conventions.

children.title: Surrogate-Gap Validity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions limiting when a proxy gap supports conclusions about the original model.

knowledge_statements.title: Surrogate-Gap Validity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that a small surrogate is meaningless outside its domination domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The implication \(\widehat G(z)\le\varepsilon\Rightarrow E(z)\le\varepsilon\) fails if domination \(E\le\widehat G\) is absent or if \(z\) lies outside its validity domain. Concretely, for \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R}x^2\), let \(E(x)=x^2\) and choose the nonnegative surrogate \(\widehat G(x)=0\). Then \(\widehat G(x)\le0\) for every \(x\), although \(E(x)>0\) whenever \(x\ne0\). Hence computability, nonnegativity, or vanishing of a surrogate does not by itself constitute an optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small nonnegative surrogate proves nothing unless a valid domination inequality links it to the target error on the candidate's domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat G(x)=0<E(x)\), so the surrogate certificate implication fails
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit elementary counterexample to an undominated surrogate

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The elementary counterexample correctly demonstrates the stated failure boundary, but the record supplies no inspectable citation as required for this knowledge layer.

children.title: Gap-Certificate Validity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Failure cases involving infeasible witnesses, invalid bounds, unstable normalization, or nonattainment.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vanishing Gaps Without an Exact Witness Under Nonattainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary example separating arbitrarily accurate gap certificates from an attained zero-gap certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}e^x\). Its infimum is \(p^\star=0\), but no finite \(x\) attains it. The constant \(d=0\) is a valid lower bound. For \(x_k=-k\), the valid gaps satisfy \[p(x_k)-d=e^{-k}\longrightarrow0,\] yet \(p(x)-d=e^x>0\) for every feasible witness \(x\in\mathbb R\). Thus arbitrarily small valid gaps do not imply existence of an exact zero-gap witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Valid gaps can tend to zero even though primal nonattainment prevents every finite witness from having zero gap.
assumptions_latex: \(d=0\) is used as a valid lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e^{-k}\to0\) but \(e^x>0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing Gaps Without an Exact Witness Under Nonattainment
Gap-Certificate Validity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collects feasibility, bound-validity, normalization, and attainment requirements for gap certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem, a reported difference \(p-d\) certifies suboptimality only when \(p\) is produced by a primal-feasible point, \(d\) is a valid lower bound, and weak duality gives \(d\le p^\star\le p\). An infeasible primal witness need not yield an upper bound, and an infeasible or otherwise invalid dual witness need not yield a lower bound; consequently \(p-d\) may even be negative. Normalized certificates additionally require a finite positive scale. Finally, nonattainment permits convergent bound sequences with gap tending to zero but prevents an exact zero-gap witness unless the relevant optima are attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A numerical gap is valid only from genuine primal and dual bounds. Invalid witnesses, degenerate scales, or nonattainment defeat stronger certificate interpretations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\le p^\star\le p\Longrightarrow 0\le p-p^\star\le p-d\); without these inequalities the conclusion is unsupported
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: weak-duality requirements and elementary nonattainment boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and weak-duality warning fit the node, but the combined claims about witness validity, normalization, and nonattainment lack a supporting locator.

children.top_down_role: Certificate families supporting quantified near-optimality under analytic or numerical error notions.

children.title: Approximate KKT Certificates
children.top_down_role: Residual-based approximations to primal-dual optimality systems.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximate KKT Residuals Depend on Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Raw residual magnitudes are meaningful only after norms and constraint scaling are fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an equality constraint \(h(x)=0\), replacing it by the equivalent equation \(\alpha h(x)=0\), where \(\alpha>0\), changes the raw feasibility residual from \(\|h(x)\|\) to \(\alpha\|h(x)\|\). With the multiplier transformation \(\widetilde\nu=\nu/\alpha\), the exact Lagrangian and KKT system are unchanged. Thus an unnormalized approximate-KKT tolerance is not invariant under equivalent constraint rescaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent constraint scaling preserves exact KKT conditions but can arbitrarily change raw approximate residuals.
assumptions_latex: h(x)=0\text{ and }\alpha h(x)=0\text{ represent the same equality constraint}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|\alpha h(x)\|=\alpha\|h(x)\|\text{ although the exact feasible set and KKT system are unchanged}.

notation.meaning: Multipliers for the original and scaled constraints

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate KKT Residuals Depend on Scaling
Approximate KKT Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines residual-based approximate KKT evidence for a finite-dimensional convex program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(\min_x f_0(x)\) subject to \(f_i(x)\le0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\) and \(Ax=b\), where all \(f_i\) are proper convex functions. A triple \((x,\lambda,\nu)\), with \(\lambda\ge0\), is an \((\varepsilon_p,\varepsilon_s,\varepsilon_c)\)-KKT certificate when
\[\left\|(f(x))_+\right\|\le\varepsilon_p,\quad \|Ax-b\|\le\varepsilon_p,\]
\[\operatorname{dist}\!\left(0,\partial f_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\partial f_i(x)+A^T\nu\right)\le\varepsilon_s,\quad \max_i|\lambda_i f_i(x)|\le\varepsilon_c.\]
At zero tolerances these are the KKT conditions. Positive residuals imply quantitative optimality only with an additional error bound or regularity estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate KKT certificate reports primal feasibility, stationarity, dual nonnegativity, and complementarity residuals; converting them to objective error requires additional regularity.
assumptions_latex: \(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_m\) are proper convex functions on \(\mathbb R^n\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,\lambda,\nu)\) satisfies the displayed KKT residual tolerances

notation.meaning: Componentwise positive part of the inequality residual vector.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard residual relaxation of convex KKT conditions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Approximate KKT evidence belongs in this container, but the exact residual system is convention-dependent. The tolerances, multiplier space for ν, norms, definition of f(x), and subdifferential-sum conventions need authoritative specification.

children.title: Approximate Subgradient Certificates
children.top_down_role: Near-optimality evidence based on relaxed convex-analytic stationarity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completes the seed implication with its converse in finite-dimensional dual pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be proper and convex, let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}F\), and let \(\varepsilon\ge0\). If \(F(x)\le\inf_yF(y)+\varepsilon\), then \(0\in\partial_\varepsilon F(x)\). Together with the seed implication, \[0\in\partial_\varepsilon F(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F(x)\le\inf_yF(y)+\varepsilon.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is epsilon-optimal exactly when zero belongs to its epsilon-subdifferential.
assumptions_latex: F:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\text{ is proper and convex}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(x)\le\inf_yF(y)+\varepsilon\Longrightarrow0\in\partial_\varepsilon F(x).
knowledge_statements.title: Epsilon-Subgradient Optimality Equivalence
Approximate Subgradient Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses an epsilon-subgradient containing zero to certify objective near-optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be proper and convex on a real vector space \(X\). For \(x\in\operatorname{dom}F\) and \(\varepsilon\ge0\), define
\[\partial_\varepsilon F(x)=\{g: F(y)\ge F(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle-\varepsilon\ \text{for every }y\in X\}.\]
If \(0\in\partial_\varepsilon F(x)\), then \(F(x)\le F(y)+\varepsilon\) for every \(y\in X\), and therefore \(F(x)-\inf_XF\le\varepsilon\). Thus membership of zero in the epsilon-subdifferential is directly verifiable near-optimality evidence whenever that membership itself can be certified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If zero is an epsilon-subgradient at a point, that point's objective value lies within epsilon of the global infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\partial_\varepsilon F(x)\Longrightarrow F(x)-\inf_{y\in X}F(y)\le\varepsilon\)

notation.meaning: Epsilon-subdifferential of the convex function at the candidate.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The epsilon-subgradient implication is standard and fits the certificate leaf, but g must be placed in an appropriate dual space and the definition requires a supporting source with a precise ambient-space convention.

children.title: Feasibility-plus-Objective Certificates
children.top_down_role: Joint evidence combining controlled constraint violation with objective-quality information.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective Quality Does Not Repair Infeasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows why feasibility and objective components must be reported separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{x:x\ge0\}\), whose optimal value is \(p^\star=0\). For every \(\delta>0\), the point \(x=-\delta\) has constraint violation \(\delta\) and objective value \(-\delta<p^\star\). Thus a small feasibility residual together with an apparently better objective value does not make the candidate feasible or optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A slightly infeasible point can have an objective value better than the feasible optimum, so objective quality cannot substitute for feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x=-\delta\text{ has violation }\delta\text{ and }f(x)=-\delta<p^\star.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective Quality Does Not Repair Infeasibility
Feasibility-plus-Objective Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines explicit constraint-violation tolerances with a certified objective lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(p^\star=\inf\{f_0(x):f_i(x)\le0,\ Ax=b\}\), let \(\ell\le p^\star\) be a certified lower bound. A candidate \(x\) has a \((\delta,\varepsilon)\) feasibility-plus-objective certificate if
\[\max_i(f_i(x))_+\le\delta,\qquad \|Ax-b\|\le\delta,\qquad f_0(x)-\ell\le\varepsilon.\]
The first two inequalities certify \(\delta\)-feasibility, while \(\ell\le p^\star\) and the third imply \(f_0(x)-p^\star\le\varepsilon\). When \(\delta>0\), this objective comparison does not assert that \(x\) is feasible; feasibility and objective quality remain separately reported components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The certificate pairs bounded constraint violation with an objective value close to a verified lower bound, keeping feasibility and objective claims distinct.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is }\delta\text{-feasible and }f_0(x)-p^\star\le\varepsilon\)
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct combination of residual feasibility and lower-bound objective certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The joint certificate kind fits and the lower-bound inference is plausible, but a source is needed for this certificate convention and for the required finiteness of the objective values and primal infimum.

children.title: Residual-to-Value-Error Certificates
children.top_down_role: Routes converting computable residuals into objective-value error estimates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-error conversion under a PL inequality without requiring strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable with finite infimum \(F^\star\), and suppose that on a set \(U\), \[\frac12\|\nabla F(x)\|_*^2\ge\mu_{\mathrm{PL}}\bigl(F(x)-F^\star\bigr),\qquad \mu_{\mathrm{PL}}>0.\] Then every \(x\in U\) with \(\|\nabla F(x)\|_*\le r\) satisfies \[0\le F(x)-F^\star\le\frac{r^2}{2\mu_{\mathrm{PL}}}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a PL inequality, a gradient residual of size r certifies objective error at most r squared over twice the PL constant.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ is differentiable and }F^\star=\inf F\in\mathbb R.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in U,\ \|\nabla F(x)\|_*\le r\Longrightarrow F(x)-F^\star\le\frac{r^2}{2\mu_{\mathrm{PL}}}.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyak–Łojasiewicz Gradient-Residual Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: No Uniform Value Bound from Residual Alone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that a residual magnitude needs a conditioning modulus to yield a uniform value-error certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(r>0\). For every \(R>0\), let \(F_R(t)=\frac{r}{2R}t^2\) and evaluate it at \(t=R\). Then \(F_R^\star=0\), \[|F_R'(R)|=r,\qquad F_R(R)-F_R^\star=\frac{rR}{2}.\] Thus a fixed gradient-residual bound is compatible with arbitrarily large objective error as \(R\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Across convex objectives with no common conditioning modulus, the same gradient residual can accompany arbitrarily large value error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |F_R'(R)|=r\quad\text{while}\quad F_R(R)-F_R^\star=\frac{rR}{2}\to\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: No Uniform Value Bound from Residual Alone
Residual-to-Value-Error Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converts a subgradient residual into objective error under strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be proper, closed, and \(\mu\)-strongly convex with \(\mu>0\), and let \(x^\star\) be its unique minimizer. For any \(x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial F\) and any computable \(g\in\partial F(x)\),
\[0\le F(x)-F(x^\star)\le\frac{\|g\|_*^2}{2\mu}.\]
Consequently, the residual bound \(\|g\|_*\le r\) certifies the value error \(F(x)-F(x^\star)\le r^2/(2\mu)\). The modulus \(\mu\) and the norm-dual-norm pair are part of the certificate data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a strongly convex objective, a subgradient of dual norm at most r certifies objective error at most r squared over twice the strong-convexity modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, closed, and \(\mu\)-strongly convex with \(\mu>0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|g\|_*\le r\Longrightarrow F(x)-F(x^\star)\le r^2/(2\mu)\)

notation.meaning: Dual norm paired with the strong-convexity norm.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard strong-convexity subgradient error bound

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual-to-value bound is mathematically standard and fits the leaf, but its constant depends on the declared strong-convexity and dual-norm conventions, for which no locator is supplied.

children.title: Residual-to-Solution-Error Certificates
children.top_down_role: Routes converting residual evidence into distance-to-solution information under additional regularity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General local residual-to-solution conversion encompassing the strong-monotonicity specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\), let \(S=T^{-1}(0)\ne\varnothing\), and suppose that on a neighborhood \(U\), \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,T(x)).\] If \(x\in U\) and a computable \(u\in T(x)\) satisfies \(\|u\|\le r\), then \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa r.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A metric-subregularity error bound converts a graph residual of size r into distance at most kappa times r from the solution set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|u\|\le r\Longrightarrow\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa r.

notation.meaning: Zero set of the optimality operator
Neighborhood on which the error bound holds

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Subregularity Residual Certificate
Residual-to-Solution-Error Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converts an inclusion residual into distance to the solution under strong monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) be \(\mu\)-strongly monotone with \(\mu>0\), meaning
\[\langle u-v,x-y\rangle\ge\mu\|x-y\|^2\]
for all \(u\in T(x)\) and \(v\in T(y)\). If \(0\in T(x^\star)\) and a candidate supplies \(u\in T(x)\), then
\[\|x-x^\star\|\le\frac{\|u\|_*}{\mu}.\]
Thus \(\|u\|_*\le r\) certifies solution error at most \(r/\mu\). Without strong monotonicity or another metric error bound, a small residual need not control distance to the solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong monotonicity converts a residual of dual norm at most r into distance at most r divided by the monotonicity modulus.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|u\|_*\le r\Longrightarrow\|x-x^\star\|\le r/\mu\)
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard strong-monotonicity residual error bound

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual-to-solution estimate fits the leaf, but the strong-monotonicity pairing and norm conventions underlying the bound require an authoritative source locator.

children.title: Exact versus Numerical Certificates
children.top_down_role: Distinction between exact witnesses and tolerance-dependent floating-point evidence.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States when numerical evaluation rigorously establishes exact verifier predicates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose outward-rounded interval arithmetic establishes h_i(D,\widehat w)\in[\underline h_i,\overline h_i]. Then \overline h_i\le0 certifies the exact inequality h_i(D,\widehat w)\le0. An equality h_i(D,\widehat w)=0 is certified only by exact evaluation or by a validated singleton enclosure [0,0]. Numerical computation therefore supports an exact certificate only when every verifier predicate is validated in its required logical direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validated enclosures can certify exact inequalities, while exact equalities require exact evaluation or a singleton zero enclosure.
assumptions_latex: The data and witness have declared exact interpretations.
The interval implementation guarantees outward rounding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \overline h_i\le0\Rightarrow h_i(D,\widehat w)\le0,\qquad [\underline h_i,\overline h_i]=[0,0]\Rightarrow h_i(D,\widehat w)=0.

notation.meaning: validated enclosure of a verifier expression

knowledge_statements.title: Validated Numerical Predicates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates existence of a mathematical witness from availability of a finite exact certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Existence of a real-valued witness satisfying exact predicates does not itself provide a finite exact certificate. Such a certificate additionally requires a finite representation in the declared domain—such as rational or suitably encoded algebraic data—and a verifier that decides the predicates on that representation. Otherwise only approximations may be encodable even when an exact real witness exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact real witness need not have a finite independently checkable exact encoding.
assumptions_latex: Certificates are finite strings interpreted by a specified verifier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists w\in\mathbb R^n\ C(D,w)\not\Rightarrow\exists e\in\{0,1\}^*\ V(D,e)=1\text{ without finite representability and decidable predicates}.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Exact-Encoding Boundary
Exact versus Numerical Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes exact acceptance from tolerance-dependent evidence for a fixed convex-program verifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) encode a convex program, \(w\) a witness, and \(V\) a specified verifier. An exact certificate is a pair \((D,w)\) for which \(V(D,w)=1\) using exact predicates over the declared number domain; acceptance certifies the nominal conclusion \(C(D)\). A numerical certificate is a tuple \((D,\widehat w,\varepsilon)\) accepted through tolerance tests such as \(r(D,\widehat w)\leq\varepsilon\). Without validated rounding and conditioning bounds, this acceptance establishes only the stated relaxed conclusion \(C_\varepsilon(D)\), not necessarily \(C(D)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact certificates prove the nominal claim through exact predicates; numerical certificates depend on tolerances and prove only a quantified relaxed claim unless errors are rigorously bounded.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) and the verifier's arithmetic conventions are explicitly encoded.
\(\varepsilon\geq 0\) is part of the numerical certificate specification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(D,w)=1\Rightarrow C(D)\) exactly, whereas numerical acceptance generally yields only \(C_\varepsilon(D)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact verification and tolerance-based residual acceptance are standard certificate distinctions
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction fits the leaf and the definition is internally coherent, but no inspectable source is supplied for the claimed verifier semantics, especially the assertion that tolerance acceptance yields only the particular relaxed conclusion C_epsilon(D).

children.title: Global Certificates versus Residual-Only Evidence
children.top_down_role: Distinction between evidence supporting a global convex conclusion and local numerical consistency checks.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vanishing Residual without a Uniform Global Guarantee
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows why residual magnitude alone has no uniform objective meaning across differently conditioned convex programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \delta>0, let f_\delta(x)=\frac{\delta}{2}x^2 and x_\delta=\delta^{-1/2}. The unique minimizer is 0, while |f_\delta'(x_\delta)|=\sqrt\delta\to0 and f_\delta(x_\delta)-f_\delta(0)=\frac12. Thus arbitrarily small stationarity residuals do not imply a uniform vanishing objective gap without conditioning information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Across increasingly ill-conditioned convex quadratics, gradient residuals vanish while the objective gap remains fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |f_\delta'(x_\delta)|\to0\quad\text{but}\quad f_\delta(x_\delta)-\inf f_\delta=\tfrac12.
knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing Residual without a Uniform Global Guarantee

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Convexity Converts Stationarity Residuals into Global Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States a conditioning assumption under which a local residual yields a global conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f:\mathbb R^n	o\mathbb R be differentiable and \mu-strongly convex with \mu>0, and let x^* be its minimizer. Then \|x-x^*\|\le\|
abla f(x)\|/\mu and f(x)-f(x^*)\le\|
abla f(x)\|^2/(2\mu). Hence a checked residual \|
abla f(x)\|\le\varepsilon, together with a validated modulus \mu, certifies global distance and objective bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gradient residual becomes quantified global evidence when paired with a certified positive strong-convexity modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable and \(\mu\)-strongly convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|\nabla f(x)\|\le\varepsilon\Rightarrow \|x-x^*\|\le\varepsilon/\mu\text{ and }f(x)-f(x^*)\le\varepsilon^2/(2\mu).
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Convexity Converts Stationarity Residuals into Global Bounds
Global Certificates versus Residual-Only Evidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses finite-dimensional conic primal–dual feasibility to distinguish global optimality from small residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the primal problem \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\) and dual problem \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:c-A^{\mathsf T}y=s,\ s\in K^*\}\), where \(K\) is a closed convex cone. A tuple \((x,y,s)\) satisfying both feasibility systems and \(c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y\) is a globally checkable optimality certificate: weak duality makes \(x\) and \(y\) optimal. Merely small primal, dual, or complementarity residuals are local numerical consistency evidence and imply no prescribed global objective bound without additional validated error or conditioning estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact primal–dual feasibility with zero gap certifies global conic optimality. Small residuals alone do not provide a quantified global conclusion.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax=b,\ x\in K,\ c-A^{\mathsf T}y=s\in K^*,\ c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y\Rightarrow x\text{ and }y\text{ are globally optimal}\).

children.title: Robust versus Fragile Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certificate behavior under perturbation, scaling, and rounding.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives a quantitative sufficient condition for persistence under bounded data perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose certificate validity is expressed by finitely many inequalities h_i(D,w)\le0, and |h_i(D',w)-h_i(D,w)|\le L_i d(D',D). If h_i(D,w)\le-m_i with m_i>0 for every i, define \rho=\min_i m_i/L_i with m_i/0:=+\infty. Then the same witness remains valid whenever d(D',D)<\rho. Strict verifier margins and sensitivity bounds therefore provide a certified robustness radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict slack divided by sensitivity bounds gives a positive radius within which the same certificate remains valid.
assumptions_latex: The validity predicates are finitely many inequalities.
Each predicate has a declared perturbation bound with \(L_i\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d(D',D)<\rho\Rightarrow h_i(D',w)<0\quad\forall i.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Margin Perturbation Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that exact acceptance alone need not provide a positive perturbation radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the scalar claim D\le0, the exact certificate at D=0 is valid but has zero margin. For every \delta>0, the perturbation D'=\delta/2 satisfies |D'-D|<\delta and invalidates the claim. Exact validity at a boundary point therefore need not imply robustness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate accepted with zero slack can be destroyed by arbitrarily small perturbations.
assumptions_latex: Perturbations are measured by absolute distance on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D=0\text{ is valid, but no positive radius preserves }D'\le0\text{ under all perturbations in that radius}.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Margin Certificate Fragility
Robust versus Fragile Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines robustness through persistence of verifier acceptance and meaning under bounded encoded-data perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\) be a metric on encoded instances and let \(C(D,w)\) denote the conclusion attached to an accepted witness. An accepted certificate \((D,w)\) is robust if there exists \(\delta>0\) such that every admissible \(D'\) with \(d(D,D')<\delta\), including declared scaling or rounding perturbations, admits verification of the same conclusion from \(w\) or a prescribed correction of \(w\). It is fragile if no such positive radius exists: arbitrarily small admissible perturbations can invalidate acceptance or its conclusion. Robustness is always relative to the metric, perturbation model, and verifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A robust certificate remains valid within a positive perturbation radius under declared corrections; a fragile one can fail after arbitrarily small admissible perturbations.
assumptions_latex: \(d\) and the admissible perturbation set are fixed.
Any allowed witness-correction rule is part of the verifier specification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\delta>0\) with persistent validity defines robustness; failure for every \(\delta>0\) defines fragility.

children.title: Certificate Size-Verification Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: Representation size and independent verification cost of convex-program witnesses.

children.title: Certificate Representation Size
children.top_down_role: Storage requirements for points, rays, multipliers, residual data, or auxiliary witness objects.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sparse Versus Dense Fixed-Width Vector Representation Size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-length comparison under fixed-width scalar and index encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(w\in\mathbb Q^n\) have \(s\) nonzero coordinates. Suppose every stored scalar occupies exactly \(B\) bits, every index occupies \(\Theta(\log n)\) bits, and dimensions and framing occupy \(O(\log n)\) bits. Then a dense coordinate encoding has length \[\Theta(nB+\log n),\] while a sparse index-value encoding has length \[\Theta\!\left(s(B+\log n)+\log n\right).\] Hence the sparse representation is asymptotically smaller precisely in regimes where \(s(B+\log n)=o(nB)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With fixed-width scalars, sparse storage replaces one scalar per ambient coordinate by one index-value pair per nonzero coordinate.
assumptions_latex: Each stored scalar uses exactly \(B\) bits.
Each explicit index uses \(\Theta(\log n)\) bits.
Dimension and framing metadata use \(O(\log n)\) bits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_{\mathrm{dense}}=\Theta(nB+\log n),\qquad L_{\mathrm{sparse}}=\Theta(s(B+\log n)+\log n).
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Versus Dense Fixed-Width Vector Representation Size

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Few Coordinates Do Not Imply Small Bit Length
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numeric-magnitude boundary for explicit exact binary certificate storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(k\ge0\), consider the one-coordinate integer witness \(w_k=(2^{2^k})\). Under ordinary explicit binary integer encoding, the witness has one coordinate but its scalar payload has exactly \(2^k+1\) bits. Thus coordinate count, dimension, rank, or sparsity alone cannot upper-bound exact certificate representation size without controlling numeric bit length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate may contain one scalar yet require exponentially many bits because of that scalar's magnitude.
assumptions_latex: Integers are stored explicitly in binary rather than by an arithmetic expression.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \dim(w_k)=1\quad\text{but}\quad L_{\mathrm{binary}}(w_k)\ge2^k+1.
knowledge_statements.title: Few Coordinates Do Not Imply Small Bit Length

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariance of polynomial certificate-size bounds under mutually polynomially bounded instance and witness encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) be uniquely decodable encodings of the same instances and instance-witness pairs. Suppose polynomials \(p,q\) satisfy \[|E_2(D)|\le p(|E_1(D)|),\quad |E_1(D)|\le q(|E_2(D)|),\] and the analogous two bounds hold for \(|E_j(D,w)|\). Then a certificate family has total encoded instance-witness length polynomial in the corresponding encoded instance length under \(E_1\) if and only if it does under \(E_2\). Exact bit lengths and constant factors may nevertheless differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mutually polynomially related encodings preserve whether certificate families have polynomial total encoded length, although their exact lengths can differ.
assumptions_latex: \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) are fixed uniquely decodable encodings of the same instances and instance-witness objects.
Instance-only lengths and total instance-witness lengths are polynomially bounded in both directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{poly\text{-}size}_{E_1}\iff\operatorname{poly\text{-}size}_{E_2}.

notation.meaning: Two fixed encodings of the same instance and witness objects.
Polynomial bounds relating the encoded lengths.

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Equivalence of Representation-Size Measures
Certificate Representation Size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measures certificate length under a fixed finite, uniquely decodable encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a binary encoding \(E\) for a problem instance \(D\) and witness \(w\). The certificate representation size is \(L_E(D,w)=|E(D,w)|\), the number of encoded bits, optionally reported as the incremental witness length \(|E(w\mid D)|\) when \(D\) is already available to the checker. For a reduced rational \(p/q\), a standard exact contribution is \(1+\lceil\log_2(1+|p|)\rceil+\lceil\log_2(1+q)\rceil\), plus framing bits. Aggregate vector and matrix sizes include dimensions, structure tags, indices, and every encoded scalar.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certificate size is the bit length of a fixed, uniquely decodable encoding, including numeric data, dimensions, indices, tags, and framing.
assumptions_latex: Exact rationals are stored in reduced form with positive denominator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_E(D,w)=|E(D,w)|\) is a representation-dependent bit complexity measure.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: bit length under a fixed encoding is the standard representation-size measure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content_kind fits representation size, but no source supports the encoding-dependent size definition or the stated rational bit contribution. The latter also depends on a specific sign and framing convention and therefore requires a direct locator.

children.title: Certificate Encoding Structure
children.top_down_role: Dense, sparse, factored, or implicit representations affecting witness portability.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lossless sparse representation of a finite rational vector or matrix witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sparse encoding of \(w\in\mathbb Q^n\) is a tuple \((n,(i_1,w_{i_1}),\ldots,(i_s,w_{i_s}))\) with \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_s\le n\) and \(w_{i_j}\ne0\). Decoding assigns the listed values to their indices and zero to omitted coordinates. Recording the dimension and requiring ordered, in-range, unique indices makes decoding unambiguous. The analogous matrix encoding records both dimensions and ordered index pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sparse witness is losslessly decoded when its shape, ordered unique indices, values, and zero-by-omission convention are explicit.
assumptions_latex: Witness scalars have a fixed finite exact encoding.
Indices have a fixed finite integer encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Dec}(E_{\mathrm{sparse}}(w))=w.

notation.meaning: number of explicitly stored nonzero coordinates

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Coordinate Encoding

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Omitted Shape or Semantics Makes an Encoding Ambiguous
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal decoding failures caused by missing metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sparse payload \(((1,1))\) does not determine whether the decoded vector is \((1)\), \((1,0)\), or any longer vector with trailing zeros unless the ambient dimension is encoded. Likewise, a byte string denoting numeric fields does not determine whether it represents a point, ray, multiplier, or factor without a certificate-type and verifier convention. Therefore payload values alone need not define a unique certificate object or verification predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Missing dimensions or verifier semantics can make one payload denote different witnesses or certificate types.
assumptions_latex: Omitted sparse coordinates are interpreted as zero.
No external dimension, type, or verifier metadata is assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Payload-only decoding need not be a function.}
knowledge_statements.title: Omitted Shape or Semantics Makes an Encoding Ambiguous

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reconstruction of a structured witness from finitely encoded factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A factored encoding represents a witness \(W\) by finite factor data \(q\) and a declared reconstruction map \(R\), with \(R(q)=W\). For example, a positive-semidefinite witness may be encoded by a rational matrix \(U\) with \(W=UU^T\). Independent verification must either evaluate certificate predicates through factor identities valid for \(R(q)\), or reconstruct \(W\); properties not implied by the declared reconstruction require separate checks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A factored witness is portable only when its factors, dimensions, reconstruction map, and factor-level verification identities are explicit.
assumptions_latex: The factors and all dimensions have finite unambiguous encodings.
The reconstruction map and verifier semantics are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Dec}(q)=R(q)=W.
knowledge_statements.title: Factored Certificate Encoding

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite program or circuit representation whose declared evaluator supplies witness entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An implicit encoding of a finite witness \(w\in S^n\) consists of \((n,P)\), where \(P\) is a finitely encoded deterministic program or circuit such that evaluation on every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) terminates and returns \(w_i\) in the declared scalar representation. It is independently interpretable only relative to specified evaluator semantics; compact description length alone gives no bound on evaluation or verification cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An implicit witness uses a finite coordinate evaluator and requires fixed semantics, dimensions, termination, and scalar conventions.
assumptions_latex: The evaluator semantics and scalar representation are fixed.
The evaluator terminates on every valid coordinate index.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: w_i=\operatorname{Eval}(P,i)\quad(i=1,\ldots,n).

notation.meaning: finite program or circuit encoding the witness

knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Certificate Encoding

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lossless explicit coordinate representation of a finite exact vector or matrix witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(w=(w_1,\ldots,w_n)\in\mathbb Q^n\), a dense encoding records \((n,w_1,\ldots,w_n)\) using a fixed uniquely decodable scalar encoding. Decoding is lossless when exactly \(n\) scalars follow the dimension field. A dense matrix encoding analogously records both dimensions and all entries in a declared row-major or column-major order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense encoding stores every coordinate together with dimensions and a declared traversal order.
assumptions_latex: Scalar encodings are finite and uniquely decodable.
Vector dimension or matrix shape and coordinate order are explicit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Dec}(E_{\mathrm{dense}}(w))=w.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense Coordinate Encoding
Certificate Encoding Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies the fields required for an unambiguous, independently checkable certificate encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A self-contained certificate encoding may be represented as \(E(D,w)=(t,m,D,w,a,\tau)\), where \(t\) identifies the certificate type, \(m\) records dimensions and cone or domain declarations, \(a\) declares arithmetic and scaling conventions, and \(\tau\) records tolerances when verification is numerical. The encoding is well formed only if parsing is unique, all referenced indices and dimensions are valid, every scalar has a declared numeric representation, and the verifier determined by \(t\) can reconstruct its predicates without unstated metadata. Canonical ordering prevents equivalent field permutations from creating ambiguous representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate encoding must uniquely expose its type, dimensions, data, witness, arithmetic conventions, and tolerances so an independent checker can reconstruct every predicate.
assumptions_latex: All fields use a finite alphabet and explicit framing.
The certificate type determines a unique verifier version.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E(D,w)\) is independently checkable only when decoding and verifier selection are unambiguous.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: unique decoding and explicit verifier conventions are standard requirements for checkable encodings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation content_kind fits the leaf, but the proposed tuple and its mandatory fields are a design specification rather than a universal mathematical encoding structure. children.title: Certificate Checking Complexity
children.top_down_role: Computational cost of independently validating the supplied witness.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial-Time Exact Checking of Rational Linear Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-checking bound for a rational primal-dual linear-program certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the rational pair \[\max\{c^Tx:Ax\le b\},\qquad \min\{b^Ty:A^Ty=c,\ y\ge0\}.\] Given rational vectors \(x,y\), a checker can verify \(Ax\le b\), \(A^Ty=c\), \(y\ge0\), and \(c^Tx=b^Ty\) in deterministic time polynomial in the total binary encoding length \(N\) of the instance and witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and value equality for a rational linear program are checkable in polynomial bit time.
assumptions_latex: All problem data and witness entries are finitely encoded rational numbers.
The total encoded instance-and-witness length is \(N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_V(N)=\operatorname{poly}(N).

notation.meaning: total bit length of the rational instance and certificate

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial-Time Exact Checking of Rational Linear Certificates

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unit-Cost Arithmetic Does Not Bound Exact Bit Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operand-growth counterexample separating arithmetic-operation counts from bit-operation bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from the binary integer \(u_0=2\), form \(u_{j+1}=u_j^2\) for \(j=0,\ldots,k-1\). This uses exactly \(k\) arithmetic multiplications, but \(u_k=2^{2^k}\) has binary length \(2^k+1\). Consequently, a unit-cost arithmetic bound of \(O(k)\) does not imply a polynomial bit-operation bound in \(k\) when exact operand growth is uncontrolled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated squaring takes linearly many unit-cost multiplications while producing exponentially long exact operands.
assumptions_latex: Arithmetic is exact over binary integers.
The arithmetic-operation model charges one unit per multiplication regardless of operand length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \#\mathrm{arith}(k)=k\quad\text{while}\quad |u_k|_{\mathrm{bit}}=2^k+1.

notation.meaning: integer after the j-th repeated squaring

knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Cost Arithmetic Does Not Bound Exact Bit Complexity
Certificate Checking Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines checking cost in exact bit complexity for a finite encoded certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z=E(D,w)\) have bit length \(N=|z|\), and let \(V\) be a deterministic exact checker. Its checking complexity is the worst-case number \(T_V(N)\) of bit operations over well-formed inputs of length at most \(N\), including parsing and arithmetic on encoded numbers. The certificate family is polynomial-time checkable if constants \(c>0\), \(k\geq0\), and \(N_0\) exist such that \(T_V(N)\leq cN^k\) for every \(N\geq N_0\). Arithmetic-operation counts alone are not bit-complexity bounds unless operand growth is also controlled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Checking complexity counts worst-case bit operations, including parsing and growing operands; polynomial checkability requires a uniform polynomial bound in total encoded length.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is deterministic and terminates on every well-formed encoding.
The computation model uses bit operations on finite strings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_V(N)\leq cN^k\) eventually is the polynomial certificate-checking criterion.

children.title: Size–Verification Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Structural tradeoffs between compact witness representations and inexpensive checking.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that the budgeted lower envelope can have no corresponding attainable Pareto point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathcal W=(0,1], with L(w)=0 and T(w)=w. Then T^*(s)=0 for every s\ge0, but no witness attains cost 0. Moreover every w\in\mathcal W is dominated by w/2, so the attainable nondominated set is empty even though the budgeted lower envelope is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite budgeted infimum can exist without any frontier witness attaining it.
assumptions_latex: Witness costs may range over nonnegative real values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T^*(s)=0\text{ is unattained, and the attainable Pareto frontier is empty}.
knowledge_statements.title: Unattained Budget Infimum

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Budgeted Tradeoff Monotonicity and Frontier Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarifies the relation between the budgeted lower envelope and the attainable Pareto frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let T_D^*(s)=\inf\{T(w):w\in\mathcal W(D),\ L(w)\le s\}. If s_1\le s_2, then T_D^*(s_2)\le T_D^*(s_1). The graph of T_D^* describes an infimal lower envelope; a pair (s,T_D^*(s)) represents an attainable frontier point only when the infimum is attained. Thus the budget function and the attainable nondominated set are equivalent only with an appropriate attainment convention or after passing to a closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Larger size budgets cannot increase the best checking cost, but the budgeted infimum need not be realized by a certificate.
assumptions_latex: All witnesses are compared under fixed encoding and computation models.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s_1\le s_2\Longrightarrow T_D^*(s_2)\le T_D^*(s_1),\quad\text{and attainment is required to identify its graph with attainable frontier points}.

notation.meaning: infimal verification cost under size budget s

knowledge_statements.title: Budgeted Tradeoff Monotonicity and Frontier Attainment
Size–Verification Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents the Pareto tradeoff between encoded witness length and worst-case verification cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance \(D\), let \(\mathcal W(D)\) be its valid witnesses. Under encoding \(E\) and checker \(V\), associate with each \(w\in\mathcal W(D)\) the pair \((L_E(D,w),T_V(E(D,w)))\). The size–verification frontier is the set of nondominated pairs: \((L,T)\) is excluded when another valid representation has \(L'\leq L\) and \(T'\leq T\), with at least one strict inequality. Equivalently, the budgeted tradeoff function is \(T_D^*(s)=\inf\{T_V(E(D,w)):w\in\mathcal W(D),\ L_E(D,w)\leq s\}\), with value \(+\infty\) when no witness meets the budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tradeoff frontier contains certificate representations for which neither encoded size nor checking time can be improved without worsening the other.
assumptions_latex: A common computation model measures all checking times.
All compared encodings certify the same mathematical conclusion for \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_D^*(s)\) gives the least verification cost attainable under size budget \(s\).

notation.meaning: best checking time under size budget s

children.title: Termination-Cause Classification
children.top_down_role: Computational reasons for stopping, including completion, limits, interruption, or numerical failure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the recorded computational reason for stopping without imposing a universal taxonomy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed solver implementation and run transcript \(\rho\), the termination cause \(c(\rho)\) is the stopping event selected by that implementation's documented stopping and precedence rules. Common families include satisfaction of a stopping test, a resource limit, external interruption, numerical breakdown, and internal failure, but their names, granularity, and precedence are implementation-dependent. The cause records why computation ended and does not by itself determine the model's mathematical status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A termination cause is the implementation-selected reason a run stopped; common cause families exist, but their taxonomy and precedence are solver-specific.
assumptions_latex: The implementation's stopping and precedence rules are fixed.
The transcript contains the event information used by those rules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c(\rho)\text{ classifies the computational stopping event, not by itself the mathematical model status}.

notation.meaning: documented termination cause selected from the transcript

knowledge_statements.title: Interface-Relative Termination Cause
Termination-Cause Classification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies why a solver run stopped without inferring the model's mathematical status.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a solver transcript \(\rho\), its termination cause is the first decisive stopping event under a declared priority rule. Causes are classified as: certified convergence, when a stated stopping predicate is satisfied; certified model conclusion, when a valid infeasibility or unboundedness witness is accepted; resource limit, including time, iteration, or memory limits; numerical failure, including breakdown or unreliable arithmetic; user or external interruption; and internal error. The classification concerns the execution event only. In particular, resource exhaustion or numerical failure leaves the underlying feasibility and optimality questions unresolved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A run stops because of certified convergence, a certified model conclusion, a resource limit, numerical failure, interruption, or error; this alone need not classify the model.
assumptions_latex: A deterministic priority rule resolves simultaneous stopping events.
The transcript records the event used to terminate the run.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c(\rho)\) classifies the stopping event and does not by itself determine a mathematical problem status.
