children.top_down_role: Solver-facing codes or labels used to report how computation ended.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies externally returned solver codes without imposing a universal code vocabulary or inferring mathematical status.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed solver interface and version, an exit-code classification is the documented assignment \(\kappa:E\to\mathcal P\) from returned codes \(E\) to their published execution meanings \(\mathcal P\). The code and its versioned documentation jointly determine the interface meaning; the code alone does not establish feasibility, optimality, infeasibility, or unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exit code has the execution meaning assigned by its solver’s versioned interface documentation; it is not, by itself, a mathematical certificate.
assumptions_latex: A solver interface and version are fixed.
The returned code belongs to the documented code set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: e\in E\Longrightarrow \text{interface meaning }\kappa(e),\quad e\not\Longrightarrow\text{an independently unverified mathematical status}.

notation.meaning: documented exit-code set for the fixed interface version

review_flags: Revises the deferred bespoke tuple classification to an interface-relative definition.
No universal code vocabulary or evidence field is asserted.
knowledge_statements.title: Version-Scoped Exit-Code Classification
Exit-Code Classification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines exit codes as implementation-level records rather than mathematical conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An exit code \(e\) is an implementation-defined finite label returned when a solver invocation ends. Its semantic classification is the tuple \(\chi(e)=(q,c,a)\), where \(q\) records completion quality, \(c\) records the declared termination-cause class, and \(a\) records whether associated evidence is absent, approximate, or verifier-accepted. Two solvers may assign different labels to the same tuple, and one label may summarize several detailed causes. Therefore an exit code is interpretable only together with its solver version, mapping table, and returned evidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exit code is a versioned implementation label whose meaning combines completion, cause, and evidence classes; it is not intrinsically a mathematical status.
assumptions_latex: The solver version and exit-code table are fixed.
Each returned label belongs to a finite code set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e\) has portable meaning only through the declared classification \(\chi(e)\) and accompanying evidence.

notation.meaning: semantic classification of the exit code

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exit codes are implementation-defined finite labels interpreted through versioned documentation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf, but the tuple chi(e)=(q,c,a) is a proposed semantic schema, not a generally established exit-code classification. It requires a direct standard or solver-interface source with a specific locator.

children.title: Termination-to-Exit Mapping
children.top_down_role: Correspondence between internal stopping causes and externally reported exit classifications.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents how documented run conditions produce an externally returned classification without assuming totality or injectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed solver interface version, let \(T\) be the documented set of reportable termination states and \(E\) its exit classifications. The interface defines a correspondence \(M\subseteq T\times E\); when the documentation guarantees exactly one returned classification, \(M\) is a function \(M:T\to E\). The correspondence may be many-to-one, so an observed exit classification need not recover the full termination state, and changing interface versions may change \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver version documents a correspondence from reportable termination states to exit classifications; it may lose information and need not be portable across versions.
assumptions_latex: One solver interface version and its documented reportable states are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (t,e)\in M\text{ records reporting correspondence; injectivity, totality, and single-valuedness require separate interface guarantees}.
review_flags: Replaces the unsupported universally total function with a general correspondence.
Functionality, totality, and injectivity are correctly treated as interface-specific properties.
knowledge_statements.title: Versioned Termination-to-Exit Correspondence
Termination-to-Exit Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes the versioned, generally many-to-one mapping from termination events to returned codes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a solver version with termination-cause set \(\mathcal C\), diagnostic-state set \(\mathcal D\), and exit-code set \(\mathcal E\). Its termination-to-exit mapping is a total implementation function \(M:\mathcal C\times\mathcal D\to\mathcal E\). The map may be many-to-one, so observing \(e=M(c,d)\) need not identify \((c,d)\). A reliable interface must publish enough metadata to recover the intended semantic class \(\chi(e)\), preserve whether a certificate was returned, and distinguish certified stopping from limits, interruptions, and failures. Changing solver versions may change \(M\) even when the mathematical model is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A versioned function maps termination causes and diagnostics to exit codes, often many-to-one; evidence metadata is needed to recover the intended meaning.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\), \(\mathcal D\), and \(\mathcal E\) are fixed for one solver version.
Every completed invocation produces exactly one exit code.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M:\mathcal C\times\mathcal D\to\mathcal E\) represents execution reporting, not a direct map to mathematical status.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a versioned many-to-one interface map captures conventional solver exit reporting
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation content_kind fits the mapping leaf, but modeling every solver version by a total function on cause and diagnostic sets, together with the stated metadata obligations, is an unsupported interface formalization. A direct source is required.

children.title: Mathematical-Status Separation
children.top_down_role: Boundaries preventing a stopping reason from being mistaken for a conclusion about the model.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates facts about how computation ended from model-level conclusions justified by sound evidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be an execution report for encoded model \(D\). The report establishes only the execution semantics assigned by its interface. A mathematical claim \(S(D)\) follows from returned evidence \(w\) only when a sound verifier for that claim accepts the same encoded model and witness: \(V_S(D,w)=1\Rightarrow S(D)\). Hence an unverified success-like label does not imply \(S(D)\), while an independently accepted sound certificate establishes \(S(D)\) irrespective of the accompanying presentation label.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Execution labels describe a run; mathematical conclusions require evidence checked by a sound predicate for the same encoded model.
assumptions_latex: The verifier is sound for the asserted status.
The verifier checks the same encoded model and numerical interpretation used by the claim.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R\not\Rightarrow S(D),\qquad V_S(D,w)=1\Rightarrow S(D).

notation.meaning: sound verifier for status claim S

review_flags: Preserves the standard logical separation without requiring every valid status to possess a returned certificate.
Soundness and encoded-model identity are explicit assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Execution–Mathematical Status Separation
Mathematical-Status Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates execution outcomes from model-level claims supported by independently checked evidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(e\) be a solver exit code and let \(w\) be any returned witness for model data \(D\). The execution statement \(e=M(c,d)\) determines only the reported termination semantics. A mathematical status \(S\), such as optimality, infeasibility, or unboundedness, may be asserted only when a specified verifier accepts \((D,w)\) and its soundness contract gives \(V(D,w)=1\Rightarrow S(D)\). Consequently, success-like exit codes without accepted evidence do not alone establish \(S(D)\), while a valid independently checked certificate can establish \(S(D)\) regardless of the solver's presentation label.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exit codes describe execution. Mathematical status follows only from sound, accepted evidence; a success label alone is insufficient, while a valid certificate remains decisive.
assumptions_latex: The verifier and its soundness contract are fixed.
The checked witness refers to exactly the encoded model \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e=M(c,d)\not\Rightarrow S(D)\), but \(V(D,w)=1\Rightarrow S(D)\) under verifier soundness.

notation.meaning: mathematical status claim about model D

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: sound certificates support mathematical claims whereas process exit labels describe execution
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle content_kind matches the separation leaf and the conditional verifier-soundness implication is coherent. No source is supplied for the stronger operational principle that mathematical status may be asserted only through an accepted witness or for its treatment of presentation labels.

children.title: Problem-Status Classification
children.top_down_role: Model-level classifications concerning feasibility, infeasibility, boundedness, and uncertainty.

knowledge_statements.title: Problem-Status Classification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies an extended-real convex minimization problem independently of solver termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p^*=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\), where \(f:F\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is convex and \(F\) is convex, the problem is infeasible if \(F\cap\operatorname{dom}f=\varnothing\); feasible otherwise. A feasible problem is unbounded below if \(p^*=-\infty\), and bounded below if \(p^*>-\infty\). A bounded feasible problem is attained when some \(x^*\in F\) satisfies \(f(x^*)=p^*\), and unattained otherwise. Unknown is an epistemic reporting status used when available evidence certifies none of the applicable mathematical cases; it is not an additional property of the problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex minimization problem is infeasible or feasible; a feasible problem is bounded or unbounded below, and a finite optimum is either attained or unattained. Unknown describes evidence.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
\(f\) is an extended-real convex objective with declared domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model status is determined by \(F\cap\operatorname{dom}f\), \(p^*\), and attainment; “unknown” records insufficient evidence.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: feasibility, extended-real boundedness, and attainment give the standard model-level classification
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content_kind fits the model-status leaf and the extended-real classification is largely standard. An authoritative convex-analysis or optimization locator is required for feasibility, boundedness, attainment, and the distinction between mathematical status and epistemic 'unknown'.

children.title: Returned-Evidence Status Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Classification of returned primal points, dual points, rays, and certificate data.

children.title: Primal-Solution Status Classification
children.top_down_role: Labels describing the quality or usability of returned primal points.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
\(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear, \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and fixed norms are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{status}_p\in\{\text{exact},\text{approximate},\text{invalid},\text{unavailable}\}\) according to the stated predicates.

notation.meaning: status of the returned primal evidence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies a returned primal vector by feasibility residuals under fixed solver tolerances.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the conic program \(\min\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\), fix tolerances \(\varepsilon_A,\varepsilon_K\ge 0\). If a vector \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) is returned, its primal-evidence status is exact when \(Ax=b\) and \(x\in K\); approximate when \(\|Ax-b\|\le\varepsilon_A\), \(\operatorname{dist}(x,K)\le\varepsilon_K\), and at least one exact condition fails; and invalid when at least one of these two residual bounds fails. If no vector is returned, the status is unavailable. These labels concern returned evidence only and do not assert optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Returned primal evidence is exact, approximate, invalid, or unavailable according to equality and cone-feasibility residuals; this classification alone does not establish optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Solution Status Classification

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53

children.title: Dual-Solution Status Classification
children.top_down_role: Labels describing the quality or usability of returned dual points.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone and \(K^*:=\{s\in\mathbb R^n:\langle s,x\rangle\ge0\ \forall x\in K\}\).
\(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear, \(A^*:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n\) is its adjoint, \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{status}_d\in\{\text{exact},\text{approximate},\text{invalid},\text{unavailable}\}\) according to the stated predicates.

notation.meaning: status of the returned dual evidence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies returned dual variables by stationarity and dual-cone residuals.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the dual program \(\max\{\langle b,y\rangle:A^*y+s=c,\ s\in K^*\}\), fix \(\varepsilon_S,\varepsilon_{K^*}\ge0\). If a pair \((y,s)\in\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n\) is returned, its dual-evidence status is exact when \(A^*y+s=c\) and \(s\in K^*\); approximate when \(\|A^*y+s-c\|\le\varepsilon_S\), \(\operatorname{dist}(s,K^*)\le\varepsilon_{K^*}\), and at least one exact condition fails; and invalid when at least one of these two residual bounds fails. If no pair is returned, the status is unavailable. Dual feasibility alone does not establish optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Returned dual evidence is exact, approximate, invalid, or unavailable according to stationarity and dual-cone residuals, independently of optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Solution Status Classification

source_witnesses.locator: 3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191

children.title: Ray Status Classification
children.top_down_role: Labels describing returned recession directions or infeasibility rays.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone, \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear, \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
Returned directions are normalized by a fixed norm, and \(\varepsilon_A,\varepsilon_K,\varepsilon_{K^*}\ge0\) and \(\delta_d,\delta_y>0\) are fixed before classification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each requested ray receives exactly one status in \(\{\text{exact},\text{approximate},\text{invalid},\text{unavailable}\}\).

notation.meaning: dual cone of the primal cone

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies normalized returned directions intended to evidence primal unboundedness or primal infeasibility.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a returned normalized nonzero direction \(d\in\mathbb R^n\), the primal-improving-ray status is exact when \(d\in K\), \(Ad=0\), and \(\langle c,d\rangle<0\); approximate when the exact predicate fails but \(\operatorname{dist}(d,K)\le\varepsilon_K\), \(\|Ad\|\le\varepsilon_A\), and \(\langle c,d\rangle\le-\delta_d\); and invalid otherwise. For a returned normalized nonzero direction \(y\in\mathbb R^m\), the primal-infeasibility-ray status is exact when \(A^*y\in K^*\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\); approximate when the exact predicate fails but \(\operatorname{dist}(A^*y,K^*)\le\varepsilon_{K^*}\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle\le-\delta_y\); and invalid otherwise. A requested ray status is unavailable when no corresponding direction is returned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized improving or infeasibility direction is exact, approximate, invalid, or unavailable according to explicit homogeneous residual tests and a negative improvement or separation margin.
knowledge_statements.title: Ray Status Classification

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normalization Dependence of Approximate Ray Status
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explains why fixed nonzero normalization is necessary for tolerance-based classification of homogeneous rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\alpha>0\), the exact primal-ray predicate \(d\in K,\ Ad=0,\langle c,d\rangle<0\) and the exact infeasibility-ray predicate \(A^*y\in K^*,\langle b,y\rangle<0\) are invariant under \(d\mapsto\alpha d\) and \(y\mapsto\alpha y\). In contrast, \(\|A(\alpha d)\|=\alpha\|Ad\|\), \(\operatorname{dist}(\alpha d,K)=\alpha\operatorname{dist}(d,K)\), \(\operatorname{dist}(A^*(\alpha y),K^*)=\alpha\operatorname{dist}(A^*y,K^*)\), and both strict margins scale by \(\alpha\). Therefore an approximate ray status based on absolute residual and margin thresholds is not a property of an unnormalized ray class; a fixed nonzero normalization must precede classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact ray validity is invariant under positive scaling, but absolute residual and margin tests are not; approximate ray classification therefore requires fixed nonzero normalization.
assumptions_latex: Distances and operator residuals use positively homogeneous norms.
Approximate tests use fixed absolute residual bounds and positive margin thresholds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Approximate status of }[d]\text{ or }[y]\text{ is well-defined only after fixing a normalized representative.}
knowledge_statements.title: Normalization Dependence of Approximate Ray Status

children.title: Certificate Status Classification
children.top_down_role: Labels describing the validity, accuracy, or completeness of returned certificate data.

assumptions_latex: \(Z\) is the certificate-object space, and \(z\in Z\) contains every field required by the certificate predicate.
\(\varepsilon\ge0\) and margins \(\eta_j>0\) are fixed before classification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each requested certificate receives exactly one status in \(\{\text{valid},\text{approximate},\text{invalid},\text{unavailable}\}\).

notation.meaning: combined equality and positive-part inequality residual

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates exact certificates, tolerance-qualified evidence, rejected evidence, and absent evidence.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P:Z\to\mathbb R^p\) and \(Q:Z\to\mathbb R^q\) encode the equality and non-strict inequality conditions \(P(z)=0\) and \(Q(z)\le0\), and let \(H_j:Z\to\mathbb R\), \(j=1,\ldots,k\), encode required strict conditions \(H_j(z)<0\). Define \(r(z):=(P(z),[Q(z)]_+)\). A returned object \(z\) has valid status when \(r(z)=0\) and \(H_j(z)<0\) for every \(j\); approximate status when it is not valid, \(\|r(z)\|\le\varepsilon\), and \(H_j(z)\le-\eta_j\) for every \(j\); and invalid status otherwise. If no object is returned, the status is unavailable. Approximate status is numerical evidence, not an exact mathematical certificate, unless a validated error bound upgrades it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate object is valid when every exact predicate holds, approximate when explicit residual and margin tests hold without exact validity, invalid otherwise, and unavailable when absent.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Status Classification

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53

children.title: Solution–Certificate Consistency
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between reported solution statuses and the accompanying evidence.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution–Certificate Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Requires outcome labels to agree with all returned solutions, rays, and certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A solver outcome is solution–certificate consistent when every asserted label is entailed by the strongest returned evidence under the same tolerances. In particular, an exact-optimal label requires exact primal and dual feasibility with \(\langle c,x\rangle=\langle b,y\rangle\); an exact-infeasible label cannot coexist with a primal-feasible \(x\); and an exact-unbounded label cannot coexist with a dual-feasible \((y,s)\). Approximate evidence may support only an accuracy-qualified label unless a validated error bound upgrades it. Conflicting exact predicates force the composite outcome to inconsistent, regardless of the solver's headline status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A headline outcome is consistent only when returned solutions and certificates support it at the same accuracy level and contain no exact logical conflict.
assumptions_latex: The primal–dual pair is \(Ax=b,\ x\in K\) and \(A^*y+s=c,\ s\in K^*\).
All evidence is evaluated using one declared tolerance profile.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{conflicting exact evidence}\Rightarrow\text{status}=\text{inconsistent}\).

source_refs.locator: 3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191

source_witnesses.locator: 3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191

children.title: Solver Outcome Families
children.top_down_role: High-level mathematical outcome classes reported by convex optimization software.

children.title: Optimality Accuracy Regimes
children.top_down_role: Successful classifications distinguished by certificate accuracy and tolerance level.

children.title: Optimal Outcomes
children.top_down_role: Successful classifications supported at the solver's strongest reported certificate level.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone, \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear, \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
\(A^*\) is the adjoint of \(A\), and \(K^*\) is the dual cone under the stated inner products.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in K,\ Au=b}\langle c,u\rangle\), \((y,s)\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{v,t}\{\langle b,v\rangle:A^*v+t=c,\ t\in K^*\}\), and \(p^*=d^*=\langle c,x\rangle=\langle b,y\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact primal-dual feasibility and zero gap certify a globally optimal conic outcome.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53
4.4. Existence of Dual Optimal Solutions p. 149

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the primal problem \(p^*:=\inf\{\langle c,u\rangle:Au=b,\ u\in K\}\) and its dual \(d^*:=\sup\{\langle b,v\rangle:A^*v+t=c,\ t\in K^*\}\). Suppose returned \((x,y,s)\) satisfies \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), \(A^*y+s=c\), \(s\in K^*\), and \(\langle c,x\rangle=\langle b,y\rangle\). Then \(x\) is primal optimal, \((y,s)\) is dual optimal, and the common objective value is finite and attained. Consequently the returned outcome may be classified as exact optimal. No constraint qualification is needed for this certificate because simultaneous feasibility and objective equality directly establish optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exactly feasible primal-dual pair with equal objective values certifies attained global optimality and a common finite optimal value.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimal Outcomes

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53
4.4. Existence of Dual Optimal Solutions p. 149

children.title: Approximately Optimal Outcomes
children.top_down_role: Successful classifications supported only within stated numerical tolerances.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone, \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear, \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
Residual norms and tolerances \(\varepsilon_p,\varepsilon_d,\varepsilon_g\ge0\) are declared before classification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_p\le\varepsilon_p\), \(r_d\le\varepsilon_d\), and \(r_g\le\varepsilon_g\), with at least one failed exact condition, imply an approximately optimal evidence status.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual and gap thresholds define a numerical, not automatically rigorous, optimality outcome.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a returned triple \((x,y,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n\), define \(r_p:=\|Ax-b\|+\operatorname{dist}(x,K)\), \(r_d:=\|A^*y+s-c\|+\operatorname{dist}(s,K^*)\), and \(r_g:=|\langle c,x\rangle-\langle b,y\rangle|\). The triple supports an approximately optimal outcome when \(r_p\le\varepsilon_p\), \(r_d\le\varepsilon_d\), and \(r_g\le\varepsilon_g\), and at least one exact primal-feasibility, dual-feasibility, or zero-gap condition fails. If all exact conditions hold, the outcome is exact optimal. This residual-based numerical certificate implies a rigorous objective-error or solution-distance bound only when an applicable conditioning or error-bound result is additionally available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicitly defined primal, dual, and gap residuals support an approximately optimal label when all declared thresholds hold but exact optimality conditions do not; stronger error guarantees require conditioning information.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximately Optimal Outcomes

source_witnesses.locator: 3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191

children.title: Optimality Accuracy Regimes
children.top_down_role: Levels of primal, dual, residual, or value accuracy attached to successful outcomes.

assumptions_latex: \(r_p,r_d,r_g\) are finite nonnegative residuals computed consistently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb R_+^3=R_{\mathrm{exact}}\mathbin{\dot\cup}R_{\mathrm{approx}}\mathbin{\dot\cup}R_{\mathrm{unresolved}}\).

notation.meaning: exact, approximate, and unresolved residual regions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partitions optimality evidence by exact predicates and declared residual thresholds.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(r:=(r_p,r_d,r_g)\in\mathbb R_+^3\) and \(\varepsilon:=(\varepsilon_p,\varepsilon_d,\varepsilon_g)\in\mathbb R_+^3\), define \(R_{\mathrm{exact}}:=\{(0,0,0)\}\), \(R_{\mathrm{approx}}:=\{r: r_p\le\varepsilon_p,\ r_d\le\varepsilon_d,\ r_g\le\varepsilon_g\}\setminus R_{\mathrm{exact}}\), and \(R_{\mathrm{unresolved}}:=\mathbb R_+^3\setminus(R_{\mathrm{exact}}\cup R_{\mathrm{approx}})\). These are respectively the exact, approximate, and unresolved optimality-evidence regimes. An implementation may subdivide the unresolved regime, but it must not report exact optimality from positive residuals or approximate optimality when a declared threshold is exceeded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimality evidence is exact only at zero residual, approximate when every declared nonnegative threshold is met but some residual is positive, and unresolved otherwise.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimality Accuracy Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Representation Dependence of Absolute Accuracy Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of absolute residual classifications on units, norms, and equivalent model scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r_p=\|Ax-b\|\). Replacing the equality by the equivalent system \(D(Ax-b)=0\), with \(D\) nonsingular, gives \(r'_p=\|D(Ax-b)\|\). In general \(r'_p\ne r_p\); for \(D=\alpha I\), \(r'_p=|\alpha|r_p\). Hence an absolute test \(r_p\le\varepsilon_p\) is not invariant under equivalent changes of units or constraint scaling. A reproducible accuracy regime must fix the representation and residual norms or prescribe compatible scaled or relative tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Absolute residual regimes depend on units and equivalent constraint scaling; reproducibility requires fixed conventions or compatible scaled or relative tolerances.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is nonsingular, so the original and scaled equality systems have the same solution set.
The same absolute numerical threshold is used before and after scaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D=\alpha I\Longrightarrow r'_p=|\alpha|r_p,\qquad \{r_p\le\varepsilon_p\}\text{ is not representation invariant in general}.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation Dependence of Absolute Accuracy Regimes

children.title: Optimality Status Transition Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Tolerance-sensitive boundaries between full and approximate optimality labels.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimality Status Transition Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies residual surfaces where an arbitrarily small perturbation changes the reported accuracy regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed positive tolerances, the boundary between approximate and unresolved optimality evidence is contained in \(\{r_p=\varepsilon_p\}\cup\{r_d=\varepsilon_d\}\cup\{r_g=\varepsilon_g\}\). The exact-to-approximate boundary is the singleton residual triple \((0,0,0)\): any positive residual destroys exact status while possibly retaining approximate status. Therefore a status is numerically fragile when its residual vector lies on, or within the residual-evaluation uncertainty of, one of these surfaces. If threshold comparison or residual computation is not reproducible at that scale, the outcome must be downgraded to unresolved rather than assigned the stronger label.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Status changes occur at zero residual or a declared tolerance surface; uncertainty crossing such a surface requires the weaker unresolved label.
assumptions_latex: The regime predicates use non-strict acceptance inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial R_{\mathrm{approx}}\subseteq\{r_p=\varepsilon_p\}\cup\{r_d=\varepsilon_d\}\cup\{r_g=\varepsilon_g\}\cup\{(0,0,0)\}\).

source_refs.locator: 3.1.9 Basic Elements of Primal-Dual Methods p. 191

children.title: Feasible but Nonoptimal Outcomes
children.top_down_role: Returned feasible solutions without a completed global optimality certificate.

assumptions_latex: The primal problem is \(\min\{\langle c,u\rangle:Au=b,\ u\in K\}\), where \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
All returned evidence has been checked under one declared solution-certificate consistency policy.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A solver outcome is feasible but not certified optimal when it returns \(x\in K\) satisfying \(Ax=b\), while no returned and validated evidence establishes that \(x\) globally minimizes \(\langle c,u\rangle\) over \(\{u\in K:Au=b\}\). In particular, an exact dual-feasible pair \((y,s)\) satisfying \(A^*y+s=c\), \(s\in K^*\), and \(\langle c,x\rangle=\langle b,y\rangle\) would be a completed optimality certificate, so the label cannot be assigned if such a pair is returned and validated. The label does not prove that \(x\) is strictly suboptimal; strict nonoptimality requires a feasible point with lower objective value or another valid argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The solver returned a feasible point but no validated evidence certifying its global optimality; the point may nevertheless be optimal.

children.title: Infeasible Outcomes

knowledge_statements.title: Infeasible Outcomes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An exact conic separation certificate establishes that the primal feasible set is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal system \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), a returned vector \(y\) with \(A^*y\in K^*\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\) is an exact infeasibility certificate. Its existence implies that no \(x\in K\) can satisfy \(Ax=b\), so the primal outcome is exactly infeasible. The certificate must be checked in the original, unscaled model or transformed back with a verified equivalence. Mere failure to find a feasible point, termination of an algorithm, or a small but nonzero certificate residual does not establish this exact outcome.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual separating vector with exact cone membership and a strict negative pairing certifies that the primal constraint system has no solution.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
\(A^*\) is the adjoint of \(A\) under the stated inner products.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A^*y\in K^*,\ \langle b,y\rangle<0\Rightarrow\{x\in K:Ax=b\}=\varnothing\).

children.title: Approximately Infeasible Outcomes
children.top_down_role: Infeasibility classifications supported only within relaxed numerical criteria.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximately Infeasible Outcomes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A normalized near-separating vector supplies tolerance-qualified evidence of infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\varepsilon_c\ge0\) and \(\eta>0\). A normalized returned vector \(y\), with \(\|y\|=1\), supports an approximately infeasible outcome when \(\operatorname{dist}(A^*y,K^*)\le\varepsilon_c\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle\le-\eta\), but exact cone membership is not established. This evidence becomes a rigorous infeasibility certificate only if a validated perturbation bound shows that the cone-membership error can change the separating pairing by less than \(\eta\) over every feasible candidate. Without such a bound, the label describes strong numerical evidence rather than exact emptiness of the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized near-separating vector supports approximate infeasibility, but exact infeasibility requires an error bound preserving its negative separation margin.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone and \(K^*\) its dual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(A^*y,K^*)\le\varepsilon_c,\ \langle b,y\rangle\le-\eta\Rightarrow\text{approximately infeasible evidence}\).

children.title: Infeasibility Evidence Strength
children.top_down_role: Distinctions among exact, numerical, partial, or heuristic support for infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Infeasibility Evidence Strength
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact and residual-based certificates for primal infeasibility in finite-dimensional conic form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the feasibility system \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), where \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a closed convex cone, \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear, and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\). A strong exact infeasibility certificate is a vector \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfying \(A^{\mathsf T}y\in K^*\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\). For prescribed tolerances \(\varepsilon_d\ge 0\) and \(\varepsilon_g>0\), a residual-based witness may instead satisfy \(\operatorname{dist}(A^{\mathsf T}y,K^*)\le\varepsilon_d\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y\le-\varepsilon_g\). Such a residual-based witness supplies only tolerance-dependent evidence unless a stated perturbation analysis shows that its negative separation margin dominates the effect of the dual-cone residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact separating multiplier proves infeasibility. A multiplier with cone residual supplies only tolerance-dependent evidence unless a perturbation bound shows that its strictly negative separation margin dominates the residual error.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a closed convex cone.
\(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A^{\mathsf T}y\in K^*,\ b^{\mathsf T}y<0\Longrightarrow\{x\in K:Ax=b\}=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scale Invariance of Infeasibility Witness Strength
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization required when comparing residual-bearing homogeneous infeasibility witnesses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\alpha>0\), \(\operatorname{dist}(A^{\mathsf T}(\alpha y),K^*)=\alpha\operatorname{dist}(A^{\mathsf T}y,K^*)\) and \(-b^{\mathsf T}(\alpha y)=\alpha(-b^{\mathsf T}y)\). Thus exact certificate validity is invariant under positive scaling, whereas separate absolute residual and margin values are not intrinsic measures of approximate-witness strength. Approximate witnesses must be normalized or compared using a scale-invariant quantity such as \(\operatorname{dist}(A^{\mathsf T}y,K^*)/(-b^{\mathsf T}y)\) when \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive scaling preserves exact certificate validity and scales both residual and separation margin. Approximate witness strength therefore requires normalization or a scale-invariant residual-to-margin ratio.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a closed convex cone.
The distance is induced by a norm, \(\alpha>0\), and \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{\operatorname{dist}(A^{\mathsf T}(\alpha y),K^*)}{-b^{\mathsf T}(\alpha y)}=\frac{\operatorname{dist}(A^{\mathsf T}y,K^*)}{-b^{\mathsf T}y}.
knowledge_statements.title: Scale Invariance of Infeasibility Witness Strength

children.title: Infeasibility Status Downgrade Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which an infeasibility classification must be weakened or withdrawn.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits the status inference supported by a particular returned infeasibility witness without prescribing a solver-wide status vocabulary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), let \(y\) be a candidate infeasibility witness expressed in the original model. It supports exact infeasibility when \(A^{\mathsf T}y\in K^*\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\). If exact validity fails but a declared normalization, cone-residual bound, and strictly negative separation-margin test all hold, the witness supports only tolerance-qualified infeasibility evidence. If those approximate tests fail, their evaluation uncertainty crosses an acceptance boundary, or the witness cannot be recovered in original-model coordinates by a verified equivalence, no infeasibility classification follows from that witness alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A returned witness supports exact infeasibility only when its exact predicates hold, approximate evidence only when all declared normalized tolerance tests hold, and otherwise no infeasibility conclusion by itself.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a closed convex cone.
Normalization, norms, residual tolerances, and margin tolerances are declared before classification.
Any transformation back to the original model is verified to preserve the certificate predicates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \neg E(y)\land A_{\varepsilon}(y)\Rightarrow\text{tolerance-qualified evidence only},\qquad \neg A_{\varepsilon}(y)\Rightarrow\text{no infeasibility inference from }y\text{ alone},

Infeasibility Status Downgrade Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between certified infeasibility and approximate or inconclusive solver status.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), an infeasible status is justified only when a returned multiplier \(y\) passes the exact certificate tests \(A^{\mathsf T}y\in K^*\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\), after accounting for representation and arithmetic. Downgrade the claim to approximately infeasible when only prescribed residual and separation tolerances are met. Downgrade it to unknown when \(b^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\), the cone-membership residual exceeds tolerance, the witness cannot be mapped to the original model, or numerical error can reverse the separation sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infeasibility becomes approximate or unknown when certificate residuals, separation margin, model recovery, or numerical reliability fail their declared acceptance tests.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a closed convex cone.
Certificate acceptance tolerances and scaling conventions are fixed before classification.

children.title: Unbounded Outcomes
children.top_down_role: Solver classifications indicating objective recession in the designated primal model.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Outcomes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal unboundedness certificate for a feasible finite-dimensional conic minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a convex cone, let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, and let \(b\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\). For \(P=\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\), a certified unbounded outcome consists of \(x_0\in K\) and \(d\in K\) satisfying \(Ax_0=b\), \(Ad=0\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\). Then \(x_0+td\in K\) and \(A(x_0+td)=b\) for every \(t\ge0\), while \(c^{\mathsf T}(x_0+td)\to-\infty\) as \(t\to\infty\). A ray without a verified feasible base point does not by itself certify that the primal optimal value is \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible base point together with a feasible recession ray of strictly negative cost certifies that the conic minimization problem is unbounded below.
assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear, \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
The problem uses the minimization convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax_0=b,\ x_0\in K,\ Ad=0,\ d\in K,\ c^{\mathsf T}d<0\Longrightarrow p^*=-\infty\).

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Infeasible Outcomes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate connecting a primal improving ray to infeasibility of the standard conic dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a closed convex cone, let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, and let \(b\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\). Consider \(P=\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\) and \(D=\sup\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\in K^*\}\). Any vector \(d\in K\) satisfying \(Ad=0\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\) certifies that the displayed dual feasible set is empty. This dual-infeasibility certificate does not require a primal feasible base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector in the primal cone with zero constraint displacement and strictly negative cost certifies infeasibility of the displayed conic dual, even if primal feasibility has not been established.

\(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear, \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
Primal and dual signs follow the displayed minimization–maximization convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Convention Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Status translation under standard conic primal–dual naming and sign conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a closed convex cone, let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, and let \(b\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\). Under \(P=\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\) and \(D=\sup\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\in K^*\}\), a vector \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfying \(A^{\mathsf T}y\in K^*\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\) is a primal-infeasibility certificate. A vector \(d\in K\) satisfying \(Ad=0\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\) is a dual-infeasibility certificate; when a primal feasible point is also verified, the same ray certifies primal unboundedness. If primal and dual labels or optimization signs are changed, certificate names and inequalities must be recomputed from the explicitly transformed pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the displayed minimization convention, a separating dual multiplier certifies primal infeasibility and a strictly improving primal-cone ray certifies dual infeasibility. Other conventions must be translated algebraically from their displayed problems.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a closed convex cone.
\(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear, \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
The displayed pair fixes the status convention.

children.title: Recession-Status Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Cases where available ray evidence does not uniquely support an unboundedness or infeasibility label.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession-Status Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of status inference from an approximate or incomplete recession witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a closed convex cone, let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, and let \(b\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\). For \(P=\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\), a candidate direction \(d\in\mathbb R^n\) does not certify primal unboundedness unless \(d\in K\), \(Ad=0\), \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\), and primal feasibility is independently established. Without a feasible base point, an exact improving ray satisfying those three ray conditions certifies only infeasibility of the displayed dual. If cone membership or \(Ad=0\) is only approximate, or if the sign of \(c^{\mathsf T}d\) is unresolved at the declared tolerances, neither exact primal unboundedness nor exact dual infeasibility follows from that candidate ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact improving ray can prove dual infeasibility without proving primal unboundedness, which additionally requires primal feasibility. A residual-bearing or zero-margin candidate ray leaves the exact statuses inconclusive.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a closed convex cone.
\(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear, \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
Status claims refer to exact mathematical feasibility unless explicitly tolerance-qualified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An improving ray without a verified feasible base point cannot by itself establish \(p^*=-\infty\).

notation.meaning: primal optimal value in the extended real line

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unboundedness Without a Strict Improving Recession Ray
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that absence of a strict ray certificate need not imply boundedness for a nonpolyhedral conic slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{(t,z,x)\in\mathbb R^3:t\ge0,\ z\ge0,\ 2tz\ge x^2\}\), and consider \(\inf\{x:(t,z,x)\in K,\ z=1\}\). The points \((u^2/2,1,u)\) are feasible for every \(u\in\mathbb R\), so the optimal value is \(-\infty\). However, every recession direction \(d=(d_t,d_z,d_x)\in K\) satisfying \(d_z=0\) has \(d_x=0\); hence no feasible recession direction has strictly negative objective slope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rotated-second-order-cone slice can be unbounded below although its recession cone contains no strictly improving direction, so failure to return such a ray does not prove boundedness.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is the displayed closed rotated second-order cone.
The equality constraint is \(z=1\), and the objective is the third coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p^*=-\infty\quad\text{and}\quad \nexists d\in K:\ d_z=0,\ d_x<0.

children.title: Unknown Outcomes
children.top_down_role: Outcomes for which the solver cannot assign a supported mathematical classification.

knowledge_statements.title: Unknown Outcomes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical meaning of an unknown solver termination status.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An unknown outcome means that the returned data establish none of the accepted predicates for a feasible optimal point, a primal-infeasibility certificate, a dual-infeasibility certificate, or a verified unbounded ray. Formally, if \(V_{m opt}\), \(V_{m pinf}\), \(V_{m dinf}\), and \(V_{m unb}\) denote the corresponding verifier predicates, unknown records \(
eg V_{m opt}\land
eg V_{m pinf}\land
eg V_{m dinf}\land
eg V_{m unb}\). It is an absence of a validated conclusion, not a mathematical assertion that the model lacks any of these properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unknown means no accepted witness validates a conclusive status. It does not imply infeasibility, unboundedness, feasibility, or absence of an optimum.
assumptions_latex: Each conclusive status has a fixed verifier predicate.
Returned data are assessed under the model's declared scaling and tolerances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \({\rm status}={\rm unknown}\not\Longrightarrow\) any mathematical feasibility, optimality, or boundedness claim.

children.title: Interrupted Outcomes
children.top_down_role: Outcomes caused by external cancellation, user interruption, or execution termination.

knowledge_statements.title: Interrupted Outcomes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification when termination is caused externally before a conclusive certificate is validated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\) be the final completed iteration and let \(I\) denote an external stop event, such as user cancellation or process interruption. The outcome is interrupted when \(I\) causes termination before any conclusive verifier predicate is accepted. Any returned iterate \(x_k\), multiplier, or ray retains only the properties independently checked from its data. Thus interruption describes the cause of termination and cannot itself imply optimality, infeasibility, or unboundedness; a separately verified witness may be reported alongside the interruption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interrupted identifies an external stop before conclusive validation. Returned points or certificates carry only properties that can still be independently verified.
assumptions_latex: The solver distinguishes external interruption from internal numerical failure.
Witness verifiers can be evaluated independently of the termination cause.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\land\neg V_{\rm conclusive}\Longrightarrow{m status}={\rm interrupted}\), with no additional model-level conclusion.

notation.meaning: disjunction of accepted conclusive verifier predicates

review_flags: solver-neutral interruption semantics require an authoritative specification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed meaning and precedence of an interrupted outcome are interface-dependent and unsupported by a cited solver-neutral or solver-specific status specification.

children.title: Resource-Limit Outcomes
children.top_down_role: Outcomes caused by time, memory, iteration, or evaluation limits.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Limit Outcomes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification when a declared computational budget expires before conclusive validation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be the event that a declared resource bound is reached, including a time, iteration, memory, or evaluation limit. The outcome is resource-limited when \(R\) causes termination and no conclusive certificate has already passed its verifier. The status identifies budget exhaustion, not a property of the convex program. A returned point \(x_k\) may still be reported as an incumbent if its feasibility residuals satisfy declared tolerances, but the resource-limit event alone supplies no optimality guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A resource-limit outcome records exhausted computation, not a model property. A returned incumbent remains usable only to the extent independently verified.
assumptions_latex: Resource bounds and feasibility tolerances are declared.
Conclusive certificate checks are independent of the stopping trigger.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\land\neg V_{\rm conclusive}\Longrightarrow{m status}={\rm resource\mbox{-}limited}\), without a conclusive model-level claim.
review_flags: resource categories and precedence are solver-interface dependent

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Resource-limit categories, their precedence relative to validated certificates, and incumbent-reporting semantics depend on the solver interface. No authoritative source is supplied.

children.title: Diagnostic-Limit Outcomes
children.top_down_role: Inconclusive outcomes caused by insufficient or conflicting solver diagnostics.

knowledge_statements.title: Diagnostic-Limit Outcomes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary created when numerical diagnostics cannot distinguish competing mathematical statuses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A diagnostic-limit outcome applies when computation terminates because available arithmetic or diagnostics cannot reliably evaluate a required verifier predicate. Examples include nonfinite quantities, unresolved cone-membership tests, severe scaling, or residuals lying within uncertainty of an acceptance boundary. If an evaluated quantity \(q\) has error bound \(\delta\) and the status requires \(q<0\), then \(|q|\le\delta\) is insufficient to certify the strict sign. The appropriate conclusion is inconclusive unless an independently verified witness establishes a stronger status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When diagnostic uncertainty overlaps a certificate boundary, the solver cannot infer the required strict predicate and must leave the mathematical status inconclusive.
assumptions_latex: Diagnostic uncertainty bounds refer to the quantities used by the verifier.
No independently validated conclusive witness is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|q|\le\delta\Longrightarrow\) the sign condition \(q<0\) is not certified from that diagnostic.
review_flags: diagnostic-limit taxonomy requires a solver-neutral authoritative source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strict-sign observation is mathematically sound, but the broader diagnostic-limit outcome category and its status precedence are unsupported by an authoritative specification.

children.title: Incumbent Evidence at Early Exit
children.top_down_role: Interpretation of partial points, bounds, residuals, or certificates retained at inconclusive termination.

knowledge_statements.title: Incumbent Evidence at Early Exit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: What a returned primal point can certify when optimization stops early.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a feasible set, let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\), and define \(p^*=\inf\{f(x):x\in C\}\). An early-exit incumbent \(\hat x\) certifies an attained feasible objective value only if \(\hat x\in C\) is verified, either exactly or under explicitly stated feasibility tolerances. Exact feasibility gives \(p^*\le f(\hat x)\). For \(\varepsilon\ge0\), the incumbent certifies \(\varepsilon\)-optimality when an independently valid lower bound \(L\le p^*\) is available and \(0\le f(\hat x)-L\le\varepsilon\). Early termination alone supplies neither feasibility nor an optimality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A verified feasible incumbent gives an upper bound on a minimization optimum. It is epsilon-optimal only when paired with an independently valid lower bound whose gap is at most epsilon.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is the feasible set and \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is the objective.
The problem uses the minimization convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\hat x\in C,\ L\le p^*,\ f(\hat x)-L\le\varepsilon\Longrightarrow 0\le f(\hat x)-p^*\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: independently valid lower bound on the optimal value
optimal value of the minimization problem

children.title: Returned Witness Classification
children.top_down_role: Identification of whether returned data represent points, multipliers, rays, or residual evidence.

knowledge_statements.title: Returned Witness Classification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Type-directed interpretation of data returned by a convex solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a conic primal–dual pair, classify returned data by the predicates they satisfy, not by array position or solver label. A primal point satisfies the primal domain and constraint predicates; dual multipliers and slacks satisfy the dual domain and stationarity predicates; an infeasibility witness satisfies a separating alternative; an unboundedness witness satisfies recession and strict-improvement predicates; residual evidence consists only of numerical values measuring violations of these predicates. One object may support multiple classifications, but no model-level status follows until the corresponding predicate is verified in the intended model coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Returned arrays are points, multipliers, rays, or residual evidence according to verified mathematical predicates. Their labels alone do not establish a status.
assumptions_latex: The canonical primal–dual convention and original-to-canonical variable map are known.

children.title: Canonical-Model Certificate Verification

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent verification against fixed canonical data after witness type and coordinate convention are known.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given canonical data \(D_c\), a declared witness type \(t\), and candidate \(w\), form the complete predicate list \(\mathcal P_t(D_c,w)\) prescribed for that type. Recompute from \(D_c\) every equality residual, objective relation, normalization, and primal or dual cone-membership test, without relying on cached solver flags. Exact verification accepts exactly when every exact predicate holds. Numerical verification accepts only the explicitly stated approximate predicate \(\mathcal P_t^{\varepsilon}(D_c,w)\) under declared norms, scaling, and tolerances; missing required components are unavailable evidence, while present components failing the tests are invalid evidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independently recompute every type-specific predicate from canonical data; approximate acceptance must disclose its norms, scaling, and tolerances.
assumptions_latex: The witness type and canonical sign convention are declared.
Canonical data and all components required by the selected predicate are available for exact verification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{accept}_t(D_c,w)\iff\mathcal P_t(D_c,w),\qquad \operatorname{accept}^{\varepsilon}_t(D_c,w)\iff\mathcal P_t^{\varepsilon}(D_c,w).

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
All canonical data and certificate components are available in a common coordinate system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed equalities and cone memberships certify primal-dual optimality for the canonical model.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conic weak duality and exact primal-dual certificate algebra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact primal-dual optimality certificate for a canonical conic minimization model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the canonical problem \(\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax+b\in K\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(K^*=\{y\in\mathbb R^m:\langle y,s\rangle\geq 0\text{ for every }s\in K\}\), a tuple \((x,y)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\) is an exact optimality certificate when \[Ax+b\in K,\qquad y\in K^*,\qquad c-A^{\mathsf T}y=0,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x+b^{\mathsf T}y=0.\] These conditions are independently checkable from the canonical data \((A,b,c,K)\). Weak duality then identifies \(x\) as primal optimal, \(y\) as dual optimal, and their common objective value as \(c^{\mathsf T}x=-b^{\mathsf T}y\). A numerical certificate must instead report the residuals and cone-membership tolerances used for acceptance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Check primal cone membership, dual cone membership, stationarity with c minus the transpose of A times y equal to zero, and zero duality gap directly against the canonical data; approximate checks must disclose their tolerances.

children.title: Original-Model Certificate Recovery

knowledge_statements.title: Original-Model Certificate Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery criterion for transferring canonical evidence to the user-facing model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) map each feasible original point \(u\) to a feasible canonical point \(x=T(u)\), and let \(R\) reconstruct an original point from an eligible canonical point. A canonical certificate \(w\) yields an original-model certificate only if a recovery map \(Q\) produces \(v=Q(w)\) and the recovered tuple \((u,v)=(R(x),Q(w))\) directly satisfies every original feasibility, sign, stationarity, and objective-gap predicate claimed by the certificate. Verification must use the original functions and data, not merely the transformed residuals. If any required component lacks a defined recovery map, no corresponding original-model claim follows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recover primal and dual objects, then recheck every claimed condition using the original variables, functions, and data; unrecoverable components support no original-model certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(T\), \(R\), and \(Q\) are recorded with their domains.
The transformation preserves the objective on points eligible for recovery.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A canonical certificate supports the original claim exactly when its recovered tuple passes the original-model predicates.

children.title: Model-Level Claim Scope

knowledge_statements.title: Model-Level Claim Scope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical scope of conclusions drawn from transformed-model and finite-accuracy evidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a solver verifies a predicate \(P_c(w;D_c,\varepsilon)\) for canonical data \(D_c\), witness \(w\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon\). This evidence justifies an original-model predicate \(P_o\) only when the recorded transformation and recovery maps establish \[P_c(w;D_c,\varepsilon)\Longrightarrow P_o(Q(w);D_o,\delta)\] for a stated original tolerance \(\delta\). Without this implication, the valid conclusion is restricted to the canonical model and its reported numerical accuracy. In particular, an approximate residual does not by itself establish exact feasibility, exact optimality, infeasibility, or unboundedness of the original mathematical model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solver evidence supports only predicates preserved by documented transformations and tolerance transfer; approximate canonical evidence alone does not prove exact original-model claims.
assumptions_latex: \(D_o\) and \(D_c\) denote the original and canonical data.
All numerical predicates state their norms and tolerances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The justified claim is limited to the strongest predicate connected by the displayed implication.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed specialization concerning transfer from an outer relaxation to an intended minimization model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_o\subseteq F_r\) be original and relaxed feasible sets for the same minimization objective \(f\). Certification of \(v_r=\inf_{x\in F_r}f(x)\) implies \(v_r\le v_o:=\inf_{x\in F_o}f(x)\), and original optimality requires additional evidence that an original-feasible point attains \(v_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certified relaxation optimum is only a bound on the original optimum unless an original-feasible point attains that bound.
assumptions_latex: The original problem is a minimization problem.
The relaxation retains the original feasible set and objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v_r\le v_o,\qquad [\bar x\in F_o\land f(\bar x)=v_r]\Rightarrow v_r=v_o=f(\bar x).

children.title: Canonicalization Certificate Mapping
children.top_down_role: Correspondence between solver-form certificates and the original expression structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic reverse traversal of a retained canonicalization graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Traverse the canonicalization trace in reverse topological order. At each node, apply the recorded inverse primal relation to recover model-facing values and the adjoint of the recorded affine relation to propagate dual contributions. Sum contributions entering a shared original expression, restore the declared ordering, scaling, and sign conventions, and finally test the recovered primal and dual objects against the original model. If a required inverse relation or adjoint metadata is absent, return recovery unavailable rather than a certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reverse the canonicalization graph, using recorded inverse primal relations and adjoint dual maps, aggregate shared-node contributions, restore conventions, and validate the original model.
assumptions_latex: The canonicalization trace is a finite directed acyclic transformation graph.
Each traversed transformation records the maps needed for primal and dual recovery.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns a native certificate only after successful reconstruction and native validation; missing trace data produce an unavailable recovery.
knowledge_statements.title: Reverse Certificate Mapping Procedure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Canonical Feasibility Is Not Native Certificate Validity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary created by relaxations, discarded trace information, or unvalidated auxiliary evidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A solver-form feasible point or dual vector alone need not certify the original model. Certificate preservation can fail if the canonical model is only a relaxation, if the objective relation is not exact, if transformation metadata needed for recovery is discarded, or if the reconstructed objects fail a native feasibility, sign, stationarity, complementarity, or value check.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solver-form validity does not by itself establish a native certificate when canonicalization is inexact, recovery metadata is missing, or native checks fail.
assumptions_latex: A claimed certificate is being transferred from solver form to the original expression structure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of exactness, recoverability, or native validation prevents publication of the solver-form object as an original certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Feasibility Is Not Native Certificate Validity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mapping solver-form primal and dual evidence through an exact, retained canonicalization trace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an exact canonicalization encode an original variable \(u\) by canonical variables \(w\in\widehat F\), with recovery map \(R\) satisfying \(R(\widehat F)=F\), and let the transformation trace retain every introduced affine map, cone constraint, and objective relation. A canonical primal witness \(w\) maps to \(u=R(w)\). Dual contributions are pulled backward through the adjoints of the retained affine maps and added when several canonical constraints descend from the same original expression node. The mapped objects constitute an original certificate only if they satisfy the original feasibility, sign or cone-membership, stationarity, complementarity, and objective-consistency predicates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recover original variables through the recorded primal map and propagate dual contributions backward through adjoint affine maps, combining contributions at shared expressions; then validate every native certificate condition.
assumptions_latex: The canonicalization is exact, not a relaxation.
The complete transformation trace and sign conventions are retained.
The original certificate predicates are explicitly specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Canonical evidence is certificate-preserving only after the recovered objects satisfy every native certificate predicate.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate-Preserving Canonicalization Trace
Canonicalization Certificate Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pullback of canonical certificates through an exact extended-form canonicalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the original feasible set be represented exactly by \[F=\{u:\exists z,\ G(u,z)\in K\},\] with canonical variable \(x=(u,z)\). A canonical primal witness maps to its original component by \(R(u,z)=u\). A canonical dual certificate maps to original expression nodes by applying the adjoints of the affine maps introduced during canonicalization and summing contributions at shared subexpressions. The mapping is certificate-preserving only when the resulting multipliers satisfy the original sign, domain, and stationarity conditions and the canonical objective equals the original objective at \(u\). Auxiliary-variable feasibility alone is not an original certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Project canonical primal variables and pull dual multipliers backward through adjoint affine maps, then verify the reconstructed certificate at the original expression nodes.
assumptions_latex: The extended representation is exact rather than a relaxation.
Every introduced affine map and auxiliary constraint is retained in the transformation record.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recovered objects certify the original model only after satisfying its native certificate conditions.

children.title: Presolve Certificate Mapping

knowledge_statements.title: Presolve Certificate Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compositional recovery of certificates through reversible presolve transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent a presolve sequence by maps \(S_1,\ldots,S_k\), with each step carrying a certificate pullback \(Q_i\). If \(w_k\) is a certificate for the final reduced model, its recovered certificate is \[w_0=(Q_1\circ Q_2\circ\cdots\circ Q_k)(w_k).\] The recovery is valid only when every \(Q_i\) is defined for the certificate class returned, restores eliminated primal or dual components, and preserves the relevant feasibility and objective identities. Verification applies each map in reverse presolve order and finally evaluates the recovered certificate against the unpresolved model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recover a reduced-model certificate by applying every recorded presolve pullback in reverse order, then verify it against the unpresolved problem.
assumptions_latex: The presolve log records every transformation and its pullback.
\(w_k\) belongs to the domain of every required pullback.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The composite pullback produces a valid original certificate precisely when all stepwise identities and final predicates hold.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: recovery through transformations is composition of reverse certificate maps

children.title: Variable-Elimination Mapping
children.top_down_role: Recovery of evidence associated with variables removed from the solver representation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit recovery of the eliminated-equality multiplier from reduced stationarity data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the eliminated equality be \(v-Pu-q=0\), and let \((g_u,g_v)\) collect all other Lagrangian stationarity contributions. If \(g_u+P^{\mathsf T}g_v=0\), then choosing the equality multiplier \(\lambda=-g_v\) gives \[g_u-P^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0,\qquad g_v+\lambda=0.\] Thus reduced stationarity lifts to original stationarity whenever \(g_v\) is recoverable and the remaining primal, dual-feasibility, and complementarity predicates are preserved by substitution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the convention v-Pu-q=0, the eliminated equality multiplier is minus the eliminated-coordinate stationarity contribution.
assumptions_latex: The equality uses the Lagrangian term \(\langle\lambda,v-Pu-q\rangle\).
The separate contribution \(g_v\) is available after witness reconstruction.
The reduced stationarity equation is \(g_u+P^{\mathsf T}g_v=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda=-g_v\) lifts reduced stationarity to the original coordinatewise stationarity equations.

notation.meaning: Multiplier of the eliminated affine equality.
Stationarity contributions excluding the eliminated equality.

knowledge_statements.title: KKT Lifting Through Affine Elimination
Variable-Elimination Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal and stationarity recovery after affine variable elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose presolve eliminates \(v\) using the exact affine identity \(v=Pu+q\), producing reduced objective \(\widehat f(u)=f(u,Pu+q)\). A reduced primal witness \(u\) recovers as \(R(u)=(u,Pu+q)\). If \((g_u,g_v)\) is a subgradient or Lagrangian-gradient contribution before elimination, its reduced contribution is \[\widehat g=g_u+P^{\mathsf T}g_v.\] Conversely, recovering separate dual or stationarity components requires the eliminated equality's multiplier or another recorded right inverse; \(\widehat g\) alone generally does not determine \((g_u,g_v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Substitute the eliminated affine variable to recover primal values; gradients pull forward by the transpose, while separate dual components need additional recorded data.
assumptions_latex: The identity \(v=Pu+q\) is exact on the original feasible set.
The reduced model was formed by direct substitution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal recovery is unique, but full dual recovery may be underdetermined without elimination metadata.

children.title: Constraint-Aggregation Mapping
children.top_down_role: Recovery of certificate contributions after constraint combination or redundancy removal.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Aggregation Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-certificate pullback through linear aggregation of constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an original residual vector be \(r(x)\in\mathbb R^m\), and let presolve replace it by the aggregated residual \(\widehat r(x)=Mr(x)\). For a reduced multiplier \(\widehat y\), the corresponding original multiplier is \[y=M^{\mathsf T}\widehat y,\qquad \langle\widehat y,\widehat r(x)\rangle=\langle y,r(x)\rangle.\] This pullback preserves the Lagrangian contribution exactly. It is a valid dual-certificate mapping only if \(M^{\mathsf T}\widehat y\) lies in the original multiplier cone. Aggregation that discards constraint directions can prevent recovery of certificates not contained in \(\operatorname{range}(M^{\mathsf T})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pull an aggregate multiplier back with the transpose of the aggregation matrix; validity additionally requires membership in the original multiplier cone.
assumptions_latex: Constraint aggregation is linear and represented by \(M\).
The original and reduced dual pairings are Euclidean.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transpose mapping preserves the Lagrangian pairing but may not recover every original multiplier.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: adjoint identity for linear constraint aggregation
